rule_name: High Humidity Fungal Disease Risk During Vegetative Stage
reason: In Dharwad's Kharif season (June–October), prolonged relative humidity above 85% combined with temperatures of 22–30°C creates optimal micro-climatic conditions for germination of fungal spores, particularly Exserohilum turcicum (Northern Leaf Blight) and Cercospora zeae-maydis (Gray Leaf Spot). The moist canopy promotes spore dispersal and infection cycle completion within 48–72 hours, causing rapid spread across maize fields common in Dharwad taluk.
actions: Apply Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/litre as a preventive foliar spray to all maize leaves from bottom to top canopy
Ensure inter-row spacing allows air circulation; remove lower senescent leaves manually to reduce humidity within the canopy
Avoid evening or night irrigation which prolongs leaf wetness period; shift irrigation to early morning hours

rule_name: Heat Stress During Silking Stage
reason: Dharwad Rabi maize (November–March) is vulnerable to heat stress when day temperatures exceed 38°C. During silking, pollen viability drops sharply above 35°C and silk desiccation occurs within 2–4 hours of exposure. Poor pollen-silk synchrony leads to tip barrenness and direct yield loss of 25–40%. Low humidity below 40% accelerates silk wilting, making this a compounding stress event critical in Dharwad's dry post-monsoon months.
actions: Provide immediate light irrigation of 25–30 mm to cool the root zone and raise local field humidity around the tassels and silks
Apply 1% potassium chloride foliar spray in the early morning (before 8 AM) to enhance heat tolerance and maintain cell turgor in silks
Mark affected plots for potential pollination supplements; hand-pollinate if natural pollen drop appears inadequate after visual check of pollen shed

rule_name: Cold Night Temperature Risk During Germination
reason: In Dharwad's Rabi season (November–February), night temperatures frequently drop below 12°C, especially in December–January. Maize seed germination requires a minimum soil temperature of 10–12°C; below this threshold, germination is uneven, takes 12–18 days instead of the optimal 5–7 days, and seedling emergence is patchy. Chilling injury at this stage reduces shoot and root meristem viability, leading to poor stand establishment and erratic crop populations in Dharwad's loamy soils.
actions: Delay sowing by 5–7 days if forecast predicts minimum temperatures below 12°C for more than 3 consecutive nights to allow soil warming
Treat seeds with Thiram 75 WS @ 3 g/kg seed as a fungicide seed treatment to protect against damping-off fungi that proliferate in cold, wet soils
Use light irrigation (15–20 mm) the day before sowing to warm the seed zone slightly and create uniform moisture for germination initiation

rule_name: Excess Rainfall Waterlogging Risk in Heavy Soils
reason: Dharwad district has significant areas of deep black cotton (Vertisol) soils with slow drainage. When rainfall exceeds 60 mm/day for 3 or more consecutive days, these soils saturate and waterlogging occurs within 24–48 hours. Maize is highly sensitive to waterlogging at seedling and early vegetative stages — root oxygen deprivation for more than 48 hours causes complete root death, nitrogen leaching, and anaerobic fermentation in the rhizosphere. Crop survival rates fall below 40% if waterlogging continues beyond 5 days at this stage.
actions: Open field drainage channels immediately along field borders and mid-field furrows at 3–4 m intervals to facilitate excess water drainage within 24 hours
Spray 1% urea solution as foliar application once waterlogging recedes to compensate for nitrogen loss due to leaching and denitrification
Monitor for yellowing from the lower leaves which indicates nitrogen deficiency post-waterlogging; apply 20 kg/acre urea top-dress once soil drains and supports field entry

rule_name: Dry Spell Stress During Grain Filling
reason: During grain filling (approximately 60–90 days after sowing in Kharif), maize requires 5–8 mm of water daily for optimal starch synthesis and kernel weight development. A dry spell of 10 or more days with zero effective rainfall combined with temperatures above 33°C accelerates evapotranspiration to 8–12 mm/day in Dharwad conditions. This results in premature husk drying, kernel abortion in the tip rows, and reduction in 100-grain weight by 15–30%. This is the most yield-critical stress period for Dharwad maize.
actions: Apply life-saving irrigation of 40–50 mm immediately using flood or drip irrigation to replenish soil moisture deficit and prevent kernel abortion
Apply 2% potassium sulfate foliar spray to improve drought tolerance mechanisms and support assimilate transport from leaves to developing kernels
Avoid any tillage or inter-cultivation operations during dry spell to prevent further soil moisture loss through surface disruption

rule_name: Strong Wind Lodging Risk at Tasseling
reason: In Dharwad, pre-monsoon and early Kharif season (May–July) experiences sudden squall events with wind speeds exceeding 40 km/h. During tasseling and silking, maize plants are at their maximum height (180–240 cm for most Dharwad varieties), making them biomechanically vulnerable. High soil moisture above 75% reduces root anchorage strength in Dharwad's medium-deep soils. Wind-induced lodging at this stage breaks stalks, disrupts pollen shed, and prevents proper silking, causing 30–50% yield loss on lodged plants.
actions: Hill up soil around the base of plants to a height of 15–20 cm using inter-row soil to provide mechanical support and improve root anchorage before forecast wind events
Avoid applying heavy irrigation within 48 hours before a forecast wind event to reduce soil saturation and improve root-soil mechanical resistance
After lodging, carefully upraise fallen plants within 24 hours and provide temporary staking for plants at 45° or less to vertical; plants beyond 60° tilt rarely recover economic yield

rule_name: Humid Night Conditions Promoting Downy Mildew Sporulation
reason: Peronosclerospora sorghi, the causal agent of Sorghum Downy Mildew, is endemic in the Dharwad region and causes 20–60% yield losses in susceptible maize varieties. Sporangiophore emergence and sporangiospore liberation are maximised when night relative humidity exceeds 90% and temperatures are between 18–24°C for 4 or more consecutive nights. These conditions are characteristic of Dharwad's early Kharif (June–July) and late Rabi (February) periods, making this a seasonally predictable, high-priority risk window.
actions: Apply Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP (Ridomil Gold) @ 2 g/litre as a foliar spray covering both leaf surfaces thoroughly, focusing on the youngest whorl leaves
Drench the base of symptomatic plants with Metalaxyl 25 WP @ 1 g/litre at 250 ml per plant to suppress systemic mycelium spread
Remove and destroy severely infected plants (those showing complete leaf chlorosis or white downy growth) by burying at 30 cm depth or burning outside the field to reduce inoculum load

rule_name: Low Minimum Temperature Pollen Viability Reduction in Rabi
reason: Dharwad Rabi maize tasseling typically occurs in January–February when minimum temperatures can drop to 10–15°C during cold wave events. Pollen germination requires a minimum temperature of 15°C; below this threshold, pollen tube elongation is inhibited and fertilisation does not occur, leading to silk-pollen asynchrony. Even 2–3 days of cold nights during anthesis can cause 15–25% kernel set failure, manifesting as unfilled cob tips and patchy kernel rows in Dharwad Rabi maize.
actions: Schedule protective light irrigation of 20–25 mm to maintain soil warmth around the root zone and raise micro-climate temperature within the crop canopy by 1–2°C
Spray 0.5% boron solution (Borax) at tasseling initiation to enhance pollen viability and pollen tube germination under sub-optimal temperature conditions
Document the number of cold nights during tasseling for yield forecasting; if minimum temperature drops below 10°C for more than 3 nights, notify extension officer for crop loss assessment

rule_name: Intense Rainfall Causing Soil Erosion and Nutrient Runoff
reason: Dharwad district's laterite and sandy-loam soils in the eastern taluks (Navalgund, Kundgol) have low structural stability and high erosion potential. Rainfall intensities above 80 mm/day cause significant surface runoff, carrying away the top 2–5 cm of nutrient-rich topsoil and recently applied fertilizers, particularly urea and di-ammonium phosphate (DAP). This results in nutrient deficiency appearing 10–15 days post-event and can reduce fertilizer use efficiency by 30–50%, directly impacting maize yields.
actions: Create contour bunds or mini-bunds across slopes at every 20–25 m interval before heavy rainfall season to intercept runoff and retain topsoil and nutrients
Apply a split dose of 15 kg/acre urea 5–7 days after heavy rainfall event to compensate for leached nitrogen, placing it 5 cm deep in inter-rows to reduce further runoff loss
Sow green manure or cowpea between rows during establishment period to provide ground cover and reduce erosion kinetic energy of raindrops on bare soil

rule_name: Post-Harvest Rain Risk During Maturity Stage
reason: Late Kharif or early Rabi rainfall during the maturity and harvest stage (100+ days after sowing) when grain moisture is 25–35% creates serious post-harvest quality risks. In Dharwad, October–November can bring unseasonal rainfall. High humidity and wet cobs promote rapid colonisation by Aspergillus flavus (aflatoxin producer) and Fusarium verticillioides (fumonisin producer), particularly in dehusked or partially dried cobs. Grain moisture above 18% at harvest is the primary trigger for mycotoxin accumulation that renders grain unfit for human and animal consumption.
actions: Harvest immediately when grain moisture is between 20–25% without waiting for field drying; use mechanical or manual shelling within 48 hours of harvest to reduce moisture rapidly
Dry harvested cobs and grain on raised platforms or tarpaulins, not on bare soil, targeting grain moisture below 12% before storage using sun drying for 5–7 sunny days
Treat dried grain with 5 ml of phosphine tablets (Celphos 3 g tablet per 100 kg grain) before storage in sealed bags to prevent aflatoxin-producing insect and fungal activity during storage

rule_name: Dry Hot Wind Stress During Vegetative Elongation
reason: Hot dry winds (locally called 'loo' conditions) during April–May in Dharwad's transition period between Rabi harvest and early Kharif preparation create severe vapour pressure deficit stress on maize. When maximum temperature exceeds 36°C with wind speeds above 25 km/h and humidity below 35%, transpiration demand exceeds root water uptake capacity by 3–5 times. This leads to leaf rolling, reduced photosynthetic rate by 40–60%, and if uncorrected, permanent wilting and leaf tip burning, especially on the topmost leaves of elongating plants.
actions: Apply immediate furrow irrigation of 35–40 mm during early morning (5–8 AM) to replenish soil moisture and mitigate the vapour pressure deficit stress before peak afternoon heat
Spray kaolin clay particle film (5% solution) on leaf surfaces to reflect solar radiation and reduce leaf temperature by 2–4°C, reducing transpiration rate
Apply 2% potassium nitrate foliar spray to improve stomatal regulation and reduce water loss under high vapour pressure deficit conditions characteristic of Dharwad hot-dry periods

rule_name: Monsoon Break Stress During Tasseling
reason: Dharwad's Kharif season occasionally experiences monsoon breaks of 7–14 days (August–September) coinciding with the tasseling-silking window (50–70 days after sowing). This is agronomically the most sensitive period. A 7-day monsoon break with temperatures above 32°C causes soil moisture depletion to below critical threshold in Dharwad's red laterite soils, which have low water-holding capacity. Pollen shed and silk reception occur simultaneously, so even 3–5 days of moisture stress reduces kernel set by 30–50%. This is the number one Kharif yield loss cause in Dharwad.
actions: Trigger life-saving protective irrigation of 40–50 mm within the first 2 days of identifying the dry spell; repeat every 7–8 days as long as dry spell continues during this critical window
Spray 100 ppm salicylic acid solution (dissolve 1 g salicylic acid in 10 litres water) to activate plant stress response pathways and maintain silk receptivity under moisture deficit

Notify nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) Dharwad for drought advisory and check eligibility for Karnataka Raitha Suraksha Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) crop insurance claim if more than 30% damage is visible

rule_name: Excessive Humidity at Maturity Causing Ear Rot
reason: At physiological maturity (black layer formation, approximately 100–110 days after sowing in Dharwad Kharif), if the cob moisture combined with high ambient humidity (>85%) and temperatures of 20–28°C persists for 5+ days, Gibberella ear rot (Fusarium graminearum) and Diplodia ear rot (Stenocarpella maydis) proliferate. These pathogens are present in Dharwad's maize-growing soils and infect through the silk channel. The resulting mycotoxin contamination and grain quality degradation cause significant income loss when grain is marketed.
actions: Harvest at first opportunity when black layer forms on kernels, even if grain moisture is 25–28%; do not wait for field drying under humid conditions
Remove husk from cobs immediately after harvest to expose grain to air and facilitate faster drying, reducing fungal colonisation time
Apply 0.1% sodium hypochlorite solution (2 ml bleach in 1 litre water) wash to harvested cobs before drying to reduce external fungal spore load on the cob surface

rule_name: Thermal Inversion Cold Night After Warm Day Stress at Emergence
reason: In Dharwad's Rabi season (November–February), clear-sky winter nights create large diurnal temperature ranges of 15–20°C, with warm days (28°C+) and cold nights (10–15°C). Emerging seedlings are particularly vulnerable to this thermal cycling. Rapid temperature fluctuations disrupt chloroplast development in the first true leaves, causing chlorotic striping, reduced photosynthetic rate, and purple coloration due to anthocyanin accumulation associated with phosphorus uptake inhibition at cold temperatures. Seedling establishment takes 3–5 days longer in these conditions.
actions: Apply 19:19:19 NPK water-soluble fertilizer @ 5 g/litre as a foliar spray once seedlings have 2 true leaves to overcome phosphorus immobility under cold soil conditions and restore green colour
Delay inter-cultivation and weeding operations until minimum temperatures consistently stay above 14°C to avoid additional stress on already thermally stressed seedlings
Increase seed rate by 10% (from standard 8 kg/acre to 8.8 kg/acre) when Rabi sowing is planned under forecast cold conditions to compensate for expected uneven germination and seedling mortality

rule_name: Pre-Sowing Heavy Rainfall Delaying Optimal Sowing Window
reason: The optimal Kharif maize sowing window in Dharwad is June 10–July 10. Prolonged pre-sowing rains above 40 mm/day for 5 consecutive days saturate the soil beyond 85% field capacity, making field entry impossible and delaying sowing. Every week of delay beyond July 10 reduces yield potential by 5–8% because late-sown Kharif maize faces monsoon recession before completing the grain-filling stage. Additionally, excessive moisture before sowing promotes soil-borne damping-off pathogen build-up (Pythium spp., Fusarium spp.).
actions: Open surface drainage channels in fields to hasten soil drainage; plan to sow within 24–48 hours of soil reaching trafficable moisture (soil sticks but does not smear when squeezed)
Use ridge-and-furrow planting method on a 60 cm ridge spacing to ensure seeds are placed on raised ridges above waterlogged furrow level, preventing direct seed contact with saturated soil
Treat seeds with Metalaxyl 35 SD @ 6 g/kg + Thiram 75 WS @ 3 g/kg seed combination before sowing in wet soil conditions to protect against both Oomycete (Pythium) and fungal damping-off pathogens

rule_name: Optimal Rainfall for Kharif Vegetative Growth
reason: The optimal conditions for maize vegetative growth in Dharwad Kharif are well-distributed rainfall of 8–25 mm/day providing 5–7 mm of effective soil recharge, with temperatures in the 24–30°C range. These conditions maximize leaf area development, stalk elongation, and nitrogen uptake. In Dharwad's typical Kharif (July–August), such conditions produce the fastest biomass accumulation rates and set the foundation for high yield potential. Farmer advisory should reinforce beneficial agronomic practices during this window.
actions: Apply the second top-dress nitrogen dose of 30 kg urea per acre at knee-high stage (30–35 days after sowing) to capitalise on optimal growth conditions and maximise leaf area
Complete inter-row cultivation and earthing-up during this window while soil is moist but trafficable to control weeds and improve soil aeration around roots
Record crop growth stage and plant height for crop performance benchmarking; optimal knee-high target is 60–75 cm by 35 days after sowing in Dharwad conditions

rule_name: Fog and Low Visibility Disease Spread Risk in Winter
reason: Dharwad experiences dense fog events in December–January, particularly in the morning hours, when relative humidity reaches 92–100% and temperatures are 12–16°C. These fog episodes last 2–6 hours and deposit substantial free water on leaf surfaces, equivalent to light drizzle. This leaf wetness at cool temperatures is ideal for Cercospora zeae-maydis (Gray Leaf Spot) and Bipolaris maydis (Southern Corn Leaf Blight) spore germination and infection. Successive foggy mornings for a week can initiate disease epidemics that reach economic threshold within 2–3 weeks.
actions: Apply protectant fungicide Chlorothalonil 75 WP @ 2 g/litre before the forecast fog period to establish a protective chemical barrier on leaf surfaces
Increase row spacing by 15–20% in fog-prone areas of the field (low-lying spots) to improve canopy ventilation and reduce duration of leaf wetness following fog events

Scout for initial lesions (grey to tan spots with yellow halos) every 3–4 days during fog period; if more than 5 lesions per leaf are found on lower 3 leaves, upgrade to curative fungicide (Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/litre)

rule_name: High Wind Speed Causing Pollen Dispersal Disruption
reason: Maize pollination in Dharwad's Kharif season (July–September) depends on wind-mediated pollen dispersal from the tassel to the silk. When wind speeds exceed 30 km/h with low humidity below 45%, pollen grains desiccate within 30–60 minutes of release (normal viability window is 2–4 hours at 60–70% humidity). Additionally, high winds disperse pollen outside the crop canopy, reducing effective pollen density within the field by 40–60%. This results in poorly filled cobs with missing kernel rows, particularly in small plots common in Dharwad smallholder farms.
actions: Plant wind-break strips of sorghum or napier grass on the windward boundary of the maize field before tasseling to reduce in-field wind speed by 30–50%
If possible, delay or bring forward irrigation to increase ambient humidity within the crop canopy during peak pollen shed hours (8–11 AM)
Consider supplementary hand-pollination on border rows by collecting fresh pollen from central rows and applying it to exposed silks in the early morning when wind is calmer

rule_name: Moderate Humidity and Temperature Optimal for Leaf Blight Spread
reason: Exserohilum turcicum, causal agent of Turcicum Leaf Blight (TLB), is the most economically important foliar disease of maize in Dharwad and North Karnataka. The pathogen's sporulation and infection cycle is optimised at 75–85% RH and 25–32°C, conditions that are common for 6–8 weeks during Dharwad's Kharif season (July–August). When these conditions persist for 6 or more consecutive days, secondary infection cycles multiply exponentially, and disease progress can reduce green leaf area by 40–60% within 2–3 weeks, directly reducing photosynthate supply for grain filling.
actions: Apply Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1 ml/litre as a systemic fungicide with curative and preventive action, targeting the upper canopy leaves which are the primary photosynthetic source
Add a sticking agent (0.5 ml/litre Triton or any agricultural surfactant) to the fungicide solution to improve adhesion on the waxy maize leaf surface and extend residual activity
Maintain detailed spray records (date, product, dose, weather) for insurance purposes and to plan spray intervals at 10–14 days if conducive weather persists

rule_name: Flash Flood Risk on Slopes During Kharif
reason: Dharwad district's undulating topography in the eastern ghats transition zone includes many fields with 2–8% slopes. When rainfall exceeds 100 mm/day on already saturated loamy soils (>80% field capacity), surface runoff velocity exceeds the soil infiltration rate by 5–10 times, creating sheet flow that uproots seedlings and young vegetative plants. This is particularly damaging in June–July when crop canopy is minimal and soil is left bare. Post-flood silt deposition over the growing point (2–4 cm) can smother seedlings and cause 60–80% stand loss in affected areas.
actions: Install semi-circular bunds (nallahs) at 15–20 m intervals across slopes before Kharif onset to intercept runoff and prevent downstream flooding of lower fields
Re-gap missing plants within 5 days of flood by transplanting spare seedlings raised in nursery trays (15 days old) to maintain plant population above 85% of target density
Apply 10 kg/acre gypsum to flood-affected soil after water drains to reclaim any structural damage and correct potential secondary sodicity from deposited fine silts

rule_name: Sustained High Humidity Increasing Anthracnose Risk
reason: Colletotrichum graminicola, which causes both Anthracnose leaf blight and Anthracnose stalk rot, thrives in Dharwad under sustained high humidity (>82%) and temperatures of 26–32°C. During grain filling, the pathogen infects stalk nodes, causing pith discolouration and stalk rot that leads to premature plant death before grain physiological maturity. This 'greensnap' or premature dying syndrome is often confused with nutrient deficiency in Dharwad fields, delaying appropriate response. Stalk rot reduces harvestable plant population by 10–25%.
actions: Apply Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/litre as a systemic fungicide with dual action against both stalk and foliar pathogens, ensuring thorough coverage of the lower stalk nodes (first 3 nodes above ground)
Conduct push test on 20 random plants: if more than 10% of plants topple or visibly bend at the nodes, schedule early harvest even if grain moisture is above 25% to salvage yield
Balance potassium nutrition with top-dress muriate of potash (MOP) @ 10 kg/acre to strengthen stalk cell walls and reduce susceptibility to Anthracnose stalk rot infection

rule_name: Cool Wet Conditions Increasing Pythium Root Rot Risk at Sowing
reason: Pythium aphanidermatum and Pythium ultimum are ubiquitous soil-borne Oomycete pathogens in Dharwad's maize-growing soils. They cause damping-off and seed rot under cool (below 18°C), wet (>80% soil moisture) conditions common in early Rabi sowing (November). Seeds germinating slowly in cold soils are exposed to these pathogens for 10–15 days instead of the usual 5–7 days, dramatically increasing infection probability. Pre-emergence damping-off can destroy 30–50% of seeds before any visible plant emerges, appearing as a patchy, uneven field.
actions: Treat all seeds with Metalaxyl 35 SD @ 6 g/kg seed (not granule form) as a film coating before sowing to provide systemic Oomycete protection throughout the germination period
Sow seeds at 4–5 cm depth (not deeper) to minimise the period of seed exposure to cool saturated topsoil layer and facilitate faster shoot emergence

Apply Trichoderma viride bioagent @ 4 kg/acre mixed with 400 kg well-decomposed farmyard manure and incorporate into the seed zone 7–10 days before sowing to establish biological suppression of Pythium

rule_name: Cyclone Depression Wind Damage Risk
reason: Dharwad can be affected by the outer circulation of Bay of Bengal depressions and low-pressure systems that move inland through coastal Karnataka between October–December. Wind speeds exceeding 55 km/h combined with heavy rainfall (>50 mm/day) cause catastrophic lodging, stalk breakage, and root-pull events in maize. The combination of waterlogged soil weakening root anchorage and the wind force creates a compound physical disaster that can destroy 50–90% of crop in a single event, particularly in late Kharif and early Rabi maize.
actions: Activate PMFBY insurance claim process immediately; photograph crop damage from multiple angles with date-stamp for documentation and contact the insurance company within 72 hours of the event
After water drainage, assess percentage lodging: if more than 50% of plants are lodged, apply a nitrogen boost of 25 kg urea per acre to encourage recovery growth on plants that are still upright
Procure crop loss assessment from local agriculture department (Raita Samparka Kendra) within 7 days of the event for eligibility for Karnataka government disaster relief compensation

rule_name: Optimal Temperature Window for Maximum Grain Starch Synthesis
reason: Grain filling in Dharwad maize (75–100 days after sowing in Kharif) achieves maximum starch synthesis rate at temperatures of 22–28°C, humidity of 60–75%, and gentle rainfall of 5–20 mm/day. These conditions maintain active source-sink balance with high photosynthesis rates and efficient phloem transport of sucrose to the developing endosperm. This weather pattern, typical of Dharwad's September conditions in a good monsoon year, can produce 100-grain weights of 30–35 g versus the 22–25 g common under stress conditions.
actions: Ensure no interruption in irrigation schedule during this period; maintain soil moisture at 70–80% field capacity to sustain the high metabolic demand of grain filling
Apply 1% potassium chloride foliar spray once during mid grain filling to enhance sugar translocation from flag leaves to kernels and improve grain density
Protect the crop from any pest or disease outbreak during this window; any defoliation above 15% during grain filling reduces final yield by 12–20% in Dharwad conditions

rule_name: Sudden Temperature Drop Causing Starch Paste Incomplete Filling
reason: Rabi maize grain filling in Dharwad (January–February) can be interrupted by cold spells where average temperatures drop below 20°C and minimum temperatures fall below 16°C. Starch synthase enzyme activity drops sharply below 18°C, reducing starch deposition rate by 50–70%. Kernels that begin filling but encounter sustained cold periods develop chalky, incompletely filled grain with reduced specific weight (test weight falls from 70+ kg/hl to below 60 kg/hl). This reduces market price by 15–25% and affects suitability for poultry and industrial starch uses.
actions: Apply warm (30–35°C) irrigation water if well water is available to maintain root zone temperature above 16°C and sustain enzyme activity during cold spells
Spray 1% potassium nitrate solution during cold spells to activate alternative metabolic pathways and partially compensate for reduced starch synthase activity
Plan harvest at physiological maturity (black layer formation) as soon as temperature recovers above 20°C; cold-stressed grain has reduced standing ability and is prone to ear rot if delayed

rule_name: Continuous Cloud Cover Reducing Photosynthetic Active Radiation
reason: In Dharwad's peak Kharif monsoon (August–September), extended cloudy periods with high humidity reduce photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) by 40–60% below clear-sky values. Maize is a C4 plant with high light saturation requirements (1500–2000 µmol/m²/s PAR at full sun). Under persistent cloud cover for 8+ days during tasseling and grain filling, carbon assimilation drops significantly, reducing the supply of photosynthates to developing kernels. Combined with tasseling, this causes incomplete pollen maturation and reduced pollen count, leading to poor pollination and lower kernel set.
actions: Avoid any additional plant stresses (water deficit, nutrient deficiency) during prolonged cloudy periods as the plant's reduced carbon budget makes it less tolerant to compound stresses
Supplement with micronutrient spray of zinc sulfate 0.5% + boron 0.2% solution during cloudy period to maintain pollen formation efficiency even under reduced light conditions
Record cloud cover days accurately for yield forecasting; every week of <50% sunshine during grain filling reduces expected yield by 8–12% from the season's potential

rule_name: High Night Temperature Reducing Grain Weight During Filling
reason: Maize grain filling requires cool nights for effective respiration-to-photosynthesis balance. When minimum (night) temperature exceeds 27°C for 5 or more consecutive nights (common in late September–October in Dharwad when monsoon withdrawal warming occurs), nighttime respiration consumes 30–45% of the day's photosynthate accumulation. This significantly reduces the net carbon available for grain starch deposition, resulting in reduced final 100-grain weights and lower test weight. Yield reductions of 10–20% have been documented in Dharwad trials under this heat accumulation scenario.
actions: Apply irrigations in late afternoon (4–6 PM) to cool the crop canopy through evaporative cooling and reduce nighttime leaf and canopy temperature by 2–3°C
Apply 2% potassium chloride foliar spray which reduces heat stress-induced respiration losses by strengthening stomatal closure efficiency in maize under high night temperature
Harvest at the earliest physiological maturity (grain moisture 25–28%) in high night temperature years to prevent continued heat-driven respiration losses in standing crop

rule_name: Early Season Drought Stress Delaying Tasseling
reason: Extended drought of 14+ days during vegetative growth (25–50 days after sowing) with soil moisture below 40% field capacity in Dharwad's red laterite soils inhibits floral induction processes in maize. ASI (Anthesis-Silking Interval) normally 1–3 days, increases to 7–14 days under severe early vegetative drought, causing pollen to shed before silks are fully emerged. This temporal mismatch is a primary cause of poor pollination and dramatically reduced kernel set per cob. Dryland Dharwad farms without irrigation access are most vulnerable.
actions: Apply maximum available water (50 mm) as a single life-saving irrigation if even limited water sources are available, prioritising crops in vegetative stage over those at other stages
Apply 100 ppm brassinolide (1 ml 0.1% solution per litre) as foliar spray to modulate floral development timing and partially correct ASI under moisture-stress conditions
Contact Dharwad District Agriculture Department for drought declaration status; if declared drought, PMFBY claims should be initiated and free seed replacement schemes may be available

rule_name: Heavy Dew Formation Increasing Leaf Rust Infection
reason: Puccinia sorghi (Common Rust) and Puccinia polysora (Southern Rust) are foliar rust pathogens commonly found in Dharwad maize crops. Heavy dew formation under high humidity (>88%), cool nights (16–22°C), and warm days (26–30°C) creates conditions ideal for rust uredospore germination. Dew periods of just 6–8 hours are sufficient for infection. Rust pustule development in these conditions can be visible within 7–10 days of infection, and under severe pressure, canopy defoliation of 20–40% can occur before physiological maturity in Dharwad's September–October period.
actions: Apply Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/litre at first sign of rust pustules (small circular orange-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces) to halt further sporulation and prevent secondary spread
Supplement with Zineb 75 WP @ 2 g/litre as a protectant tankmix if rust is spreading rapidly and covering more than 10% of leaf area of upper 3 leaves
Ensure foliar spray coverage reaches both upper and lower leaf surfaces as rust pustules develop on both sides; use a fine nozzle (hollow cone or flat fan) to achieve complete coverage

rule_name: Waterlogged Anaerobic Conditions Causing Nitrogen Loss
reason: In Dharwad's black cotton soil areas (Hubli taluk and adjacent areas), waterlogging of 4+ days under heavy rainfall creates anaerobic soil conditions that trigger denitrification. Nitrate nitrogen (NO3-N) from applied urea and DAP is rapidly converted to nitrogen gas (N2 and N2O) by anaerobic bacteria, causing 40–60% loss of applied nitrogen. The concurrent inhibition of root nitrogen uptake under anaerobic conditions means maize plants show acute nitrogen deficiency (yellowing from lower leaves, reduced growth) within 5–7 days of waterlogging, even if fertilizer was recently applied.
actions: Immediately open field furrows and drainage channels to reduce waterlogging duration; even 1 day of earlier drainage saves 10–15% of the nitrogen that would otherwise be denitrified
Apply foliar urea spray (2% = 20 g per litre) once water drains and field is trafficable, providing emergency nitrogen through leaf absorption to compensate for soil nitrogen loss
After field drainage and soil drying (2–3 days), apply 20–25 kg urea per acre as top-dressing with earthing-up to restore nitrogen supply for recovery growth

rule_name: Temperature Optimum for Maximum Tiller Formation
reason: In Dharwad maize, tillers (suckers) form most actively at 15–30 days after sowing when temperatures are in the 25–30°C range and soil moisture is comfortable at 55–70% field capacity. While tillers are generally not productive in improved hybrid maize, their presence indicates the crop is growing in optimal conditions. The tiller formation period coincides with the critical weed competition window (10–30 days after sowing) and the timing of the first nitrogen top-dress. Advisory actions should capitalise on this vigorous growth period.
actions: Apply 20 kg urea per acre as the first top-dress dose at 20–25 days after sowing (4–5 leaf stage) to leverage optimal plant metabolism and maximise nitrogen use efficiency
Complete inter-row weeding (manual hoeing or tractor cultivation at 20 cm depth) before 30 days after sowing to eliminate weed competition during the most active root and shoot growth period
Remove tillers (suckers) manually if they exceed 3 per plant, as excessive tillers on hybrid maize divert nutrient resources from the main stalk, especially in narrow-spaced plantings

rule_name: Extended Saturation Risk Causing Phosphorus Fixation
reason: Dharwad's black cotton soils (Vertisols) have a high phosphorus fixation capacity that increases dramatically under waterlogged conditions. When soil saturation exceeds 95% for 6+ days, iron and manganese reduction under anaerobic conditions creates a pH shift that promotes the formation of insoluble iron phosphates, effectively locking applied phosphatic fertilizers (DAP, SSP) in unavailable forms. This is particularly critical at sowing and early emergence when phosphorus is essential for root development and energy metabolism (ATP synthesis), and immobility of soil phosphorus cannot be corrected by additional application without drainage.
actions: Drain fields to below 80% soil moisture before applying phosphatic fertilizers; defer any planned DAP application until soil oxygen status recovers

Apply phosphorus fertilizer as a liquid solution (mono-ammonium phosphate 12-61-0 dissolved at 2 g/litre) as foliar spray post-waterlogging to deliver available phosphorus directly to plant tissue bypassing the fixed soil phosphorus
Use mycorrhizal inoculant (Glomus fasciculatum @ 5 kg/acre) as a soil treatment to establish phosphorus-mobilising mycorrhizal networks that can access fixed soil phosphorus pools once soil aerates

rule_name: Onset of Monsoon Optimal Sowing Window Signal
reason: The optimal Kharif maize sowing window in Dharwad opens when the Southwest Monsoon reliably establishes (typically June 5–15). Three consecutive days of 20–50 mm rainfall bringing soil moisture to 60–80% field capacity signals adequate moisture for germination without waterlogging risk. Sowing within this window (targeting June 10–25) allows the crop to complete tasseling and silking (50–70 days after sowing) in late July–August when Dharwad receives peak rainfall, maximising natural water availability during the most critical pollination and grain-filling windows.
actions: Sow immediately within 24–48 hours of the 3rd consecutive adequate rainfall day to capture the optimal sowing window; delay beyond July 10 will reduce yield potential by 5–8% per week
Sow hybrid seeds at 25 cm inter-plant and 60 cm inter-row spacing at 4–5 cm depth using a seed drill to ensure uniform depth and spacing for even emergence
Apply 75 kg DAP per acre as basal fertilizer in the furrow below the seed (5 cm below seed) during sowing to provide phosphorus for early root and shoot development

rule_name: Late Monsoon Withdrawal Heat Spike During Grain Filling
reason: In Dharwad, monsoon withdrawal (normally October) sometimes causes a temporary heat spike where maximum temperatures rise to 35°C+ with rapidly falling humidity (from 80%+ to below 55%). This occurs precisely during Kharif maize grain filling (70–95 days after sowing). The sudden shift to hot-dry conditions dramatically accelerates grain moisture loss from 40% to below 20% in 5–7 days, prematurely terminating kernel filling before maximum starch synthesis is complete. Kernels formed under this stress are lighter (reduced 100-grain weight), wrinkled, and may have chalky endosperm, reducing market quality.
actions: Apply emergency supplementary irrigation of 30–40 mm to buffer soil moisture and slow down grain desiccation, extending the effective grain-filling period by 5–7 days
Apply 1% potassium sulfate foliar spray to improve cell wall integrity in developing kernels and slow premature desiccation of the pericarp
Harvest at 25–28% grain moisture (before natural field drying completes) and dry artificially or under shade to preserve kernel density and prevent harvest quality loss

rule_name: Pre-Monsoon Summer Shower Creating False Sowing Opportunity
reason: In May–June, Dharwad receives isolated pre-monsoon thunderstorm showers (25–50 mm) that temporarily wet the soil but are not followed by reliable monsoon rains. Farmers who sow after these showers risk germination without subsequent reliable moisture supply. Seeds that germinate and reach the 2–3 leaf stage without adequate follow-up rainfall suffer irreversible seedling drought stress (soil moisture crashes rapidly in 3–5 days under high temperatures). Re-sowing at this point costs seed, labour, and time and shifts the sowing date outside the optimal window.
actions: Wait for at least 3–4 consecutive rainy days (25+ mm/day each) before sowing to confirm reliable monsoon onset rather than isolated pre-monsoon shower activity
Check IMD Dharwad weather forecast for the next 10 days; sow only if probability of continued rainfall is above 70% for the following week post-sowing
If sowing must occur during uncertain rainfall (water constraints or field preparation timing), keep 1.5 kg of spare seed per acre for re-gapping or re-sowing if emergence is less than 60% by day 12

rule_name: Temperature and Humidity Synergy for Charcoal Rot Infection
reason: Macrophomina phaseolina, causal agent of Charcoal Rot in maize, is an aggressive soil-borne pathogen in the Dharwad agro-climatic zone. It infects plants under hot (35°C+) and drought-stressed (soil moisture <35%) conditions after 75 days of crop growth. The pathogen colonises the stalk and root system, producing microsclerotia (giving the characteristic charcoal-gray discolouration of pith), leading to premature plant death before grain physiological maturity. In Dharwad's post-monsoon withdrawal period, both temperature elevation and rapid soil drying create ideal Charcoal Rot conditions.
actions: Apply immediate irrigation to bring soil moisture above 50% field capacity; adequate water supply is the single most effective management tool for limiting Charcoal Rot severity

Avoid applying excessive nitrogen fertilizer late in the season (after 60 days after sowing) as lush, nitrogen-driven vegetative growth increases plant water demand and exacerbates drought stress that triggers Charcoal Rot

Harvest any fields with more than 15% visibly lodged or dead-standing plants immediately at whatever moisture level, as Charcoal Rot-affected stalks become brittle and harvest losses increase with every day of delay

rule_name: Ideal Soil Moisture for Maximum Fertilizer Uptake
reason: Maximum nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium uptake by maize roots occurs at soil moisture levels of 55–75% field capacity (field capacity at 100%, permanent wilting point at 0% in this scale). Below 55%, mass flow and diffusion of nutrients to roots are slowed by reduced soil water continuity. Above 75%, anaerobic zones inhibit root aerobic function and nutrient carrier activity. This optimal soil moisture window, combined with 24–30°C for active root enzyme systems, represents the peak fertilizer-use efficiency window in Dharwad's Kharif and Rabi seasons.
actions: Apply second top-dressing of nitrogen (30–35 kg urea per acre) immediately during this optimal window to maximise nitrogen use efficiency and plant uptake
Apply zinc sulfate heptahydrate @ 10 kg/acre in soil or 0.5% as foliar spray if soil is in this optimal moisture range, as zinc mobility and uptake are maximised under these conditions
Document spray and fertilizer application dates and weather conditions on this day for precision agriculture records and to build historical correlation between application timing and yield outcomes

rule_name: Waterlogging Causing Iron Toxicity in Sandy Soils
reason: In Dharwad's sandy and laterite soils found in Kundgol and Navalgund taluks, prolonged waterlogging triggers iron reduction (Fe3+ to Fe2+) under anaerobic conditions. The highly soluble ferrous iron (Fe2+) accumulates to toxic levels in soil solution, being taken up by maize roots and causing bronzing syndrome — characteristic orange-brown discolouration of leaf tips and margins progressing inward. Iron toxicity at this severity reduces photosynthesis by 30–50% and impairs phosphorus metabolism, resulting in stunted plants that never fully recover to their yield potential.
actions: Drain fields to restore aerobic conditions; once oxygen returns to the root zone, iron re-oxidises to Fe3+ and toxicity symptoms stop progressing within 3–5 days

Apply 10 kg lime per acre after waterlogging drains in affected fields to raise pH slightly (from 5.5 to 6.0–6.5 range), which reduces iron solubility and prevents recurrence in subsequent rain events
Spray 1% zinc sulfate + 0.5% lime solution (Bordeaux mixture variant) to counteract iron toxicity symptoms on leaves and restore normal chlorophyll synthesis in affected maize plants

rule_name: Cyclone Season Harvest Timing Risk
reason: October–November in Dharwad can coincide with late Kharif maize maturity and simultaneously with cyclone season from the Bay of Bengal. When maturity-stage maize (100+ days after sowing) faces pre-cyclone conditions of rain, strong winds, and high humidity, there is a critical decision window. Delay in harvesting mature maize under these conditions risks complete crop loss due to stalk lodging from wind, ear rot from humidity, and grain rewetting reducing market quality. The economic cost of early harvest (higher drying cost) is always less than total loss from delayed harvest.
actions: Harvest all fields showing physiological maturity (kernel black layer visible, husk drying, grain moisture between 20–30%) immediately within 24–48 hours of first cyclone warning for the region
Arrange additional labour and mechanical harvesters through local Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) in Dharwad for emergency rapid harvesting before the cyclone event
Inform the Dharwad District Agricultural Office of harvest status and potential crop loss for cyclone event documentation which forms the basis for insurance claims and government relief

rule_name: Excessive Irrigation Leaching Risk on Sandy Soils
reason: Sandy soils in parts of Dharwad's eastern region have high hydraulic conductivity (5–20 cm/hour) and low cation exchange capacity (CEC <5 cmol/kg). When rainfall exceeds 35 mm/day on already moist sandy soils (>80% FC) and is further supplemented by flood irrigation, percolation losses carry away mobile nutrients — especially nitrate-N, sulfur, and boron — below the root zone within 24 hours. Farmers who apply flood irrigation during or after rain on sandy soils effectively waste both water and nutrients, and the crop shows deficiency symptoms within 7–10 days.
actions: Immediately suspend flood irrigation on sandy fields when rainfall exceeds 20 mm/day; irrigate only when soil moisture drops below 50% field capacity to avoid leaching cycles

Switch to split application of nitrogen: instead of 50 kg urea in one dose, apply 3 split doses of 15–17 kg urea at 20, 35, and 50 days after sowing to reduce leaching risk from single large applications
Consider converting to drip irrigation on sandy fields in Dharwad where available, as drip reduces percolation losses by 60–70% and nutrient leaching by 50% compared to flood irrigation

rule_name: Heat Accumulation Accelerating Crop Development Beyond Calendar
reason: Maize development is driven by heat accumulation measured as growing degree days (GDD). When both maximum (>34°C) and minimum (>22°C) temperatures remain elevated for 10+ consecutive days, GDD accumulation in Dharwad can be 30–40% higher than average, causing the crop to reach tasseling and silking 7–14 days earlier than calendar predictions. This early tasseling can shift the critical pollination window to an unplanned period, potentially coinciding with a dry spell, or causing the crop to mature 2–3 weeks before the expected harvest equipment and market availability, disrupting the farming schedule.
actions: Update crop stage estimates: under sustained heat accumulation, advance all stage predictions by 7–10 days and schedule irrigation, fertilization, and harvesting accordingly
Prepare for earlier tasseling by ensuring irrigation is available and scheduled to meet the higher water demand that accompanies accelerated tasseling and silking under heat
Contact grain buyers or commission agents in Dharwad APMC for adjusted market dates to ensure harvest logistics (shelling, drying, transport) are planned 2 weeks earlier than originally scheduled

rule_name: Cool Optimal Temperature for Maximum Seedling Vigour
reason: Maize seedling establishment is most vigorous at 22–28°C average temperature with 60–75% soil moisture field capacity. In Dharwad's early Kharif (June–July), these conditions occur naturally after monsoon establishment, providing ideal seedling growth conditions with high photosynthesis rates from the first true leaves and rapid root architecture development. Stand establishment under these conditions achieves 90–95% of target plant population, and seedling vigour scores are highest, predicting lower disease susceptibility and higher final crop performance.
actions: Ensure gap-filling of any missing plants using seedlings raised in poly bags or nursery trays is completed before 15 days after sowing while optimal temperatures maintain vigorous transplant recovery
Apply first hoeing and inter-cultivation at 10–12 days after sowing to remove early weed competition; this is the critical weed-free window that determines the first 60 days of crop performance
Take a plant count per 10-metre row at this stage to verify target population (> 27,000 plants per acre for 60x25 cm spacing); record for yield prediction baseline

rule_name: Pre-Rain Nitrogen Application Volatilisation Risk
reason: When urea fertilizer (the primary nitrogen source used in Dharwad maize farming) is applied on soil surfaces immediately before heavy rainfall (>30 mm/day), urea hydrolysis is rapid under warm (>28°C), humid (>75%) conditions, producing ammonia (NH3) that volatilises into the atmosphere before soil incorporation. Heavy rain then washes away any remaining surface urea before leaching can bring it into the root zone. This combination can cause 30–50% loss of surface-applied urea, meaning the intended nutrient dose is not delivered to the crop.
actions: Delay nitrogen top-dressing by 24–48 hours if rain forecast exceeds 30 mm/day; apply only when weather is dry with no rain expected for 6–8 hours post-application
Incorporate surface-applied urea immediately with a light soil disturbance (hoe or cultivator pass at 5 cm depth) to place urea below the soil surface and reduce volatilisation by 60–70%

Use ammonium sulfate (21% N) instead of urea during periods of heavy rainfall risk, as sulfate ion adsorption to soil reduces leaching and ammonium form is less volatile than urea under wet conditions

rule_name: Wind-Assisted Fungal Spore Transport Between Fields
reason: Moderate winds (15–35 km/h) combined with high humidity (>80%) and favourable temperatures (22–30°C) create optimal conditions for long-distance transport of maize foliar pathogen spores — particularly Exserohilum turcicum (Turcicum Blight), Puccinia sorghi (Common Rust), and Bipolaris zeicola (Eye Spot). Spores can travel 2–10 km on these wind currents between fields, initiating new infection foci in previously disease-free plots. This airborne inoculum transport is the primary mechanism for disease epidemic development across Dharwad's maize-growing landscape.
actions: Coordinate preventive fungicide spraying at the village or watershed level where multiple farmers grow adjacent maize fields, to prevent re-inoculation from neighbouring untreated fields
Apply protectant fungicide (Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/litre) before the forecast wind event to establish protective residue on leaf surfaces before spores arrive from neighbour fields
Report visible disease outbreaks to the local Raita Samparka Kendra to trigger a collective spray advisory for the cluster of maize farmers in the affected hobli of Dharwad taluk

rule_name: Saturated Soil Impeding Harvesting Operations
reason: Black cotton soils in Dharwad become extremely plastic and sticky when saturated above 85% field capacity. Tractor-mounted harvesters and threshers sink into saturated soil, causing wheel compaction to 30–40 cm depth, creating hardpans that damage soil structure for subsequent cropping seasons. Manual harvesting also becomes extremely difficult and slow on waterlogged black soils. Furthermore, harvested cobs placed directly on wet soil rapidly absorb moisture, compromising drying efficiency and increasing post-harvest disease risk.
actions: Wait for 3–4 dry days after cessation of rains before entering the field with mechanical harvesting equipment; test field trafficability by walking without sinking more than 5 cm
If forced to harvest in wet conditions, use narrow-track mechanisation or bullock-drawn harvesting equipment which exerts lower ground pressure than tractor systems
Harvest in morning hours when temperature is lower and surface soil is slightly firmer from overnight cooling; avoid harvesting in the heat of the day when wet black soil is at maximum plasticity

rule_name: Humidity Spike After Dry Period Creating Disease Reactivation
reason: Maize fields that appear to have low disease pressure during a dry phase often carry dormant pathogen populations (latent infections, dormant conidia in residue). When humidity spikes suddenly above 82% with temperatures of 24–30°C during the later crop stages (grain filling and maturity), these dormant pathogens rapidly reactivate and generate high sporulation, causing disease outbreaks that can damage the uppermost leaves (ear leaf and above) that are critical for grain filling. This late-season disease resurgence is underestimated in Dharwad but accounts for 8–15% yield losses in some years.
actions: Apply broad-spectrum strobilurin fungicide Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/litre mixed with Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 0.5 ml/litre as a combination spray to arrest rapid disease reactivation across multiple pathogen species
Ensure the ear leaf (leaf adjacent to the uppermost ear) is specifically targeted in fungicide application, as its green area duration directly correlates with final grain weight
If the crop is within 14 days of planned harvest, skip fungicide application and plan for immediate harvest to reduce crop residue in the field that serves as inoculum for the next crop

rule_name: Optimal Rabi Sowing Temperature Window
reason: The optimal Rabi maize sowing window in Dharwad is October 15–November 10, when average temperatures are 20–26°C and minimum temperatures are above 15°C. These conditions allow rapid germination (5–7 days) and establishment before the onset of cooler December–January temperatures that slow early growth. Post-sowing temperature trajectory is critical: crops sown in October complete their germination and early vegetative stages in warm conditions, reach tasseling in January at 12–16°C (manageable), and grain filling in February–March at gradually warming temperatures, producing the highest Rabi yields in Dharwad.
actions: Sow Rabi maize between October 15–31 targeting this optimal temperature window; maintain 60 x 20 cm spacing (tighter than Kharif) to compensate for lower Rabi plant vigour
Apply 70 kg DAP per acre as basal fertilizer during Rabi sowing as phosphorus availability is lower in cooler soils and higher basal application is needed to sustain early root development

Choose hybrid varieties recommended by UAS Dharwad for Rabi season (e.g. GANGA-5, DKC varieties recommended for Dharwad conditions) that are adapted to the day-length and temperature regime of the Rabi season

rule_name: Sustained High Soil Moisture and Humidity Promoting Banded Leaf Blight
reason: Rhizoctonia solani AG-1 causes Banded Leaf and Sheath Blight (BLSB) in maize, a disease of increasing significance in Dharwad's irrigated and high-rainfall Kharif maize areas. BLSB development is strongly associated with high soil moisture (>80% FC), humid conditions (>85% RH), and temperatures of 26–32°C — all conditions common in Dharwad's August–September monsoon period. The pathogen spreads as sclerotia in soil and surface residue, climbing the plant via the sheath and causing characteristic banded lesions that can envelope the ear, significantly reducing cob quality and kernel filling.
actions: Apply Validamycin 3 L (Kitazin) @ 2 ml/litre as a soil drench at the base of plants for direct contact with sclerotia and ascending mycelium; repeat at 10-day intervals if conditions persist
Reduce canopy density in severely affected areas by removing the bottom 2–3 leaves (which are non-photosynthetically active) to improve air circulation and reduce sheath-level humidity
Avoid excessive nitrogen application in the late vegetative and silking stages in wet years as lush, dense canopies with high humidity support BLSB epidemic development

rule_name: Diurnal Temperature Range Stress on Newly Sown Seeds
reason: A diurnal temperature range exceeding 16°C (e.g. 30°C day, 14°C night) during Rabi sowing and emergence (October–November) creates significant seed and seedling stress in Dharwad. While daytime temperatures favour germination trigger, cool nights extend the germination period and subject partially germinated seeds to thermal shock at the most vulnerable radicle-emergence stage. This results in uneven, staggered germination spread over 10–15 days, creating non-uniform crop stands with multiple physiological age classes, making uniform crop management (irrigation, fertilizer timing, spray) difficult throughout the growing season.
actions: Increase seed rate by 8–10% (from 8 kg to 8.7 kg per acre) to compensate for expected uneven germination and achieve target plant population despite patchy establishment
Apply 5 g/litre humic acid solution as a soil drench over the seed zone after sowing to buffer soil temperature fluctuations and improve seed-to-soil contact for even germination

Conduct plant count at 15 days after sowing; if population is below 85% of target, gap-fill using seedlings from nursery poly bags sown 10 days after main field to ensure uniform plant age across the field

rule_name: Monsoon Onset Delay Reducing Kharif Yield Potential
reason: Dharwad's normal monsoon onset is June 5–10; if the Southwest Monsoon is delayed beyond June 20–25 (indicated by 20+ days of negligible rainfall below 5 mm/day in June), farmers face a critical sowing dilemma. Delayed sowing beyond June 25 shifts tasseling and silking to September–October when monsoon is typically receding, subjecting the most critical yield-determining stage to moisture stress during monsoon withdrawal. Each week of sowing delay after June 15 reduces expected yield by 5–8% due to reduced growing season thermal time and suboptimal water availability at flowering.
actions: Do NOT sow with pre-monsoon soil moisture alone; use IMD and private weather service 15-day rainfall forecast to confirm reliable monsoon onset before committing seed to the soil
If monsoon is delayed beyond July 1, switch from a full 115-day hybrid maize variety to a shorter-duration hybrid (85–90 days) to complete grain filling before the monsoon fully withdraws in October

Plan contingency: if monsoon delayed beyond July 10, consider switching the field to short-duration sorghum or tur (pigeon pea) which are better adapted to late and unreliable Kharif rainfall in Dharwad conditions

rule_name: Turcicum Leaf Blight High Risk Window
reason: Exserohilum turcicum, causal agent of Turcicum Leaf Blight (TLB), is the single most economically damaging foliar disease of maize in Dharwad and North Karnataka. Conidia of E. turcicum germinate and penetrate maize leaves optimally at 80%+ relative humidity and temperatures of 20–28°C. Infection cycles complete in 4–5 days under these conditions, and secondary sporulation builds epidemic pressure exponentially when this weather persists for 5+ consecutive days. UAS Dharwad trials consistently identify TLB as responsible for 20–45% yield loss in susceptible hybrids in high-risk years. Long cigar-shaped grey-green lesions (5–15 cm) that run parallel to leaf veins on mid-canopy leaves are the diagnostic signature.
actions: Apply Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1 ml/litre as a systemic curative fungicide targeting mid and upper canopy; ensure spray reaches both leaf surfaces using a high-volume knapsack sprayer at 200 litres per acre
Follow up with a second spray of Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/litre at 10–12 days interval if conducive weather persists, rotating mode of action to prevent fungicide resistance
Remove and bury severely infected lower leaves (showing >50% lesion area) to reduce the in-field sporulation load and slow the upward progression of infection toward the ear leaf

rule_name: Downy Mildew Critical Infection Period
reason: Peronosclerospora sorghi causes Sorghum Downy Mildew (SDM), an obligate systemic pathogen that can destroy 30–70% of susceptible maize crops in Dharwad. The critical infection window is 7–30 days after sowing when oospores in the soil germinate and systemically colonise young seedlings. Infection success rate is maximised at RH above 90% and temperatures of 20–30°C. Once systemic infection establishes, no fungicide can cure the plant; prevention at the seedling window is the only viable management strategy. Dharwad's Kharif conditions of June–July create this high-risk period annually, and SDM is endemic in many Dharwad taluk fields due to oospore build-up from previous crops.
actions: Apply Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP (Ridomil Gold MZ) @ 2.5 g/litre as a soil drench at 250 ml per plant base at 10 and 20 days after sowing to suppress oospore germination and early systemic infection

Treat seeds mandatorily with Metalaxyl 35 SD @ 6 g/kg seed before sowing in fields with known SDM history; seed treatment is the most cost-effective single intervention in Dharwad's high-risk SDM zones
Uproot and destroy (bury or burn) all 'crazy top' symptom plants (excessive tillering, leaf strapping, white downy growth on underside) immediately on identification to prevent oospore return to soil

rule_name: Gray Leaf Spot Epidemic Development Conditions
reason: Cercospora zeae-maydis, causal agent of Gray Leaf Spot (GLS), has become a significant yield-reducing pathogen in Dharwad maize over the past decade, associated with increased adoption of maize monoculture and minimum tillage practices that increase crop debris. Sporulation and infection are optimised at 85%+ RH and 25–30°C. A 7-day window of these conditions is sufficient to establish visible disease and begin the secondary epidemic cycle. GLS lesions (narrow, rectangular, grey-tan bounded by leaf veins) first appear on lower leaves, progressing upward, causing premature senescence of leaves critical for grain filling. In severe years, GLS can cause 20–35% yield loss in Dharwad.
actions: Apply Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1 ml/litre or Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1 ml/litre at first appearance of lesions on lower leaves, as early intervention prevents upward spread to economically important upper leaves

Incorporate previous crop maize residue thoroughly (minimum 15 cm deep) in fields with GLS history as surface residue is the primary overwintering inoculum source for Cercospora zeae-maydis in Dharwad
Avoid dense planting (below 50 cm row spacing) in known GLS-prone fields during Kharif; wider rows of 65–70 cm improve air circulation, reduce humidity within canopy, and reduce GLS progression rate

rule_name: Common Rust Rapid Spread Under Moderate Temperature
reason: Puccinia sorghi (Common Rust) is a cool-temperature pathogen with uredospore germination and infection optimised at 16–23°C and RH above 85%. In Dharwad, these conditions are common during September–October (Kharif) and January–February (Rabi). Unlike Turcicum Blight, Common Rust is a polycyclic disease with a very short latent period of 5–7 days at optimal temperatures, allowing 5–6 infection cycles within a season. Round to oval, brick-red or brown powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces are diagnostic. Heavy rust infection during grain filling reduces 100-grain weight by 10–20% in Dharwad susceptible hybrids.
actions: Apply Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/litre at first pustule appearance; rust responds rapidly to DMI fungicides and early treatment prevents the exponential secondary infection cycle

Check the registered variety's rust resistance rating from UAS Dharwad seed catalogue; if the variety is rated as susceptible, lower the threshold for fungicide application and spray preventively once environmental conditions meet the criteria
Ensure all foliar spray applications for rust cover the undersides of leaves where uredospores are released, as standard topside-only coverage misses 40–50% of pustule-producing leaf surface area

rule_name: Southern Corn Leaf Blight Warm Humid Risk
reason: Bipolaris maydis (Helminthosporium maydis), causal agent of Southern Corn Leaf Blight (SCLB), thrives in Dharwad's warm-humid Kharif conditions. SCLB development is maximised at 25–35°C with humidity above 82%, conditions that coincide with Dharwad's July–September peak monsoon. Diagnostic symptoms are tan-coloured, elongated lesions (2–3 cm) parallel to leaf veins with distinct yellow halos on younger leaves and tan borders on older leaves. In SCLB-susceptible hybrids grown at high density in Dharwad's irrigated tracts, disease can cause 15–30% yield loss, particularly by destroying the ear leaf which contributes 30–35% of photosynthate to grain filling.
actions: Apply Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/litre + Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/litre as a combination spray covering both curative and protectant activity against Bipolaris, especially targeting the upper two-thirds of the plant canopy

Ensure basal dose of potassium (30 kg MOP per acre) was applied at sowing; potassium-deficient plants show significantly higher SCLB severity as cell wall integrity is compromised, reducing the plant's physical barrier to fungal penetration

Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation during SCLB outbreak conditions as sprinkler water disperses Bipolaris conidia from infected lower canopy leaves to upper healthy leaves, accelerating epidemic progress

rule_name: Banded Leaf and Sheath Blight High Humidity Ground-Level Risk
reason: Rhizoctonia solani AG-1 IA causes Banded Leaf and Sheath Blight (BLSB), an emerging and increasingly economically significant disease in Dharwad's irrigated and high-rainfall Kharif maize growing areas. Sclerotia in soil and previous crop residue initiate infection at the base of the plant; the pathogen then climbs the sheath system under warm (28–34°C), saturated soil and high aerial humidity (>88%) conditions. BLSB can reach the ear sheath and ear within 2–3 weeks of initial infection, causing ear rot and kernel discolouration. Dharwad UAS data show BLSB causing 15–40% yield loss in dense, irrigated Kharif stands in high-risk years.
actions: Apply Validamycin 3L (Validacin) @ 2 ml/litre as soil drench at the base of affected plants and as sheath spray targeting the lower 50 cm of the plant stem at first symptom appearance
Avoid lodging of plants and physical damage to the lower sheaths during inter-cultivation operations as wounds provide entry points for Rhizoctonia infection at the sheath level

Reduce plant density in fields with BLSB history during the following Kharif season (increase row spacing from 60 cm to 70–75 cm) to lower canopy humidity and reduce sheath contact between adjacent plants

rule_name: Charcoal Rot Risk Under Late Season Heat and Drought
reason: Macrophomina phaseolina causes Charcoal Stalk Rot, a soilborne disease with severe pathogenic potential in Dharwad's post-monsoon heat conditions. The pathogen's sclerotia dormant in soil become virulently active under heat (>34°C) and drought stress (<35% soil moisture FC) after 70 days of crop growth. Colonising the stalk pith, it causes rapid tissue breakdown producing the characteristic ash-grey, charcoal-like discolouration of internal stalk tissue. Infection results in premature plant death — stalks break at ground level — before grain reaches physiological maturity, causing 10–30% plant stand loss and yield reductions in Dharwad's October-period post-monsoon crops.
actions: Apply immediate irrigation at 40–50 mm to alleviate drought stress; water stress is the primary trigger and sustained soil moisture above 50% FC reduces Charcoal Rot incidence by 60–70%

Conduct push test: push the top of each plant with one hand 30 cm from vertical; if plant bends or breaks at the base, it is stalk-rotted; harvest any field with >15% push-test failure immediately to prevent total harvest loss from collapsed plants

Apply Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/litre as a prophylactic soil drench at 60 days after sowing in fields with previous Charcoal Rot history, before heat and drought conditions establish to reduce pathogen activation

rule_name: Pythium Stalk Rot Waterlogging Risk in Young Crop
reason: Pythium aphanidermatum thrives in warm (25–35°C), waterlogged soil conditions and is a primary cause of stalk rot and damping-off in Dharwad's young maize crops during Kharif. Unlike cool-temperature Pythium species that cause seed rot, P. aphanidermatum attacks the stalk base and roots of established seedlings (2–6 leaf stage) under warm, flooded conditions. Infected plants collapse suddenly at the soil line with soft, water-soaked stalk tissue, often collapsing in 24–48 hours after visible symptoms. Entire rows or patches can collapse, creating obvious circular dead zones in the field. Losses of 20–50% stand in poorly drained areas are documented in Dharwad.
actions: Drain standing water immediately by opening drainage furrows; Pythium spread halts as soon as aerobic soil conditions are restored and soil moisture drops below 80% field capacity
Apply Fosetyl-Al (Aliette 80 WP) @ 3 g/litre as a preventive soil drench in waterlogging-prone field spots (low areas, compacted zones) before predicted heavy rainfall events

Re-gap collapsed plants within 7 days of waterlogging using transplants from a nursery or healthy plants from overcrowded rows, maintaining target population above 85% to prevent yield loss from reduced stand

rule_name: Fusarium Ear Rot Risk During Humid Silking
reason: Fusarium verticillioides (formerly Fusarium moniliforme) is the dominant ear rot pathogen in Dharwad maize. The pathogen infects through the silk channel during silking, colonising the developing cob from the tip downward. Infection is maximised when silking coincides with humid (>80% RH), moderate temperature (20–30°C), and rainfall conditions that facilitate spore splash and silk infection. Beyond visible pink-white mould on kernels, F. verticillioides produces fumonisins — mycotoxins that cause leukoencephalomalacia in horses and oesophageal cancer risks in humans — making contaminated grain unmarketable and dangerous. This is both a yield and a food safety risk in Dharwad.
actions: Apply Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/litre at early silking (when silks are freshly emerged and sticky) to prevent Fusarium spore germination on silk tissue before husk closure

Ensure tight husk cover varieties are selected in the following season; open-husk types common in traditional Dharwad varieties allow greater silk and kernel exposure to Fusarium spores during rain splash

Harvest at first physiological maturity (black layer visible at kernel base) without delaying for field drying; every week of post-maturity standing under humid conditions increases fumonisin accumulation by 30–50%

rule_name: Aspergillus Ear Rot and Aflatoxin Risk During Hot Dry Grain Filling
reason: Aspergillus flavus is the primary aflatoxin-producing pathogen in Dharwad maize, particularly dangerous in late Kharif or early Rabi conditions where high temperatures (>36°C) and moderate humidity (70–85%) coincide with grain filling. Aflatoxin B1, produced during fungal colonisation of stress-damaged kernels, is a potent Group 1A carcinogen and the most regulated agricultural mycotoxin globally. India's PFA standards limit aflatoxin to 30 ppb total in maize for human use and 20 ppb for food-grade processing. Aflatoxin-contaminated grain from Dharwad has been rejected by poultry compound feed buyers, causing significant economic losses to farmers.
actions: Apply biocontrol agent Aflasafe KE01 (Afla-Guard) @ 10 kg/acre as a soil broadcast 2 weeks before tasseling to establish a competitive atoxigenic Aspergillus population that outcompetes aflatoxin-producing strains

Harvest at first physiological maturity; do not leave mature grain standing in field under high-temperature conditions as aflatoxin synthesis accelerates in standing, dehydrating kernels under heat stress

Dry harvested grain rapidly to below 12% moisture on clean, raised drying platforms within 5 days of harvest; aflatoxin production in stored grain above 14% moisture and above 30°C storage temperature is irreversible and compounds with storage duration

rule_name: Northern Corn Leaf Spot Cool Season Risk
reason: Bipolaris zeicola (syn. Helminthosporium carbonum) causes Northern Corn Leaf Spot (NCLS) under cool, humid conditions characteristic of Dharwad's Rabi season (December–February). Unlike SCLB which prefers warmth, NCLS is favoured by 18–24°C with high humidity for 5+ days. Diagnostic lesions are small (0.5–1.5 cm), elongated, tan to buff-coloured spots with brown borders, distributed across all canopy levels but most concentrated on mid-canopy leaves. NCLS is generally less severe than TLB in Dharwad but can cause 10–20% yield loss in susceptible Rabi hybrids during cool, cloudy post-monsoon conditions.
actions: Apply Chlorothalonil 75 WP @ 2 g/litre as a broad-spectrum protectant fungicide during Rabi cool-humid periods before lesion development reaches more than 2% leaf area on mid-canopy
Select Rabi hybrids with known NCLS resistance from UAS Dharwad variety trials; NCLS resistance in newer hybrids significantly reduces the need for fungicide intervention in Rabi seasons

Monitor Rabi maize fields during December–January foggy periods every 5–7 days for early NCLS lesion appearance on lower leaves; early detection allows single targeted application before epidemic buildup

rule_name: Stalk Rot Complex Risk at Post-Tasseling Stage
reason: Stalk rot complex in Dharwad maize is caused by multiple pathogens acting together — primarily Fusarium graminearum, Colletotrichum graminicola, and Diplodia maydis. During grain filling (70–95 days after sowing), the massive carbohydrate demand of developing kernels depletes root and stalk reserves, reducing the plant's defensive capacity. Pathogens enter through natural senescence of lower stalk tissue under warm, humid conditions. The resulting stalk softening (pinch test: soft pith in inter-nodes) leads to lodging before harvest, preventing mechanical harvest and causing significant harvest losses in Dharwad's commercial maize farms.
actions: Conduct pinch test on 30 random plants at 80 days after sowing: squeeze the second or third internode above the ground; if it collapses easily, stalk rot is present and immediate harvest planning is essential
Apply Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/litre + Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 2 g/litre as a stalk drench at first sign of lower leaf yellowing (senescence) which precedes stalk rot by 10–14 days

Ensure balanced nitrogen-to-potassium ratio in fertilizer programme (N:K ratio should not exceed 2:1 in Dharwad soils); excessive nitrogen relative to potassium increases stalk rot susceptibility by stimulating lush tissue with thinner cell walls

rule_name: Damping Off Risk in Newly Emerged Seedlings
reason: Post-emergence damping-off in Dharwad maize is caused by Fusarium spp. (primarily F. oxysporum and F. semitectum), Pythium spp., and Rhizoctonia solani acting either alone or in complex. Newly emerged seedlings (5–18 days after sowing) are most vulnerable during the cotyledon and first true leaf stage when the mesocotyl is still green and soft. High soil moisture (>85%) combined with warm temperatures (22–32°C) creates the optimal disease environment. Infected seedlings show a pinched, water-soaked mesocotyl at or just below the soil surface, toppling over or failing to produce a second leaf. Patchy stands with circular clusters of dead seedlings indicate damping-off.
actions: Drench affected seedling rows with Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/litre at 200 ml per plant immediately on identifying collapsed seedlings to prevent spread to adjacent healthy plants
Improve drainage in affected low spots of the field immediately by opening sub-surface channels; reducing soil saturation below 75% FC halts new infection within 48 hours

For the next sowing season, apply Trichoderma harzianum @ 2.5 kg/acre mixed in 200 kg compost as a soil treatment 15 days before sowing to establish biological suppression of damping-off complex pathogens

rule_name: Eye Spot Disease Risk Under Sustained Leaf Wetness
reason: Kabatiella zeae (syn. Aureobasidium zeae) causes Eye Spot of Maize, characterised by tiny, circular lesions (1–4 mm) with a clear or pale centre and a narrow yellow-green halo — resembling a bird's eye. The pathogen requires sustained leaf wetness and high humidity (>88%) at moderate temperatures (22–28°C) for spore germination and infection. Eye Spot is primarily a cool monsoon disease in Dharwad, occurring in the July–August cloudy, rainy period. While rarely causing severe standalone yield loss, Eye Spot weakens the cuticle and creates entry points for secondary Bipolaris and Fusarium infections in stressed plants.
actions: Apply Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/litre which provides excellent control against Eye Spot as a DMI fungicide; combine with sticker-spreader to improve adhesion under rainy conditions
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation in Eye Spot-prone Dharwad fields during the cool-wet season; switch to furrow or drip irrigation to reduce the leaf wetness period that drives infection

Ensure plant population does not exceed 28,000 per acre in fields with Eye Spot history; dense canopies with restricted air circulation dramatically increase the duration of leaf wetness and accelerate Eye Spot progression

rule_name: Crazy Top Downy Mildew Wind-Spread Risk
reason: Sclerophthora macrospora causes Crazy Top Downy Mildew — a morphologically distinct syndrome from SDM with characteristic abnormal proliferation of tassel bracts into leafy structures and multiple ears forming abnormally. Sporangia produced on infected plants are wind- and splash-dispersed under humid (>85% RH) conditions with moderate winds (10–30 km/h) and temperatures of 20–28°C. Secondary spread within a field occurs rapidly once primary infection sources (infected plants from systemically infected seed or previous season oospores) are sporulating. Dharwad black cotton soil areas with poor drainage have higher endemic Crazy Top pressure due to oospore persistence in permanently wet zones.
actions: Immediately rogue out all Crazy Top-symptomatic plants (plants showing leafy tassel, multiple ear proliferation, abnormal stunting) before sporulation to remove secondary inoculum source from the field

Apply Metalaxyl 35 SD seed treatment @ 6 g/kg for the next sowing season in fields where Crazy Top incidence exceeded 3% this season; systemic seed treatment is the most cost-effective prevention in endemic Dharwad fields

Improve field drainage by installing permanent bunds and drainage channels in low-lying field areas where standing water accumulates, as waterlogging enables oospore germination and perpetuates the disease cycle

rule_name: Diplodia Ear Rot and Stalk Rot Post-Silking Risk
reason: Stenocarpella maydis (Diplodia maydis) causes two overlapping diseases — Diplodia Ear Rot and Diplodia Stalk Rot — both of which are prevalent in Dharwad's post-silking maize at 75–105 days after sowing. Ear rot initiates through husk infection at high humidity (>85%) and warm temperatures (28–35°C), causing premature bleaching of husks and a white mycelial growth under husks with embedded black pycnidia. Stalk rot causes premature plant death with brown discolouration of stalk vascular tissue. Both phases cause 10–25% yield loss in Dharwad and render infected grain unfit for seed use due to seed viability reduction.
actions: Apply Thiram 75 WP @ 2 g/litre as a husk spray targeting the ear zone at 80 days after sowing to reduce Diplodia pycnidiospore germination on husk surfaces in high humidity conditions
Harvest without delay at physiological maturity (black layer stage); delayed harvest under humid conditions multiplies pycnidia production on infected cobs, contaminating the seed lot for next season

Avoid using grain from Diplodia-infected lots as seed in the next season; even lightly infected seed carries the pathogen systemically into the next crop seedlings, perpetuating the disease cycle in the field

rule_name: Bacterial Stalk Rot Hot Humid Waterlogged Risk
reason: Erwinia chrysanthemi (Dickeya zeae) causes Bacterial Stalk Rot of maize, a fast-progressing disease under extremely hot (>30°C), waterlogged (>90% soil moisture), and highly humid (>90% RH) conditions.
