The bacteria enter through wound sites (insect feeding, hail damage, inter-cultivation wounds) or natural openings and cause rapid maceration of stalk tissue from the base upward. Infected stalks emit a foul, fishy odour and collapse within 3–5 days. This disease causes sudden death syndrome in Dharwad Kharif fields, particularly in July–August when waterlogging and heat coincide. Entire patches of 50–200 plants can collapse within a week during severe outbreaks.
actions: Drain waterlogged fields immediately; bacterial stalk rot spreads exclusively under anaerobic, waterlogged conditions and halts almost entirely once soil drainage is restored

Apply Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/litre as a soil drench around the base of plants adjacent to collapsed patches to create a copper barrier zone that prevents bacterial spread to healthy neighbouring plants

Remove and destroy (burn or deep bury) collapsed rotted plants immediately; do not incorporate bacterial stalk rot-infected tissue into soil as decomposing infected plant material serves as a bacterial reservoir for next season

rule_name: Smut Gall Formation Risk at Silking
reason: Ustilago maydis causes Common Smut of Maize, forming characteristic white-silver galls on ears, tassels, stalks, and leaves. Infection by teliospores occurs through meristematic (actively dividing) tissue during tasseling and silking at temperatures of 26–34°C with moderate humidity (60–80%). The galls expand rapidly from 2 cm to 15 cm diameter within 2 weeks, replacing grain with masses of black teliospores. Smut incidence in Dharwad maize fields ranges from 2–15% depending on mechanical wound incidence (hail, insect feeding, inter-cultivation cuts) which create infection entry points. Each smut-infected ear represents complete yield loss for that plant's grain contribution.
actions: Remove smut galls when they are still white-silver (before the gall turns black and ruptures) by cutting and placing in a closed bag; do not allow black spore masses to reach the soil as teliospores persist for 5–7 years

Avoid mechanical injury to plants during inter-cultivation and earthing-up operations in Dharwad Kharif season as wounds are the primary infection routes for U. maydis during the susceptible tasseling-silking period
Apply Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/litre as a preventive spray at tassel emergence targeting the ear zone and tassels in fields with smut history in previous seasons to reduce teliospore germination

rule_name: Head Smut Systemic Infection Risk at Sowing
reason: Sporisorium reilianum causes Head Smut of Maize, a systemic smut where teliospores in the soil infect the seedling radicle at germination (0–10 days after sowing). The pathogen grows systemically within the plant without visible symptoms until tasseling and ear formation, when it replaces both tassel and ear with smut galls filled with teliospores. Diagnosis only at tasseling means intervention is too late; management must be preventive at sowing. In Dharwad fields with a history of Head Smut, soil teliospore populations can be high enough to cause 5–20% plant infection rates without seed treatment.
actions: Treat all maize seed with Carbendazim 50 WP @ 2 g/kg + Thiram 75 WS @ 1.5 g/kg combination seed treatment before sowing in all fields with Head Smut history in Dharwad; this dual treatment suppresses both smut teliospore germination and damping-off
Avoid deep sowing (more than 6 cm) in known Head Smut-endemic fields as deeper sowing increases seedling emergence time and duration of contact between the emerging radicle and soil teliospores

Practice crop rotation by sowing pulses (tur, chickpea) or sunflower in place of maize for one season in fields where Head Smut incidence exceeded 5%; these non-host crops starve the soil teliospore population and reduce inoculum density

rule_name: Maize Streak Virus Risk During Dry Season
reason: Maize Streak Virus (MSV), transmitted by the leafhopper Cicadulina mbila, causes characteristic yellow-white streaks on young maize leaves. In Dharwad, dry hot conditions (RH <55%, temperature 28–36°C) during early crop growth create environmental conditions that favour leafhopper populations and reduce the plant's ability to compartmentalise viral infection. The virus is transmitted within 1–2 minutes of leafhopper feeding, making chemical vector control impractical; host plant resistance and healthy seed are the primary management tools. Early infection (before 4-leaf stage) causes severe stunting and near-complete yield loss in susceptible varieties.
actions: Use MSV-resistant hybrid varieties recommended for Dharwad region (e.g. HQPM-7, varieties with MSV tolerance ratings from IIMR or UAS Dharwad variety trial results); variety selection is the most effective and economical MSV management strategy

Apply imidacloprid 70 WS @ 5 ml/kg as a seed treatment to suppress leafhopper populations during the critical 7–21 day seedling establishment period when plants are most vulnerable to virus acquisition

Rogue out and destroy streak-affected plants before 20 days after sowing; infected plants serve as reservoir sources for leafhopper acquisition and re-inoculation of neighbouring healthy plants in the field

rule_name: Anthracnose Leaf Blight Risk in Monsoon Recovery
reason: Colletotrichum graminicola causes both Anthracnose leaf blight and stalk rot in Dharwad maize. The leaf blight phase, while less economically severe than stalk rot, reduces canopy photosynthetic capacity by 15–25% and weakens plant vascular integrity, predisposing plants to stalk rot later in the season. Leaf blight development requires high humidity (>85%), moderate temperatures (22–30°C), and active rainfall splash (10–35 mm/day) to disperse conidia from residue on the soil surface to lower leaves. In Dharwad's residue-retaining minimum-till fields increasingly adopted for soil health, Anthracnose leaf blight pressure is significantly higher than in conventionally ploughed fields.
actions: Apply Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/litre which has curative activity against Colletotrichum and simultaneously prevents early stalk infection that follows the leaf blight phase in the Dharwad cropping sequence

Plough or disc previous crop maize residue at least 30 days before the next sowing to expose and accelerate breakdown of infected straw which carries Colletotrichum conidia and sclerotia; do not retain maize stover on the surface in Anthracnose-endemic fields

Increase inter-row spacing to 65–70 cm in Anthracnose-prone fields to reduce rain splash movement of conidia from infected lower leaves to upper canopy and improve airflow that reduces leaf wetness duration

rule_name: Root Rot Complex Post-Flooding Risk
reason: Post-flooding root rot complex in young Dharwad maize crops involves Pythium spp., Fusarium spp., and Rhizoctonia solani acting synergistically on oxygen-depleted, stressed root systems. After 4+ days of flooding in the 10–40 day after sowing window, root cortical cells begin dying from oxygen deprivation, creating ideal wound sites for pathogen entry. All three pathogen groups produce enzymes (pectinases, cellulases) that rapidly macerate root tissue, leaving plants with black, rotted, odour-producing root systems. Plants may remain upright for 5–10 days post-flooding before suddenly collapsing as the root system loses all function.
actions: Drain water immediately and wait 5–7 days before applying rescue treatment of Metalaxyl + Mancozeb @ 2.5 g/litre + Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/litre combination as a soil drench to suppress the mixed Oomycete-fungal root rot pathogen community

Apply 500 g Pseudomonas fluorescens bioinoculant mixed in 20 litres water as a root zone drench after drainage; P. fluorescens produces siderophores and antibiotics that suppress Fusarium and Pythium root pathogens and stimulates root recovery

Apply 10 kg gypsum per acre to flood-affected patches after drainage to restore calcium to root zones and improve root cell wall integrity, reducing secondary infection from post-flood weakened root tissue

rule_name: Corn Lethal Necrosis Compound Virus Severe Risk
reason: Maize Lethal Necrosis (MLN) is caused by the interaction of Maize Chlorotic Mottle Virus (MCMV) and one of several potyviruses (including SCMV — Sugarcane Mosaic Virus). MCMV is primarily transmitted by thrips, which thrive under dry, hot (30–36°C) conditions with moderate winds that help them move between plants. While individual viruses cause mild symptoms, the combined infection causes complete plant death within 2–4 weeks of infection. MLN is not yet widely established in Dharwad but has been reported in parts of Karnataka, and dry-season vector conditions in Dharwad Rabi maize place this as a monitoring priority with potentially catastrophic consequences if it becomes established.
actions: Apply Thiamethoxam 25 WG @ 0.5 g/litre or Imidacloprid 17.8 SL @ 0.5 ml/litre as a foliar spray to reduce thrips populations that transmit MCMV during dry hot periods; target the whorl of young plants where thrips congregate

Rogue out any plants showing multiple symptoms (mottling, necrosis, complete yellowing from leaf tip) immediately and report to local KVK Dharwad for virus disease confirmation, as early detection is critical for MLN management
Use MLN-tolerant varieties from IIMR recommended list for Dharwad conditions in fields adjacent to sorghum, wheat, or other grass crops that serve as alternate virus hosts for MCMV and potyviruses

rule_name: Powdery Mildew Risk Under Dry Moderate Conditions
reason: Sphaerotheca fuliginea (Podosphaera xanthii) causes Powdery Mildew on maize, an unusual disease in that it does not require free water for infection — moderate humidity (60–78%) without rainfall is optimal. In Dharwad, Powdery Mildew appears during the drier parts of the Kharif season and in Rabi under conditions of moderate humidity without rain. White powdery colonies on both leaf surfaces, particularly on the upper surface, reduce photosynthesis by 10–20% in moderate infections. Though rarely a primary yield-reducing disease, Powdery Mildew weakens plants that are simultaneously experiencing other stresses, and can be confused with downy mildew by newer farmers.
actions: Apply Sulphur 80 WP @ 3 g/litre as a cost-effective contact fungicide specifically active against Powdery Mildew; do not apply when temperature exceeds 32°C as sulphur causes phytotoxicity on maize leaves under high heat

Ensure the disease is correctly distinguished from Downy Mildew: Powdery Mildew has white powdery growth on the UPPER leaf surface only, while Downy Mildew has white sporulation on the LOWER leaf surface; different pathogens require different fungicide strategies
Avoid sprinkler irrigation during Powdery Mildew development as wetting the mildew colonies with water does not control the disease and may spread other pathogens from lower canopy to upper leaves

rule_name: Brown Spot Disease Risk in Acidic Laterite Soils
reason: Physoderma maydis causes Physoderma Brown Spot, also called Yellow Spot, on maize. The pathogen produces dark brown round-to-oval spots primarily on leaf sheaths and stalk internodes under high humidity (>80%) and warm (24–30°C) conditions. It is particularly prevalent in Dharwad's eastern taluk acidic laterite and sandy soils (pH 5.2–5.8) where phosphorus availability is low and plant immune defences are compromised. In severe infections, Physoderma infection of stalk nodes weakens the internode structurally, predisposing plants to mid-stalk breakage under wind or heavy rain during grain filling.
actions: Apply Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/litre to both leaf and sheath surfaces, as Physoderma brown spot lesions on the sheath are the most damaging and often missed by top-spray-only applications

Apply lime @ 200 kg per acre in Dharwad laterite soils with pH below 5.5 to raise pH to 6.0–6.5, improving phosphorus availability and plant nutrient-based defence capacity against secondary Physoderma infection

Ensure adequate phosphorus application (75–80 kg DAP per acre as basal) in sandy acidic fields of Dharwad's Kundgol and Navalgund areas where phosphorus deficiency consistently increases Physoderma severity

rule_name: Gibberella Ear Rot Cool Wet Silking Risk
reason: Fusarium graminearum (Gibberella zeae) causes Gibberella Ear Rot, identifiable by the characteristic pink to red mould growing from the ear tip downward under the husks. Unlike Fusarium Ear Rot (which infects from the tip), Gibberella infects through the silk channel during wet, cool-moderate silking conditions (22–28°C, >82% RH). It produces deoxynivalenol (DON/vomitoxin) and zearalenone — regulated mycotoxins that cause feed refusal in livestock and reproductive disorders in swine. Gibberella Ear Rot-contaminated maize grain is routinely rejected by Dharwad poultry feed mills, causing serious income loss for Kharif maize farmers.
actions: Apply Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1 ml/litre at 50% silk emergence targeting silk bundles and husk surfaces; Tebuconazole is highly effective against Fusarium graminearum and is the fungicide of choice for Gibberella Ear Rot prevention in Dharwad conditions
Harvest within 2–3 days of black layer formation and dry cobs quickly to below 14% moisture to stop DON and zearalenone accumulation in partially-dried or field-drying cobs under humid conditions

Segregate harvested grain visually: cobs with visible pink-red mould should be dried separately and tested before marketing; do not mix visibly infected grain with clean grain as mycotoxin contamination is undetectable visually once grain is mixed

rule_name: Fusarium Root Rot Compaction Stress Combined Risk
reason: Fusarium oxysporum and F. solani f. sp. zeae cause Fusarium Crown and Root Rot in maize, a chronic, low-intensity disease in Dharwad's black cotton soil fields. Heavy Vertisol soils develop surface compaction (1–3 cm depth) under alternate wetting-drying cycles common in Kharif, restricting root penetration into deeper soil layers and creating hypoxic root conditions. Compaction-stressed roots are significantly more susceptible to Fusarium crown rot, which attacks the crown and mesocotyl producing reddish-brown discolouration. Plants show stunting, yellowing, and tillering despite adequate nutrition — a diagnostic indicator of Fusarium crown rot versus nutrient deficiency.
actions: Apply Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 2.5 kg/acre mixed with 50 kg compost as a soil treatment before sowing in black cotton soil fields with Fusarium crown rot history, to establish biocontrol suppression in the crown zone

Perform sub-soiling (chisel plowing at 25–30 cm depth) before Kharif sowing in heavily compacted black cotton soil fields to break hardpan, improve root penetration, and reduce the compaction-Fusarium interaction that drives crown rot severity

Avoid heavy pre-sowing irrigation (>50 mm) on black cotton soils that creates surface sealing and compaction when dry; use 25–30 mm irrigation to achieve field capacity without surface crust formation

rule_name: Late Wilt Disease Risk in Deep Black Soils
reason: Magnaporthiopsis maydis (formerly Harpophora maydis) causes Late Wilt of Maize — a vascular disease that wilts plants at the grain filling stage (65–90 days after sowing) without any prior visible symptoms. The pathogen colonises xylem vessels under warm (>30°C) soil conditions in deep black cotton soils, blocking water transport. Affected plants wilt suddenly despite adequate soil moisture, showing brown discolouration of vascular tissue when stalks are split longitudinally. Late Wilt has been reported from North Karnataka maize-growing areas and is a significant risk in Dharwad's irrigated Kharif black cotton soil fields. Once wilting begins, no treatment is effective.
actions: Practice 2–3 year crop rotation with non-host crops (sorghum, tur, sunflower) in fields where late wilt incidence exceeded 3% in the previous Kharif season; Late Wilt fungal population in soil declines significantly after one non-host season

Apply Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/litre as a soil drench preventively at 50 days after sowing in high-risk deep black cotton soil fields to suppress early vascular colonisation before symptom expression at 65+ days after sowing

Report late wilt incidence to KVK Dharwad for regional disease monitoring; Late Wilt is an emerging priority disease in Karnataka and regional data is needed for advisory system calibration and to identify high-risk hoblis for variety trials

rule_name: Seed Rot and Pre-Emergence Damping Off Under Cold Wet Sowing
reason: Pre-emergence seed rot under cold (<18°C), wet (>85% soil moisture) Rabi sowing conditions in Dharwad is caused by Pythium spp. and Fusarium spp. attacking seeds that germinate slowly due to cold soil temperatures. The combination of slow germination (12–15 days instead of 5–7 days) and pathogen-conducive soil conditions means seeds are exposed to rotting organisms for twice the normal duration. Seed rot causes patches of non-emergence, visible as bare soil rows in an otherwise germinated field. Affected seeds disintegrate and leave no trace, making post-emergence diagnosis impossible without digging. This is a silent, invisible yield loss in Rabi maize that is often mistakenly attributed to poor seed quality.
actions: Use only certified, high-germination (>90%) hybrid seed from KSSC or authorized dealers for Rabi sowing in Dharwad; poor germination seed is more susceptible to seed rot and provides lower initial seedling vigour

Apply combination seed treatment of Metalaxyl 35 SD @ 6 g/kg + Carbendazim 50 WP @ 2 g/kg to protect against both Oomycete (Pythium) and true fungal (Fusarium) seed rot pathogens that are active at Rabi sowing temperatures in Dharwad

Sow at 4–5 cm depth only; deeper sowing (6–8 cm) in cold soils increases transit time for the emerging coleoptile and extends exposure of the germinating seed to soil pathogens by an additional 3–5 days

rule_name: Tar Spot Complex Risk Under Frequent Rainfall Cycles
reason: Phyllachora maydis (Tar Spot) causes characteristic black, shiny, raised stroma on maize leaves resembling small tar spots. In combination with Monographella maydis (Fisheye Tar Spot complex), it causes the most yield-damaging form of this disease complex. Infection is favoured by cool-moderate temperatures (18–24°C), high humidity (>85%), and frequent light rains over 8+ consecutive days — conditions that occur in Dharwad's September–October transitional monsoon period. The Tar Spot Complex has caused significant yield losses in parts of humid maize-growing areas globally and represents a monitoring priority as it spreads geographically. Early reports from nearby IIMR trial sites in Karnataka suggest emerging presence.
actions: Apply Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/litre as a protectant spray when weather forecast indicates 8+ days of cool-humid conditions to prevent Tar Spot complex establishment during the September transitional monsoon in Dharwad

Report any unusual black, raised, shiny spots (distinct from rust pustules which are powdery) to KVK Dharwad for pathogen identification; Tar Spot Complex is distinct from other foliar diseases and requires specific diagnostic confirmation
Maintain foliar spray records and disease observations across seasons to help regional agricultural advisory services build the first local database on Tar Spot Complex occurrence in Dharwad district

rule_name: Penicillium Ear Rot During Cold Wet Harvest Season
reason: Penicillium spp. cause a blue-green mould ear rot in Dharwad Rabi maize at harvest when cool (15–24°C), humid (>80%) February–March conditions coincide with delayed harvesting of mature cobs. Penicillium enters through husk damage (insect feeding, mechanical) and colonises kernels with blue-green conidial masses visible when husks are peeled back. While Penicillium mycotoxins (ochratoxin A, citrinin) are less regulated than aflatoxins in India, they significantly reduce grain quality for poultry and livestock feed markets. Penicillium-infected grain has a characteristic musty odour and discoloured germ that reduces germination in seed lots.
actions: Harvest Rabi maize within 5 days of physiological maturity during February–March; delayed harvest under cool-humid Rabi conditions allows Penicillium to establish on intact cobs still in the field

Remove husks immediately after harvest and begin field drying in direct sunlight on elevated tarpaulins; blue-green Penicillium growth is dramatically reduced when grain moisture is brought below 16% within 7 days of harvest
Treat harvested cobs with light dusting of Mancozeb powder (0.5% w/w) or sulphur dust if stored before complete drying to prevent Penicillium spread during the storage-drying transition period

rule_name: Nematode Root Damage Compounding Disease Risk
reason: Root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne incognita) and lesion nematodes (Pratylenchus zeae) are widespread in Dharwad's sandy laterite soils in the eastern taluks. Nematode populations are highest at warm (26–32°C), moderate moisture (45–70% FC) conditions. While nematode damage alone causes 10–15% yield loss through root galling and reduced water-nutrient absorption, the primary agronomic impact in Dharwad is the creation of root wound sites that serve as entry points for Fusarium root rot and Pythium root rot pathogens — amplifying disease impact 2–3 fold compared to either nematode or fungal infection alone.
actions: Apply Carbofuran 3 G @ 8 kg/acre in the seed furrow at sowing in sandy fields with known nematode history to suppress nematode population during the critical seedling and early vegetative establishment period

Apply Paecilomyces lilacinus bioagent @ 4 kg/acre mixed with compost as a pre-sowing soil treatment to establish biological nematode suppression that persists through the crop season without chemical reapplication

Incorporate marigold (Tagetes erecta) green manure at 5 tonnes/acre and plough in 3 weeks before sowing; marigold root exudates (alpha-terthienyl) are potent nematostatic compounds reducing Meloidogyne population by 40–60% in Dharwad sandy soils

rule_name: Curvularia Leaf Spot Risk in Stressed Crops
reason: Curvularia lunata is a secondary pathogen in Dharwad maize that attacks heat-stressed and drought-stressed plants. The pathogen is always present in the environment but causes significant disease only when plant immune defences are weakened by drought stress (soil moisture <45% FC) combined with hot (28–35°C), humid (>80% RH) conditions. This paradoxical hot-humid-yet-dry scenario occurs during Dharwad's post-monsoon transition in October, when temperatures are still high and humidity remains elevated from the monsoon but rainfall has stopped and soil dries rapidly. Curvularia causes olive-brown to black oval spots on leaves and husks, reducing final grain quality and photosynthesis.
actions: Address the primary drought stress immediately with irrigation at 30–35 mm; Curvularia disease intensity reduces significantly when plant water status is restored above 55% soil moisture field capacity

Apply Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/litre if Curvularia lesions are visible on more than 5% of leaf area of upper 3 leaves, as active infection in stressed plants can spread to husks, reducing grain quality at marketing

Record occurrence of combined heat-drought-Curvularia events for future season planning; fields showing this pattern should be prioritised for assured irrigation infrastructure investment to break the drought-stress-disease cycle

rule_name: Crown Rot Fungal Complex Risk in Rabi Cold Emergence
reason: Crown rot complex in Dharwad Rabi maize involves Fusarium graminearum, F. culmorum, and F. pseudograminearum — all cool-temperature Fusarium species that are more aggressive at temperatures below 20°C than the warm-temperature Fusarium species. The crown (junction of root and shoot below soil line) is the most vulnerable infection site; infected crowns show brown-dark discolouration and constriction, stunting shoot emergence and root development simultaneously. Rabi maize in Dharwad sown in cold, moist conditions (November–December) in fields with heavy maize residue from previous Kharif is at highest risk for this crown rot complex.
actions: Apply Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1 ml/litre as a crown drench at 10 days after sowing for Rabi maize in fields with previous crown rot history; Tebuconazole is specifically effective against the cool-temperature Fusarium complex
Remove or deep-plough previous Kharif maize stubble before Rabi sowing; residue on the surface or shallowly incorporated serves as primary inoculum source for Fusarium crown rot in the Rabi crop

Add boron @ 0.5 g/litre (borax solution) to the seed treatment slurry for Rabi sowings; boron-treated seeds produce stronger cell walls in the emerging crown zone, reducing susceptibility to Fusarium crown rot infection

rule_name: Pythium Damping Off Overnight Spread After Rain
reason: Pythium aphanidermatum is uniquely dangerous in Dharwad Kharif maize because it can cause 100% damping-off in a circular spreading pattern overnight under warm-wet conditions. At temperatures of 28–36°C with rainfall >35 mm, Pythium zoospores move through film water across the soil surface and infect the emerging coleorhiza and radicle of germinating seeds (4–12 days after sowing). In Dharwad's July conditions with both warm nights and heavy monsoon rains, P. aphanidermatum can spread 2–3 metres from an initial infection focus in a single night, creating expanding circular dead patches that double in size daily if unchecked.
actions: Apply Metalaxyl 25 WP @ 1.5 g/litre as a preventive soil drench across the entire field (not just affected patches) when night temperatures exceed 28°C and heavy rain is forecasted within 24 hours of seed germination stage
Re-examine the expanding patch margin daily and apply a Metalaxyl drench 1–2 metres beyond the visible dead-plant boundary to arrest Pythium spread before new infections become visible
In fields with repeated Pythium damping-off history in Dharwad, sow maize on raised beds (15–20 cm high, 90 cm bed width) to reduce waterlogging duration and zoospore mobility in surface water

rule_name: Seed-Borne Smut Risk From Ungraded Farmer-Saved Seed
reason: In Dharwad, an estimated 30–40% of smallholder farmers use saved or informally purchased maize seed that has not undergone certified seed treatment. Farmer-saved seed from plots with smut, downy mildew, or Fusarium grain rot infections can carry pathogen teliospores or mycelium. When such untreated seed is sown in moist (55–75% FC), warm (22–30°C) soil, the co-sown pathogens have a head start over biocontrol agents. The critical seeding moment is a narrow window where proper seed treatment prevents 20–40% of early-season diseases that would otherwise require expensive curative interventions throughout the growing season.
actions: Apply combination seed treatment (Metalaxyl 35 SD @ 6 g/kg + Carbendazim 50 WP @ 2 g/kg + Thiram 75 WS @ 1.5 g/kg) to ALL maize seed — both certified and farmer-saved — before every sowing; do not skip seed treatment regardless of seed source

Source certified maize seed from KSSC outlets, Bayer, or Pioneer dealers in Dharwad town for Kharif and Rabi seasons; certified seed is tested for germination >90% and is pre-treated with fungicide at recommended doses

If farmer-saved seed must be used, float-test seeds in 10% salt water (100 g salt per litre) and discard floating seeds; treat only the sinking seeds with the above fungicide combination before sowing

rule_name: Ustilago Hyphae Spread in Moist Warm Soil
reason: Ustilago maydis teliospore germination and basidiospore production in Dharwad soils occurs optimally at 65–80% RH and 26–32°C soil temperature. During tasseling and silking when the plant has the most actively meristematic tissue, basidiospores in soil-splash can reach tassel branches and silk bundles through rain splash or dew movement, infecting multiple aerial infection sites. Field surveys in Dharwad district show Common Smut incidence of 3–8% in irrigated maize, corresponding to reduced cob counts and significant yield loss from gall-replaced ears. Mechanical damage from any field operation during this period amplifies infection.
actions: Spray Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/litre at tassel emergence (when tassels have just emerged from the whorl) targeting the tassel and upper stalk to reduce basidiospore establishment in exposed meristematic tissue

Avoid any mechanical damage to plants from inter-cultivation or earthing-up operations during the tasseling and silking period; Ustilago infection rate increases 3–5 fold in mechanically damaged plants compared to undamaged plants

Collect and count smutted ears in a 10-metre row at each harvesting; calculate smut incidence percentage and report to the district agricultural office for regional smut incidence monitoring and advisory calibration

rule_name: Blight Progression Risk on Lower Canopy Post-Tasseling
reason: Post-tasseling in Dharwad Kharif (August–October), the maize canopy reaches full closure with the top leaves maintaining active photosynthesis while lower leaves begin natural senescence. When humidity exceeds 80% and temperatures are 24–30°C, foliar pathogens (primarily TLB and GLS) that have been building up since vegetative stages accelerate their upward progression through the canopy toward the ear leaf and above. Lesion coverage exceeding 50% of the ear leaf and above at this stage directly reduces starch loading into kernels, with each 10% increase in upper canopy disease severity reducing final yield by 6–10% in Dharwad field trials.
actions: Apply Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/litre + Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2 g/litre combination spray at 75 days after sowing targeting specifically the top 3–4 leaves (including ear leaf) to protect the primary photosynthetic source for grain filling

Assess the economic threshold: if disease covers more than 20% of the ear leaf area at 75 days after sowing, a fungicide spray is economically justified at expected yield levels above 40 quintals per acre in Dharwad

Ensure sprayer nozzles reach the upper canopy (ear leaf and flag leaf level) with adequate pressure; disease on the upper canopy in a 200 cm tall Dharwad crop requires a boom sprayer or elevated knapsack sprayer to achieve effective coverage

rule_name: Helminthosporium Turcicum Sporulation Peak Window
reason: Exserohilum turcicum reaches peak conidial sporulation when night temperatures are 18–22°C (promoting sporulation) and day temperatures are 26–30°C (promoting rapid spore germination), combined with sustained high humidity (>87%) for 4+ consecutive days. This specific diurnal temperature-humidity pattern is exactly characteristic of Dharwad's August-September Kharif weather when the monsoon is active but monsoon breaks are beginning. The cigar-shaped conidia are produced in massive quantities under these conditions and released in the early morning hours, ensuring maximum airborne concentration during the peak dew period — the most efficient infection window for this pathogen.
actions: Apply systemic fungicide (Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1 ml/litre) during the evening or early morning when conidial release is lowest, to avoid spraying when spore clouds are already airborne and when spray efficacy is maximised by the next morning dew period

Double the monitoring frequency to every 3 days during this weather pattern; TLB lesion counts on the ear leaf should trigger immediate spray if more than 3 fresh lesions per leaf are visible on the top 4 leaves

Combine the systemic TLB spray with a phosphate fertilizer spray (1% mono-potassium phosphate) to simultaneously support grain filling and stimulate salicylic acid-based plant defence pathways that contribute to partial TLB tolerance

rule_name: Maize Mosaic Virus Risk in Early Kharif Seedlings
reason: Maize Mosaic Virus (MMV) is transmitted by the planthopper Peregrinus maidis, which thrives under warm (28–36°C), dry (RH <65%) conditions with moderate winds that facilitate insect movement between plants. The virus causes characteristic mosaic patterns (irregular yellow-green discolouration) on young leaves, severe stunting of infected seedlings, and complete yield loss if infection occurs before the 4-leaf stage. In Dharwad, early June Kharif sowing (before reliable monsoon establishment) places seedlings in the hottest, driest conditions — peak planthopper risk — before canopy closure provides natural microclimate buffering.
actions: Apply Imidacloprid 17.8 SL @ 0.5 ml/litre as a foliar spray at 12 and 22 days after sowing to suppress planthopper populations during the critical early seedling period; target the whorl where planthoppers shelter from direct sun

Rogue out mosaic-symptomatic plants before 25 days after sowing and before the crop reaches knee height; virusinfected plants serve as inoculum reservoirs and infected young plants never recover economic productivity

Avoid sowing maize adjacent to perennial grasses (Napier, sugarcane, ratoon sorghum) which serve as alternate hosts for both MMV and its planthopper vector; maintain a 10-metre buffer strip of open soil or legume crop between maize and grass hosts

rule_name: Pythium Root Rot Risk in Drip-Irrigated Systems
reason: Drip-irrigated maize in Dharwad creates a consistently moist, warm soil zone (a wetted bulb at 80%+ soil moisture) directly around the root zone. While drip improves water use efficiency, the persistent high moisture combined with warm soil temperatures (26–34°C) under Dharwad's Kharif conditions creates a microhabitat ideal for Pythium root rot. Unlike flood-irrigated fields where wet-dry cycles partially suppress Pythium, drip-irrigated zones have continuous moisture that enables perpetual Pythium zoospore production and infection cycles. Drip emitter blockages that create uneven wetting also concentrate Pythium at wet spots, causing patch root rot patterns along drip lines.
actions: Fertigate Fosetyl-Al (Aliette) @ 3 g/plant through the drip system at 25 and 45 days after sowing in drip-irrigated Dharwad maize fields to deliver Oomycete-specific fungicide directly to the root zone without off-target effects

Check drip emitters monthly for blockages and replace clogged emitters immediately; uneven wetting creates high-moisture spots where Pythium concentration exceeds the economic threshold for root infection

Incorporate organic matter (well-decomposed farmyard manure @ 5 tonnes/acre) into the drip zone before crop establishment to stimulate Trichoderma and Pseudomonas populations that naturally suppress Pythium in the root zone

rule_name: Phytophthora Root and Stem Rot Risk on Poorly Drained Slopes
reason: Phytophthora maydis causes root and basal stem rot in Dharwad maize on loamy soils with impeded subsurface drainage. The pathogen requires free water and extended saturation periods (>88% SM, 4+ rain days) for zoospore production and infection, similar to Pythium but more aggressive on established seedlings and early vegetative plants. Phytophthora-infected plants show brown-black lesions on the stem base at soil level, wilting from midday despite adequate soil moisture (diagnostic sign of vascular blockage), and internal brown discolouration of basal stem tissue. In Dharwad's loamy soils on lower landscape positions that receive runoff, Phytophthora incidence can reach 15–25% in wet Kharif years.
actions: Apply Fosetyl-Al 80 WP @ 3 g/litre as a crown drench at 250 ml per plant at first signs of midday wilting (with adequate soil moisture) to arrest Phytophthora vascular colonisation before complete plant collapse

Install field drainage channels at the head of each bed row on slopes to divert incoming runoff from uphill areas, preventing the prolonged waterlogging that initiates Phytophthora zoospore production

Treat seeds with Metalaxyl 35 SD @ 6 g/kg in fields with Phytophthora history; the systemic metalaxyl provides protection through the seedling and early vegetative stages when Phytophthora infection risk is highest

rule_name: Rhizoctonia Aerial Blight Risk at Canopy Closure
reason: Rhizoctonia solani AG-1 IA causes Aerial Blight of Maize under the highest-humidity conditions in Dharwad's Kharif season. When canopy closure occurs (around 40–50 days after sowing for most Dharwad maize varieties), RH within the dense plant canopy can exceed 95% even when ambient RH is 90%. The Rhizoctonia mycelium, present in soil and plant debris, grows upward through stems and sheaths, producing characteristic tan-brown banded lesions on leaf sheaths with visible aerial mycelial threads binding adjacent leaves and stems together. Aerial Blight can reach ear height within 7–10 days under peak humid conditions, severely affecting ear quality.
actions: Apply Validamycin 3L @ 2 ml/litre as a targeted sheath spray on the lower 50 cm of plants at canopy closure onset; Validamycin-based products are APEDA and BIS approved for Rhizoctonia in India and have excellent safety profiles for Dharwad farmer use

Perform a single inter-row strip weeding at canopy closure to remove excess biomass between rows that contributes to humidity elevation and Rhizoctonia spread; this is the last practical canopy-entry window before physical access becomes impossible

Avoid foliar applications of high-nitrogen fertilizers (urea sprays) during Rhizoctonia aerial blight conditions, as nitrogen-induced lush growth creates more succulent tissue that is more susceptible to Rhizoctonia infection

rule_name: Post-Harvest Storage Aflatoxin Risk in High Humidity
reason: Post-harvest aflatoxin accumulation in Dharwad maize stored under humid (>80% RH) and warm (25–38°C) conditions is a critical food safety and economic risk. Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus synthesise aflatoxin B1 exponentially when grain moisture exceeds 14% at these temperatures. Dharwad farmers storing shelled grain in gunny bags in non-ventilated rooms during October–November (pre-Diwali season) create ideal aflatoxin production environments. Poultry feed buyers in Hubli-Dharwad routinely test loads for aflatoxin, and rejection of contaminated lots causes total income loss on those consignments. Karnataka food safety standards follow FSSAI limits of 10 ppb AFB1.
actions: Dry shelled grain to below 12% moisture (test by biting a kernel — if no moisture on tooth, it is below 12%) before placing in storage; this single action prevents >90% of storage aflatoxin development
Store grain in sealed HDPE (high-density polyethylene) bags or airtight metal bins rather than jute gunny bags to prevent moisture ingress during humid October-November weather in Dharwad

Apply phosphine fumigation tablets (Celphos 3 g tablet @ 1 tablet per 100 kg grain) in sealed storage bags before the monsoon withdrawal humidity period to suppress Aspergillus growth and insect activity simultaneously

rule_name: Goss's Wilt Risk Indicator During Warm Wet Periods
reason: Clavibacter michiganensis subsp. nebraskensis causes Goss's Bacterial Wilt and Leaf Blight of maize. Entry is facilitated by physical leaf damage from wind-driven rain and hail events, creating wound sites through which the bacteria enter the vascular system. Warm (26–32°C), humid (>82% RH) conditions with wind-driven rain (25+ mm/day, 20+ km/h wind) create both the infection opportunity (wounds) and the epidemiological conditions for spread. While not yet widely confirmed in Dharwad district specifically, the agro-climatic conditions and increasing maize intensification place it as a monitoring priority. Diagnostic hallmark is tan water-soaked lesions with irregular margins running parallel to leaf veins and characteristic 'freckles' (bacterial exudate droplets).
actions: Monitor for tan lesions with watery margins and leaf-parallel progression immediately after wind-rain events; if such symptoms appear alongside bacterial ooze dried to yellow-orange 'freckles', contact KVK Dharwad for bacterial wilt confirmation
Avoid inter-cultivation operations with hoe or tractor during or immediately after wind-rain events to minimise additional mechanical wounds that serve as Goss's Wilt bacterial entry sites

Use resistant hybrid varieties that are dual-rated for both Goss's Wilt and TLB resistance where available from IIMR recommended list for Karnataka; variety resistance is the most reliable management strategy for bacterial diseases

rule_name: Storage Mould Developing Due to Incomplete Drying
reason: Post-harvest drying of maize grain in Dharwad is done predominantly by sun-drying on tarpaulins or courtyard floors. When post-harvest weather is cloudy or drizzly (>5 mm/day) with ambient humidity above 78% and temperatures of 20–30°C, grain moisture does not fall below the safe storage threshold of 12–13% within the expected 5–7 day drying period. Grain stuck at 16–20% moisture for more than 7 days under these conditions allows Aspergillus, Penicillium, and Fusarium storage moulds to establish, reducing grain weight by 2–5% through respiration and causing visible mould growth that destroys the market value of the lot.
actions: Spread grain thinly (maximum 5 cm depth) on tarpaulins and turn it 3–4 times per day to maximise evaporative surface area and reduce drying time during overcast post-harvest periods

Construct a simple raised perforated platform drying structure using bamboo and polythene to allow airflow from below the grain, achieving 30–40% faster drying than flat-tarpaulin sun drying in humid conditions

If drying cannot be completed within 10 days due to wet weather, contact local UPCL or agricultural cooperative for access to mechanical grain dryer; cost of mechanical drying (₹1–2 per kg) is always less than mould-related price discount or rejection at the buyer

rule_name: Northern Corn Leaf Blight Early Season Establishment
reason: Early establishment of Exserohilum turcicum (Turcicum Leaf Blight) in the vegetative stage (20–45 days after sowing) dramatically worsens final disease severity compared to late establishment. Primary inoculum from infected maize stubble in Dharwad fields produces conidia that infect lower leaves early in the season, establishing the secondary inoculum base that drives the mid-season epidemic. If more than 5% of lower leaf area shows TLB lesions at 35 days after sowing in Dharwad conditions, disease progression models predict upper canopy infection reaching 40–50% leaf area by tasseling, far exceeding the economic threshold. Early detection and intervention at this stage is 4–5 times more cost-effective than late-season intervention.
actions: Inspect the bottom three leaves of 20 random plants at 35 days after sowing; if TLB lesions (tan, elongated, cigar-shaped) are present on more than 3 leaves out of 20 plants, apply systemic fungicide immediately

Apply Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/litre as the first intervention at early vegetative establishment of TLB; early intervention reduces secondary inoculum production by 70–80% and prevents mid-season epidemic development

Deep-plough or incorporate maize residue from previous crops thoroughly before sowing in TLB-endemic Dharwad fields; residue incorporation reduces primary inoculum by 50–60% and delays epidemic onset by 15–20 days, compressing the disease window

rule_name: Stalk Borer Entry Wound Pathogen Colonisation Risk
reason: Chilo partellus (spotted stalk borer) is a major pest of Dharwad Kharif maize that creates feeding tunnels in the stalk and whorl. While the pest itself is a direct yield reducer, its entry holes and feeding tunnels are also important disease entry points for Fusarium spp. and Colletotrichum graminicola. Stalk borer-damaged tissue under warm (25–32°C), humid (>78% RH) conditions becomes rapidly colonised by these pathogens, converting a 10–15% direct pest yield loss into a 20–30% combined pest-disease yield loss. This disease-interaction aspect of stalk borer damage in Dharwad is underrecognised in standard pest management advisories.
actions: Apply Carbendazim 50 WP @ 1 g/litre into the whorl of plants showing fresh stalk borer feeding damage (dead heart, frass) to prevent Fusarium colonisation of the borer entry tunnels

Use Trichoderma viride granules @ 5 kg/acre applied into the whorl at 25 days after sowing to establish biocontrol agents in the whorl zone that both suppress borer egg hatching and prevent fungal colonisation of borer wounds

Apply Lambda-cyhalothrin 5 EC @ 1 ml/litre at 20 days after sowing to suppress stalk borer before whorl penetration and tunnel formation; reducing borer damage directly reduces the wound-entry disease infection pathway

rule_name: Leaf Rust Uredospore Peak Release Morning Risk
reason: Puccinia polysora (Southern Rust) differs from Common Rust in its preference for higher temperatures (optimum 25–30°C) and in producing a different pattern of smaller, densely clustered uredinia on upper leaf surfaces. It has historically been restricted to coastal Karnataka but has been spreading into North Karnataka and Dharwad division under warming trends. The specific cool-night (14–20°C) and warm-day (24–28°C) temperature pattern with high night humidity (>88%) that produces heavy dew is the peak uredospore release condition for both Common Rust and Southern Rust, creating maximum airborne spore concentrations in early morning hours just before dew dries.
actions: Schedule all rust-protective fungicide sprays in the late afternoon (3–5 PM) to ensure maximum residue on leaf surfaces during the high-infection morning dew period the following day; morning spraying during spore release reduces efficacy

Apply Flutriafol 25 SC @ 0.5 ml/litre (or Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/litre as cost-equivalent alternative) specifically targeting rust pustule suppression on both leaf surfaces at first sign of powdery rust pustule development

Document rust intensity weekly using a simple 1–5 scoring: 1 = no rust, 2 = <5% leaf area, 3 = 5–15%, 4 = 15–30%, 5 = >30%; share scores with KVK Dharwad for regional disease progression monitoring and variety performance benchmarking

rule_name: Combine Disease and Drought Compound Stress Yield Loss
reason: The most devastating yield loss scenario in Dharwad maize occurs when drought stress (soil moisture <40% FC) coincides with active disease pressure (humidity >80%) during grain filling (70–95 days after sowing). Drought-stressed plants have severely compromised physical and biochemical defences against all pathogen groups simultaneously. Charcoal Rot (Macrophomina), Fusarium Ear Rot, and Anthracnose Stalk Rot all intensify dramatically under simultaneous drought and humidity conditions — a paradox common in Dharwad's October monsoon withdrawal period when soil dries rapidly but ambient air remains humid. This compound stress-disease scenario causes 40–60% combined yield loss and is the most financially devastating weather-disease interaction in Dharwad maize.
actions: Immediately apply life-saving irrigation of 40–50 mm as the highest-priority action; alleviating drought stress is the single most effective intervention for reducing all disease severities simultaneously in this compound stress scenario

Apply Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/litre + Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 0.5 ml/litre combination systemic fungicide spray to cover the broadest possible disease complex — including Anthracnose, Fusarium Ear Rot, and foliar blights — with a single application

Harvest at the earliest possible physiological maturity; compound drought-disease stressed plants have dramatically accelerated stalk rot progression and standing delay beyond maturity can result in 100% harvesting loss from collapsed, rotted stalks in 10–15 days under these conditions

rule_name: Critical Irrigation Requirement at Silking Stage
reason: Silking is the single most water-sensitive stage of maize growth in Dharwad. When soil moisture drops below 45% field capacity during silk emergence (55–75 days after sowing) combined with negligible rainfall (<5 mm/day), silk desiccation occurs within 4–6 hours of peak afternoon temperature. Desiccated silks lose receptivity to pollen within 24 hours. Even a single day of severe water deficit at silk emergence can reduce kernel set by 20–40% per plant, manifesting as unfilled cob tips and missing kernel rows. In Dharwad's rain-fed tracts during monsoon breaks, this is the leading cause of Kharif maize yield loss, with economic impact of ₹8,000–15,000 per acre in high-yield potential seasons.
actions: Apply immediate life-saving irrigation of 50 mm (flood) or 4 hours of drip at full flow; this is the highest-priority irrigation event of the entire Dharwad maize crop season and must not be delayed by more than 12 hours after identifying this condition

If canal or borewell water is unavailable, use any available water source including farm pond, tanker water, or shared community water at whatever cost; the economic return from preventing kernel abortion far exceeds any water procurement cost at this stage

Schedule the next irrigation at 7–8 days after this application to maintain soil moisture above 55% FC through the completion of silking and early grain set — the 10-day window from silk emergence to kernel set is the most yield-critical irrigation window in Dharwad maize

rule_name: Waterlogging Risk Immediate Drainage Action
reason: Maize is among the most waterlogging-sensitive field crops, showing irreversible root damage after just 48 hours of complete soil saturation in Dharwad's black cotton Vertisol soils. These soils have a bulk density of 1.3–1.5 g/cm³ and very slow hydraulic conductivity (0.1–0.5 cm/hour) that prevents natural drainage. At 95%+ soil moisture for 2+ consecutive days, root zone oxygen depletion triggers anaerobic fermentation, ethanol accumulation in root cells, and rapid root cortical cell death. Nitrogen leaching and denitrification simultaneously deplete the soil nutrient supply. Each additional day of waterlogging beyond 48 hours reduces crop recovery probability by 15–20% in Dharwad's Kharif.
actions: Open emergency drainage channels immediately across the field at 3–4 m spacing using a spade; channels should be 20–25 cm deep and must connect to the field border outlet channel to allow active water removal within 6–12 hours

After drainage, do not apply any fertilizer for 5–7 days to allow root system recovery; then apply foliar urea spray (2% = 20 g per litre) to replenish nitrogen lost through denitrification during anaerobic waterlogging

Assess plant recovery at 5 days post-drainage: healthy recovery shows new leaf emergence from the whorl; plants showing no new growth after 7 days post-drainage are dead and should be removed and replaced with nursery transplants to restore stand population

rule_name: Drip Irrigation Scheduling at Grain Filling Stage
reason: Drip-irrigated maize in Dharwad during grain filling (75–100 days after sowing) requires daily or alternate-day irrigation scheduling to maintain soil moisture between 60–80% field capacity for maximum starch synthesis. When soil moisture drops to 50% FC under high temperatures (>32°C) with minimal rainfall, evapotranspiration demand in Dharwad conditions exceeds 8–10 mm/day. A drip system can typically deliver 4–6 mm/hour depending on emitter spacing and flow rate. Delays in drip scheduling under these conditions lead to kernel dehydration and reduced test weight, directly affecting market price at Hubli-Dharwad APMC.
actions: Run drip system for 3–4 hours daily (or 6–8 hours alternate days) to deliver approximately 25–30 mm per irrigation cycle; adjust run time based on emitter flow rate to achieve this volume in the wetted root zone
Fertigation of 2 kg potassium nitrate per acre per week through the drip system during grain filling maintains both water supply and potassium nutrition that supports assimilate transport to kernels

Check all drip emitters weekly during grain filling for blockage; even a 10% emitter failure rate creates soil moisture heterogeneity that results in uneven grain filling and increases average test weight variability in the harvested lot

rule_name: Pre-Sowing Soil Moisture Deficit for Rabi Season
reason: Rabi maize sowing in Dharwad (October–November) depends on residual soil moisture from the Kharif monsoon. When soil moisture at sowing is below 45% field capacity, germination is slow and uneven — seeds take 12–15 days to emerge instead of the optimal 5–7 days. This extended germination period exposes seeds to soil-borne pathogens and cold night temperatures that increase seedling stress. Below 40% soil moisture, germination is so poor that seed-to-soil contact is inadequate, leading to 20–30% non-germination. A pre-sowing irrigation to bring moisture to 65–75% FC is essential in Dharwad's Rabi season, particularly in red laterite soils that dry faster than black cotton soils after the monsoon ends.
actions: Apply pre-sowing irrigation of 40–50 mm (called 'paleva' or life irrigation) 3–5 days before intended sowing date to bring soil moisture to 65–75% FC; allow soil surface to dry to trafficable condition before sowing to prevent compaction
Sow within 48–72 hours of pre-sowing irrigation when the soil is moist but not sticky; correct sowing moisture ensures maximum seed-to-soil contact and uniform germination across the field

For Rabi maize in Dharwad's laterite soil eastern taluks (Kundgol, Navalgund), apply 50–60 mm pre-sowing irrigation as these soils have lower water-holding capacity than central Dharwad black cotton soils and dry out faster between irrigations

rule_name: Flood Irrigation Over-Watering Risk at Vegetative Stage
reason: Flood irrigation is the dominant irrigation method in Dharwad maize, practised on approximately 65% of irrigated area. Farmers frequently apply flood irrigation without considering the current rainfall and soil moisture status, leading to over-irrigation events where soil moisture exceeds 85% FC. When combined with active rainfall (>20 mm/day), flood irrigation during the vegetative stage creates transient waterlogging lasting 12–36 hours in low-lying field spots. This repeated over-irrigation causes nitrogen leaching, root compaction in furrows from water weight, and sub-optimal aeration around roots. In Dharwad, over-irrigation with flood systems wastes 30–40% of total seasonal water and reduces nitrogen use efficiency by 20–30%.
actions: Suspend flood irrigation immediately when rainfall exceeds 20 mm/day; rainfall above this threshold provides sufficient water for the vegetative stage and additional flood irrigation only creates waterlogging risk and nutrient leaching

Adopt scheduled irrigation based on soil moisture status: irrigate only when soil moisture drops below 55% FC for vegetative maize; use the simple 'feel method' — squeeze a handful of soil from 15 cm depth, if it forms a ball and leaves slight moisture impression on hand, irrigation is not yet needed

Convert flat-bed flood irrigation to ridge-and-furrow system (60 cm ridges, irrigation in alternate furrows) to reduce direct soil saturation on plant ridges and improve drainage response time, reducing over-irrigation damage in Dharwad's heavy soils

rule_name: Critical Irrigation at Tasseling Pollen Shed Stage
reason: Tasseling (approximately 50–65 days after sowing) is the second most water-sensitive stage after silking in Dharwad maize. Pollen production and viability require active photosynthesis and cell turgor that depend on adequate water supply. When soil moisture drops below 50% FC during tasseling with high maximum temperatures (>34°C) and low humidity (<50%), pollen count per tassel decreases by 30–50% and pollen viability drops from >90% to <50% within 2 days. This dramatically reduces effective pollination and kernel set. In Dharwad's Rabi season (January–March), this risk is acute when tasseling coincides with summer heating before the pre-monsoon season.
actions: Apply protective irrigation of 40–45 mm immediately at first sign of tassel emergence; timing is critical — irrigation after tassel emergence and before pollen shed provides maximum benefit and should be completed within 24 hours of identifying this risk condition

Schedule follow-up irrigation at 7 days after the first application to maintain moisture continuity through the complete tasseling-silking-early grain set window (approximately 15–18 days total duration in Dharwad conditions)

Apply light overhead sprinkler irrigation if available in the early morning (6–8 AM) during peak heat events to raise field humidity around tassels and extend pollen viability period during the critical morning pollen-shed hours

rule_name: Sprinkler Irrigation Timing Conflict with Fungal Disease
reason: Sprinkler irrigation in Dharwad maize fields, while improving water distribution uniformity, creates a significant disease promotion risk when operated under already humid conditions (>80% RH) with moderate temperatures (22–30°C). Each sprinkler irrigation event wets all leaf surfaces for 1–2 hours, extending the total daily leaf wetness period from 4–6 hours (dew only) to 8–12 hours. This extended leaf wetness during 4+ consecutive conducive weather days accelerates TLB, GLS, and Common Rust infection cycles by 40–60%, effectively halving the time to reach economic disease threshold. Farmers with sprinkler systems in Dharwad frequently operate them in the evening, creating the worst-case scenario of overnight wet leaves.
actions: Operate sprinkler irrigation only in the early morning (5–8 AM) to allow leaf surfaces to dry within 2–3 hours of sunrise; avoid evening or night sprinkler operation which creates 10–14 hours of continuous leaf wetness — the maximum disease-promotion scenario

When sustained humid weather (>80% RH for 4+ days) is predicted, switch from sprinkler to furrow or drip irrigation method for that period to eliminate the added leaf wetness that compounds natural dew-based infection risk
Apply preventive fungicide (Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/litre) before switching back to sprinkler operation after a disease-conducive humid period to re-establish protective residue on leaf surfaces

rule_name: Irrigation Skip During Active Heavy Monsoon Rainfall
reason: During active Kharif monsoon periods with 30+ mm/day rainfall for 3+ consecutive days, soil moisture in Dharwad maize fields exceeds 75% field capacity — well above the stress threshold for all growth stages. Applying scheduled irrigation during this period wastes water, labour, and energy (pump fuel costs), and actively increases waterlogging risk, particularly in heavy black cotton soils with limited drainage capacity. This is a common over-management error in Dharwad where farmers apply scheduled irrigations regardless of rainfall status, particularly for irrigated Rabi maize systems without rain-based irrigation controllers.
actions: Suspend all scheduled irrigations immediately when rainfall exceeds 30 mm/day for 3 consecutive days; resume only when soil moisture drops below 60% field capacity at 15 cm depth as assessed by the feel method

Record actual rainfall and irrigation volumes applied each week; in a normal Dharwad Kharif season (700–900 mm total rainfall), supplementary irrigation requirement for maize is typically only 2–3 irrigation events of 40–50 mm each during monsoon breaks

Calculate water savings from skipped irrigations and reinvest in soil health inputs (micronutrients, organic matter) that improve water-holding capacity and reduce future irrigation frequency requirements

rule_name: Furrow Irrigation Efficiency Loss on Sandy Soils
reason: Sandy laterite soils in Dharwad's eastern taluks (Kundgol, Navalgund, parts of Kalghatgi) have high percolation rates of 5–15 cm/hour. Furrow flood irrigation on these soils results in deep percolation losses of 40–60% of applied water before it can be absorbed laterally into the root zone. Under high temperatures (>30°C) that increase evapotranspiration demand, soil moisture in sandy Dharwad soils drops from 60% FC to stress threshold (40% FC) within 3–4 days of irrigation. Farmers compensate by increasing irrigation frequency, but deep-percolated water carries soluble nutrients (nitrate, sulfate, potassium) below the 45 cm root zone, permanently losing them from plant availability.
actions: Reduce single flood irrigation dose from typical 60–70 mm to 30–35 mm on sandy soils and increase frequency to every 5–6 days instead of every 10–12 days; smaller, more frequent applications prevent deep percolation and keep moisture in the root zone

Apply all nitrogen fertilizer as split doses of 10–12 kg urea per acre every 10 days rather than large single applications to match the faster leaching rate of sandy Dharwad soils; this improves nitrogen use efficiency from 35% to 55–60%

Consider drip irrigation conversion for sandy soil fields in Dharwad; Karnataka government's PMKSY (Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana) provides 45–55% subsidy for drip system installation; contact Dharwad DKVSSS office for application

rule_name: Emergency Irrigation During Monsoon Break at Grain Filling
reason: Kharif monsoon breaks of 8+ days during grain filling (August–October) are a recurring weather hazard in Dharwad, occurring in 3–4 out of every 10 years based on IMD historical data. When soil moisture drops to 45% FC or below during grain filling with no effective rainfall (<3 mm/day), kernel starch deposition rate decreases by 40–60%. Extended deficit above 10 days causes premature black layer formation — the plant cuts off kernel supply before maximum grain weight is achieved. Final 100-grain weight may be reduced by 20–35% from its potential, representing direct income loss of ₹5,000–12,000 per acre at Dharwad APMC market rates.
actions: Apply maximum available water immediately — 50–60 mm flood irrigation or run drip for 5–6 hours; even a single life-saving irrigation at the right moment during grain filling can restore 60–70% of the yield loss that would occur without any irrigation

Prioritise irrigation scheduling by stage: if water is limited and multiple fields need irrigation, prioritise grain-filling stage fields over vegetative-stage fields, as the yield impact per unit water applied is 3–4 times higher during grain filling

Apply 2% potassium chloride foliar spray alongside the irrigation to improve drought tolerance signalling and water use efficiency within the plant, partially compensating for the soil moisture deficit through enhanced stomatal regulation

rule_name: Irrigation Requirement for Uniform Seedling Emergence
reason: Uniform germination and emergence in Dharwad maize depends on maintaining seed zone moisture at 60–75% field capacity from sowing through emergence (days 1–8 after sowing). When soil moisture drops below 55% FC and maximum temperatures exceed 32°C in the first week after sowing, the top 5–10 cm of soil (seed zone) dries rapidly under evapotranspiration demand. Seeds that have already initiated germination and extended the radicle but encounter dry soil suffer irreversible desiccation injury that kills the emerging seedling before it reaches the surface. Patchy emergence — visible as rows with 40–60% gaps — is the primary result, reducing final plant population and yield potential.
actions: Apply a light irrigation of 20–25 mm within 4–5 days of sowing if rainfall has not occurred and soil surface is visually dry; use furrow irrigation only (no overhead sprinkler or flood) to avoid soil crusting that physically blocks seedling emergence

Never apply a heavy irrigation (>40 mm) in the first 10 days after sowing as soil crusting from the irrigation impact destroys soil capillary structure and physically prevents coleoptile emergence through the hardened crust

Monitor soil surface for crusting (light reddish-brown hard crust visible on laterite soils) 5–7 days after sowing; if crust forms before emergence, break it with a light rotary hoe pass at 3 cm depth to facilitate seedling emergence

rule_name: Over-Irrigation Nitrogen Leaching in Rabi Season
reason: Rabi maize irrigation in Dharwad on sandy soils uses borewell water that is pumped at high flow rates, frequently resulting in over-irrigation. When soil moisture exceeds 90% FC in sandy soils under flood irrigation, 30–50% of applied water passes through the root zone and carries nitrate-nitrogen below 60 cm where maize roots cannot access it. Rabi Dharwad temperatures are cooler (18–24°C average), so evapotranspiration is lower than Kharif (3–5 mm/day vs 7–10 mm/day), meaning irrigation needs are approximately 30–40% lower in Rabi than Kharif for the same crop stage. Farmers who use Kharif irrigation schedules for Rabi maize systematically over-irrigate and waste both water and fertilizer.
actions: Reduce flood irrigation dose for Rabi maize to 35–40 mm per application (versus 50–60 mm in Kharif) and extend intervals to 12–14 days (versus 8–10 days in Kharif) to match lower Rabi evapotranspiration demand in Dharwad

Apply nitrogen top-dressing (urea) only 24–48 hours before the next scheduled irrigation in Rabi season; this timing ensures nitrogen is carried into the root zone with the irrigation water rather than applied to dry soil where volatilisation risk is higher

Install a simple low-cost soil moisture indicator at 15 cm depth using a 30 cm wooden stick pushed into the soil; if soil clings to the stick when pulled out, do not irrigate; irrigate only when the stick comes out clean and dry

rule_name: Soil Moisture Deficit at Knee-High Stage Reducing LAI
reason: The knee-high stage (30–50 days after sowing) in Dharwad maize is a critical leaf area development period where 60–70% of the final canopy size is established. When soil moisture drops below 45% FC with high temperatures (>33°C), the plant's leaf expansion rate decreases by 40–60%. Leaves that do not fully expand during this window remain permanently undersized, reducing the total photosynthetically active leaf area index (LAI) for the rest of the season. Each unit reduction in final LAI from the optimal 3.5–4.0 for Dharwad conditions reduces final grain yield by approximately 8–12%. This growth stage stress also delays tasseling by 5–7 days, increasing ASI and pollination risk.
actions: Apply irrigation of 40–45 mm immediately to restore leaf expansion rate before permanent leaf development is compromised; leaf expansion responds to irrigation within 24–48 hours and partial recovery is possible if irrigation is applied before leaves mature to their final constrained size

Apply 1% urea foliar spray in addition to irrigation to stimulate rapid leaf area expansion and provide quick-access nitrogen during the recovery phase after soil moisture stress at the knee-high stage

Earthing-up (mounding soil around plant bases to 10–15 cm height) immediately after this irrigation to improve root anchorage, reduce soil temperature at the crown, and direct future irrigation water closer to the root zone

rule_name: High Evapotranspiration Demand Under Hot Dry Wind
reason: Under hot, dry wind conditions in Dharwad (common in March–April for Rabi maize and October for late Kharif), the combination of high temperature (>36°C), wind speed (>20 km/h), and low humidity (<40%) creates extreme evapotranspiration demand of 12–15 mm/day — far exceeding the 5–8 mm/day average. Soil moisture depletes from 55% FC to below stress threshold (40% FC) within 2–3 days under these conditions. The soil surface dries faster than water can move upward from subsoil, so even fields with adequate subsoil moisture show visible crop stress (leaf rolling, grey-blue colour change in leaves) within 24 hours of the wind onset.
actions: Apply irrigation of 50–55 mm immediately; under extreme evapotranspiration conditions, standard 40 mm doses are insufficient as 15–20 mm evaporates from the soil surface before reaching the root zone — apply the full 50–55 mm dose in one event

Reduce the irrigation interval from normal 8–10 days to 5–6 days during the hot-dry wind period to compensate for 2–3 times higher daily water demand; this temporary frequency increase is necessary until wind speed and temperature return to normal

Create windbreak rows (2–3 rows of sorghum or tall-growing cowpea) on the windward field boundary to reduce in-field wind speed by 30–50% and lower evapotranspiration demand, conserving irrigation water and reducing crop thermal stress

rule_name: Irrigation Requirement for Rabi Maturity Stage Grain Filling
reason: Rabi maize grain filling in Dharwad (January–March) coincides with the transition from cool winter to early summer conditions. As temperatures rise from 22°C in January to 30°C+ in March, daily water demand increases from 4–5 mm/day to 8–10 mm/day. Fields that were adequate on a 12-day irrigation cycle in January require irrigation every 8–9 days in March. Failure to adjust the irrigation schedule to the rising evapotranspiration demand leads to moisture stress during the critical starch accumulation phase, causing premature black layer formation 7–10 days early and reducing final kernel weight by 15–25% below potential. This is particularly acute for late-sown Rabi maize in Dharwad.
actions: Adjust Rabi irrigation schedule dynamically: February (12-day intervals, 40 mm dose), March (8-day intervals, 45 mm dose); do not maintain the same irrigation schedule across the entire Rabi season

Apply the final irrigation in Rabi maize at 90–95 days after sowing (just before physiological maturity); no benefit from irrigation after black layer formation, and late irrigation on near-mature grain increases Diplodia and Penicillium ear rot risk

Monitor soil moisture status by the feel method every 5 days during Rabi grain filling; in March heat, red laterite soils can reach stress threshold (40% FC) within 5–7 days of irrigation rather than the 10–12 days typical of cooler months

rule_name: Post-Sowing Light Irrigation for Seed-Zone Moisture in Rabi
reason: Even when pre-sowing irrigation brings Rabi Dharwad field soil moisture to 65–70% FC, the top 5–8 cm seed zone can dry to below germination threshold within 3–5 days if maximum temperatures exceed 30°C and no rainfall occurs. This is due to rapid surface evaporation from exposed soil between rows in the first week before seedling emergence. The seed zone moisture must remain above 55% FC continuously from sowing through coleoptile emergence to ensure uniform germination. A light post-sowing irrigation of 15–20 mm (called 'ankur paani' in local farming practice) at 3–5 days after sowing is a standard Dharwad farmer practice that improves germination uniformity significantly.
actions: Apply a light post-sowing irrigation of 15–20 mm at 3–5 days after sowing if soil surface has dried visually and no rainfall is expected; use furrow or drip irrigation to avoid soil surface disturbance and crusting from overhead watering

Do not apply more than 20 mm in this post-sowing light irrigation to avoid seed movement, soil crusting, or risk of overwatering that delays emergence by creating temporarily anaerobic conditions around the germinating seed

After seedling emergence (8–12 days after sowing in Rabi conditions), increase irrigation dose progressively with plant size: 20 mm at emergence, 30 mm at 2-leaf stage, 40 mm at 4-leaf stage, reaching full 45–50 mm doses only at knee-high stage

rule_name: Drip System Clogging Risk Under Hard Water Use
reason: Borewell water used for Rabi irrigation in Dharwad typically has high total dissolved solids (TDS) of 800–2000 ppm and elevated calcium-magnesium carbonate content due to basaltic geology of the Deccan Plateau. When drip emitters operate continuously for 30+ days with hard water, calcium carbonate deposits progressively block emitter orifices (0.8–1.2 mm diameter), reducing flow rate by 20–50%. Blocked emitters create highly uneven soil moisture distribution — some plants receive excess water while adjacent plants receive none. This uneven moisture leads to uneven plant growth, uneven tasseling dates, and variable grain filling completion, reducing overall field yield uniformity and average yield by 10–20%.
actions: Flush all drip laterals completely by opening the end caps for 5 minutes every 10 days to remove accumulated calcium-carbonate silt; this is the single most important drip maintenance task for Dharwad borewell water users

Inject dilute acid (phosphoric acid @ 2 ml per litre water, pH 5.5–6.0) through the drip system for 30 minutes once per month during continuous Rabi drip operation to dissolve calcium carbonate deposits in emitters before blockage becomes severe
Install a 120-mesh filter (screen filter) at the drip pump outlet and clean it every 15 days; filter cleaning prevents 70–80% of emitter blockage in Dharwad's hard borewell water systems

rule_name: Irrigation Cut-Off at Physiological Maturity
reason: Once maize reaches physiological maturity (black layer visible at kernel base, grain moisture 25–35%, husk beginning to dry), continued irrigation provides no additional grain yield benefit as kernel filling is biochemically complete. Irrigation after black layer formation in Dharwad conditions actively increases ear rot risk (Fusarium, Aspergillus) by maintaining high field humidity around maturing cobs. It also delays field drying, increases soil compaction risk for harvesting operations, and wastes expensive borewell water and electricity. Many Dharwad farmers continue irrigating past maturity out of habit, incurring ₹500–1,500 per acre in unnecessary irrigation costs per season.
actions: Stop all irrigation immediately once black layer is visible on kernels at the base of the cob (check 5–10 kernels from different cob positions); no further irrigation is needed or beneficial after black layer formation

Allow the field to dry naturally for 10–15 days after black layer formation before harvest; this field drying period reduces grain moisture from 28–35% to 20–25%, reducing post-harvest drying time and electricity cost

Calculate total seasonal water used for irrigation and compare to the recommended 250–300 mm for Kharif maize or 300–350 mm for Rabi maize in Dharwad; excess usage indicates over-irrigation in previous stages that should be corrected in the next season

rule_name: Insufficient Irrigation Leading to Prolonged Anthesis-Silking Interval
reason: Anthesis-Silking Interval (ASI) — the number of days between pollen shed and silk emergence — is the most diagnostic yield indicator in Dharwad maize. Under optimal conditions ASI is 1–3 days; under severe water stress (soil moisture <40% FC for 6+ days during 52–70 days after sowing), ASI increases to 7–14 days. This temporal mismatch means pollen has finished shedding before silks are receptive, or silks emerge but pollen viability has already declined. An ASI above 5 days in Dharwad conditions reduces kernel set by 30–60%. Prolonged ASI is observable to a trained farmer as tassels that appear brown and spent while silks are still fresh green.
actions: Apply life-saving irrigation of 50–60 mm immediately without any delay; restoring soil moisture to 65–70% FC within 24 hours of detecting this condition can partially restore ASI synchrony if irrigation occurs before tassel shed is complete

Monitor tassel pollen shed daily: fresh pollen is yellow powder visible on tassel branches and on upper leaf surfaces; if pollen shed has already ended but silks are still white (fresh), hand-collect pollen from adjacent well-irrigated plots and apply to silks to salvage kernel set

Document the ASI event with date and soil moisture readings; fields with recurring ASI problems indicate systematic irrigation scheduling failure or water supply limitation requiring infrastructure investment (borewell deepening, farm pond, drip conversion)

rule_name: Black Cotton Soil Cracking and Irrigation Loss
reason: Dharwad's black cotton Vertisol soils shrink dramatically during dry periods, developing vertical cracks 2–5 cm wide and 20–50 cm deep when soil moisture drops below 30% FC. These shrinkage cracks dramatically reduce irrigation efficiency: when flood irrigation is applied to severely cracked Vertisol fields, 40–60% of irrigation water flows directly into the cracks and percolates to below the root zone without any plant-available benefit. Additionally, cracks in the 10–20 cm root zone can physically tear and break maize root systems, directly damaging plant water and nutrient uptake capacity. This soil-crack irrigation efficiency problem is unique to Dharwad's Vertisol farming areas.
actions: Do not apply full-dose flood irrigation directly into severely cracked soil as most water will be lost through cracks; instead apply 2 small irrigations of 25 mm each with a 12-hour gap to allow gradual crack closure before applying the full moisture dose

Apply a surface mulch of dry maize stover, sorghum straw, or sugarcane trash @ 3–4 tonnes/acre between rows to slow surface evaporation and prevent crack development during dry spells; mulched fields maintain soil moisture 15–25% higher than bare soil under the same conditions

In fields prone to cracking, irrigate before soil moisture drops below 40% FC to prevent crack development; crack prevention costs less than the water efficiency losses that occur once cracks exceed 2 cm width

rule_name: Pre-Tasseling Irrigation Boost for Maximum Cob Development
reason: The 10-day window immediately before tassel emergence (approximately 40–52 days after sowing in Dharwad maize) is the period of maximum cob primordia development. During this phase, the number of rows of kernels per cob and the number of potential kernel sites per row are determined and are highly sensitive to water availability. When soil moisture is below 55% FC during this pre-tasseling window, kernel rows per cob are reduced from the variety's potential (14–16 rows) to 10–12 rows, and kernel site number per row decreases by 15–25%. These reductions in cob architecture are permanent and set the upper limit for final grain yield regardless of how well conditions improve later.
actions: Apply a full-dose irrigation of 45–50 mm at 40–45 days after sowing as a standard agronomic practice even in years with reasonable rainfall, to ensure maximum cob architecture development during this critical 10-day window

Time this pre-tasseling irrigation to coincide with the planned second or third nitrogen top-dress application (30–40 days after sowing) so that the applied urea is immediately carried into the root zone by the irrigation water, maximising nitrogen availability for cob development

Record the number of kernel rows on 10 harvested cobs at maturity each season to assess whether pre-tasseling irrigation was adequate; 14+ rows per cob indicates good water management during this window, while less than 12 rows consistently indicates pre-tasseling water stress requiring irrigation schedule adjustment

rule_name: Rainfed Field Irrigation Decision During Monsoon Break
reason: Approximately 45% of Dharwad district's maize area is rain-fed without access to well or canal irrigation. During August–September monsoon breaks (7–20 days), these rain-fed fields depend entirely on stored soil moisture. When a monsoon break of 12+ days occurs and soil moisture depletes below 40% FC during tasseling, silking, or grain filling, there is no irrigation option for most rain-fed farmers. However, for the minority of rain-fed farmers with emergency access to a shared borewell, tanker water, or water harvesting pond, making the correct decision about when a monsoon break is severe enough to justify emergency water procurement is critical for yield protection.
