actions: Contact local village panchayat or water user association immediately for shared borewell or tanker water access if soil moisture is below 40% FC for 5+ days during tasseling or silking; even a single emergency irrigation of 30–40 mm during this window can prevent 25–35% yield loss

For completely rain-fed fields without any irrigation access, apply foliar spray of 2% potassium chloride to improve drought tolerance and delay leaf rolling under moisture deficit, partially sustaining photosynthesis and pollen viability

File for PMFBY crop insurance yield loss claim if the monsoon break exceeds 15 days during tasseling-silking; document soil crack status, leaf rolling intensity, and approximate percentage of non-receptive silks for insurance assessor documentation

rule_name: Excess Irrigation Promoting Weed Flush After Application
reason: Flood irrigation in Dharwad maize fields during the first 5–25 days after sowing creates a moist seedbed that promotes germination of weed seeds throughout the field. Excess irrigation (>80% soil moisture) in this early period stimulates the weed seed bank — particularly Parthenium hysterophorus (congress grass), Cyperus rotundus (nutsedge), and Echinochloa species — to germinate and emerge rapidly in between the maize rows. These weeds, if not controlled within the first 30 days, can reduce maize yields by 30–60% through direct competition for water, nutrients, and light. The irrigation-weed flush interaction in Dharwad's weed-seed-rich Kharif soils is a compounding productivity challenge.
actions: Apply pre-emergence herbicide (Atrazine 50 WP @ 1 kg a.i./acre in 200 litres water) within 2–3 days after planting and before first irrigation to establish a chemical weed barrier that will persist through the first irrigation and prevent the weed germination flush

Schedule first post-sowing irrigation precisely at 5–6 days after sowing to coincide with maize seed germination timing; early maize establishment before weeds reach the 2-leaf stage provides competitive advantage that reduces later weed management need

Conduct first inter-row weeding by hoe within 10–12 days after irrigation-triggered weed flush; catching weeds at the white-thread (2-leaf) stage requires 50–60% less labour than waiting for weeds to establish at 4–6 leaf stage

rule_name: Borewell Water Temperature Stress on Young Roots
reason: Borewell water in Dharwad's deep aquifers (60–150 m depth) maintains a near-constant temperature of 24–28°C year-round. When this relatively warm water is applied to cold Rabi season soil (soil temperature 12–16°C in December–January) through drip emitters, it initially creates thermal contrast stress on young maize roots. However, the primary concern in very cold Rabi nights (min temp <15°C) is that drip-irrigated soil cools rapidly overnight, and young seedling roots in drip-wetted zones experience rapid temperature cycling that reduces root enzyme activity and impairs nutrient uptake. This subtle root stress contributes to the 'Rabi check' — a period of apparent growth stagnation in December–January Dharwad Rabi maize.
actions: Operate drip irrigation only in the morning hours (8 AM to 12 PM) during cold Rabi winter periods to allow the soil warming benefit of midday sun before the drip adds additional moisture that cools through overnight evapotranspiration

Reduce drip run time in December–January by 25% compared to the calculated requirement, as cold Rabi soil temperature reduces plant water demand to 60–70% of the calculated reference evapotranspiration; over-watering cold soils increases disease risk without growth benefit

Apply 5 g/litre seaweed extract solution as a foliar spray during the December–January cold period to stimulate root growth hormones (cytokinins) that partially compensate for the cold-induced suppression of root metabolic activity

rule_name: Irrigation Scheduling for Maximum Fertilizer Uptake Efficiency
reason: Nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium uptake from soil is maximised when soil moisture is at 60–75% field capacity with temperatures of 24–30°C. This is the optimal root activity window in Dharwad maize during the Kharif vegetative phase. Irrigation that brings soil moisture to 65–70% FC applied 24–48 hours before or at the time of top-dress fertilizer application provides the most efficient nutrient delivery. The active water transport in the soil-root system under this moisture-temperature combination moves nutrients to root surfaces via mass flow at the highest rate, with nitrogen use efficiency reaching 55–65% compared to 30–40% when fertilizer is applied to dry or waterlogged soil.
actions: Time top-dress urea applications (at 20–25 days and 40–45 days after sowing) to coincide with or immediately before an irrigation event that brings soil to 65–70% FC; this single scheduling change can improve urea nitrogen use efficiency by 20–30%

Apply the urea top-dress in the soil moisture range of 50–65% FC (not below 40% FC where it risks volatilisation, not above 80% FC where leaching dominates), then irrigate to bring moisture to 65–70% FC within 24 hours

Incorporate urea 3–5 cm deep in inter-row soil using a hoe rather than broadcasting on the surface; soil-incorporated urea reaches the active root zone 3–4 days faster with less volatilisation loss, especially important in the 24–30°C Kharif conditions of Dharwad

rule_name: Sprinkler System Pressure Drop Reducing Coverage Uniformity
reason: Sprinkler irrigation systems in Dharwad maize perform poorly under high wind speed conditions. At wind speeds above 20 km/h, water droplets from sprinkler heads are deflected downwind, creating a highly uneven moisture distribution pattern where the windward side of each sprinkler circle receives 150–200% of the designed dose and the downwind side receives only 40–60% of the designed dose. Under high temperature (>33°C), evaporative losses from the water jet increase by 15–25% before the droplets reach the soil surface. Together these factors can create severe within-field soil moisture variability of 30–50%, leading to patchy crop response with some plants over-watered and others stressed.
actions: Operate sprinkler systems only when wind speed is below 15 km/h, typically early morning (5–8 AM) or late evening (6–8 PM) in Dharwad; avoid operating sprinklers during peak afternoon winds common in pre-monsoon and post-monsoon transition periods

In high-wind periods, increase sprinkler system operating pressure by 10–15% (if pump capacity allows) to compensate for wind drift; smaller droplets at lower pressure are more affected by wind than larger droplets at higher pressure

For fields with persistent high-wind problems, consider converting to micro-sprinklers or drip irrigation for the most water-sensitive crop stages (tasseling and grain filling) where coverage uniformity is critical to yield

rule_name: Night Irrigation for Temperature Management at Tasseling
reason: When both maximum (>36°C) and minimum (>26°C) temperatures are elevated during tasseling in Dharwad conditions (typical of late Rabi and early summer), the 24-hour heat accumulation reduces pollen viability throughout the day. Sprinkler irrigation operated at night (10 PM to 2 AM) or very early morning provides evaporative cooling that can reduce crop canopy temperature by 3–5°C during the critical pre-dawn and early morning pollen shed hours (7–10 AM). This is a practical precision irrigation application specific to heated-tasseling conditions in Dharwad's irrigated Rabi and late-Kharif maize systems that can meaningfully improve pollination success under heat stress.
actions: Operate sprinkler irrigation in two short cycles: 10 PM to 11 PM and 4 AM to 5 AM during high-temperature tasseling events to maintain crop canopy moisture and cool the microclimate around tassels during peak pollen shed hours

Do not operate sprinklers between 11 AM to 4 PM during high-temperature tasseling days as daytime evaporative demand consumes water before it benefits the crop and the elevated humidity from daytime sprinkler operation increases fungal disease risk

Reduce night irrigation dose to 15–20 mm per cycle (not the full dose) to avoid waterlogging and early morning field ponding that increases disease risk; the primary goal of night irrigation is temperature management, not full moisture replacement

rule_name: Irrigation Scheduling Adjustment Post Heavy Rainfall Event
reason: After heavy rainfall events (50+ mm/day for 2+ days) in Dharwad, Kharif season soil moisture is replenished to near or above field capacity for most soil types. Resuming scheduled irrigations within 5 days of such events is agronomically unnecessary and economically wasteful. In Dharwad's borewell-dependent irrigation systems, each unnecessary irrigation costs ₹150–400 per acre in electricity and labour costs. Scientifically, post-heavy-rain irrigation increases soil saturation, promotes root zone anaerobiosis, and increases nitrogen leaching, all of which reduce crop productivity rather than improving it. Adjusting irrigation schedule post-rainfall is a simple practice that reduces input costs without any yield penalty.
actions: Reset the irrigation clock after any rainfall event above 25 mm and calculate days to next irrigation based on estimated daily soil moisture depletion; the next irrigation should be applied only when soil moisture drops to 55% FC, not on a fixed calendar schedule

Maintain a simple rain gauge (low-cost, ₹150–300 from agricultural stores in Dharwad market) to record daily rainfall; track cumulative rain and subtract from planned irrigation schedule to avoid over-irrigation during active monsoon periods

Share rainfall data with neighbouring farmers in the hobli to coordinate irrigation schedule adjustments at the village level; collective irrigation schedule management from shared water sources (tanks, canals) significantly improves water use efficiency across Dharwad's farming community

rule_name: Soil Moisture at Optimal Level for Herbicide Activation
reason: Pre-emergence herbicides used in Dharwad maize (Atrazine 50 WP, Pendimethalin 30 EC) require soil moisture of 55–75% FC and temperatures of 22–30°C for optimal activation and formation of the herbicidal soil barrier. These herbicides work by binding to soil organic matter and clay particles while remaining in the soil solution in sufficient concentration to kill germinating weed seeds. When soil moisture is below 50% FC, the herbicide binds excessively to dry soil particles and the effective soil solution concentration drops below the herbicidal threshold. When moisture exceeds 80% FC, herbicides leach below the weed germination zone (top 2–3 cm). The irrigation management around herbicide application thus directly determines weed control efficacy.
actions: Apply pre-emergence herbicide within 2–3 days after sowing when soil surface moisture is 55–75% FC; if soil is too dry, apply a very light 10–15 mm irrigation 24 hours before herbicide application to bring moisture to the optimal range for herbicide activation

Do not apply any irrigation for 5–7 days after pre-emergence herbicide application to avoid disturbing the herbicidal soil crust; subsequent irrigation or rainfall should be light (<25 mm) to maintain the barrier without leaching

Apply Pendimethalin 30 EC @ 1 litre/acre in 200 litres water as an alternative to Atrazine when sorghum is grown as a subsequent crop in the rotation, since Atrazine has soil persistence that can damage sorghum if the rotation interval is less than 12 months

rule_name: Deficit Irrigation Strategy for Rain-Fed Fields with Limited Water
reason: In Dharwad's dryland maize areas with limited irrigation infrastructure, the total available water from a shallow well or small farm pond may be insufficient to apply full recommended doses (45–50 mm) across the entire maize area during monsoon breaks. Deficit irrigation strategy — applying 50–60% of the full recommended dose precisely at the most critical crop stages — is scientifically proven to produce 75–85% of the yield possible with full irrigation. Specifically, prioritising 25–30 mm at silking-tasseling under deficit conditions produces far higher returns per unit water than spreading the same water equally across all field areas at inadequate doses.
actions: Under water scarcity, concentrate all available irrigation water on the portion of the field at silking or tasseling stage; a 25–30 mm application on 2 acres at tasseling produces more yield than a 12–15 mm application spread across 4 acres

Use alternate furrow irrigation technique (irrigate every other furrow instead of all furrows) to reduce water use per acre by 40–50% while maintaining 70–80% of the yield benefit; this doubles the area that can receive life-saving irrigation from limited water sources

In future seasons, create farm ponds (minimum 400 m³ capacity per acre of maize) during the pre-monsoon period to harvest monsoon runoff for storage as emergency tasseling-silking irrigation; KSRSAC/KVK Dharwad provides farm pond design templates and NABARD provides financial assistance

rule_name: Saline Irrigation Water Risk During Rabi Season
reason: Rabi season borewells in Dharwad's older geological formations (particularly in Hubli and Kundgol taluks) show increasing salinity as water tables drop in the dry season. Continuous flood irrigation of black cotton soil with moderately saline borewell water (EC 2–4 dS/m) over 45+ days accumulates salts in the upper 30 cm soil profile. Maize is moderately salt-sensitive with yield reduction beginning at soil EC above 1.7 dS/m. In Dharwad's heavy Vertisol soils with limited natural leaching, salt accumulation from Rabi irrigation can reduce yield by 10–25% and create long-term soil degradation that affects subsequent Kharif crops as well.
actions: Apply a leaching irrigation of 80–100 mm (double the normal dose) once every 30 days in Rabi season to flush accumulated salts below the root zone; this leaching event prevents salt build-up and maintains soil EC below the maize tolerance threshold

Observe leaf margins on older leaves for salt stress symptoms (brown scorched margins, called 'salt burn'); if this appears in the middle of a Rabi crop, apply a single heavy leaching irrigation immediately and supplement with 0.5% potassium chloride foliar spray to improve ion balance

Test borewell water EC once per year (before Rabi sowing) at the nearest UAS Dharwad soil testing laboratory (free service for district farmers); if EC exceeds 2.0 dS/m, plan mandatory leaching irrigations in the schedule from season start

rule_name: Post-Lodging Irrigation Management for Recovery
reason: After wind-induced lodging events in Dharwad Kharif maize, many farmers instinctively apply irrigation in an attempt to 'help the crop recover.' However, irrigating lodged maize when soil moisture is already above 75% FC further saturates the already-wet soil that caused weak root anchorage leading to lodging. This additional irrigation worsens lodging extent by keeping the soil in the plastic state that prevents fallen plants from re-anchoring. In contrast, allowing some soil drying (to 55–60% FC) after a lodging event enables soil firming around exposed roots and allows earthing-up operations to re-support fallen plants.
actions: Suspend all irrigation for 5–7 days after a lodging event when soil moisture is above 75% FC; allow soil to firm and drain naturally before any recovery management operations

Once soil firms to trafficable state (55–65% FC), conduct earthing-up on lodged plants that are still alive: push soil around exposed roots and mound 10–15 cm of soil at the plant base to provide mechanical support and encourage adventitious root development

After earthing-up, resume normal irrigation at reduced dose of 30–35 mm (not full 45–50 mm) to establish new adventitious root growth without creating the wet conditions that caused the original lodging; increase dose progressively over 2–3 irrigations

rule_name: Canal Water Availability Coordination at Critical Stages
reason: Parts of Dharwad district have access to Malaprabha and Tungabhadra Left Bank Canal (TLBC) irrigation systems. Canal water availability is scheduled in rotation turns ('warabandhi') that may not coincide with the crop's critical irrigation needs during tasseling-silking. When a farmer's scheduled turn falls 5–8 days before the critical silking window, this is insufficient as soil moisture will have depleted to stress levels by silking time. Equally, if a turn falls during or after silk desiccation has begun, the irrigation provides reduced benefit. Proactive coordination with the canal division 10–14 days in advance is essential for critical-stage irrigation with canal systems.
actions: Determine the expected tasseling date (standard day 50–55 after sowing for most Dharwad Kharif varieties) at the time of sowing and immediately inform the canal division to request a warabandhi turn in days 48–55 after sowing; advance notice of 14+ days is required for warabandhi adjustments in Dharwad canal systems

Maintain a small (100–200 m³) farm pond or storage tank to bridge the gap if canal turn does not coincide precisely with the critical tasseling-silking window; even 25–30 mm from stored water during this window can prevent the worst pollination failure

Document all canal water turn requests, scheduled dates, and actual dates received for the season; data on irrigation delivery reliability can support farmer collective bargaining with the irrigation department for priority scheduling of Kharif critical stage water turns

rule_name: Excess Moisture Before Harvest Affecting Grain Quality
reason: High soil moisture (>75% FC) combined with high ambient humidity (>80% RH) at harvest time in Dharwad creates multiple grain quality risks. Physically, wet field conditions prevent mechanical harvester entry, forcing hand harvesting which is 3–4 times more expensive. Grain harvested from high-moisture field conditions absorbs surface moisture rapidly, requiring longer and more expensive drying. Biochemically, mature kernels in high-humidity, warm conditions recommence enzymatic activity, reducing starch quality and dry matter percentage. For seed corn production (common in Dharwad KMSSCL contract farming), excess moisture at harvest critically reduces germination percentage of the seed lot.
actions: Stop irrigation at black layer formation (approximately 98–105 days after sowing) and allow 10–15 days of field drying before harvest; this drying period reduces grain moisture from 28–32% to 20–24%, significantly reducing post-harvest drying cost and disease risk

Harvest during the driest part of the day (11 AM to 3 PM) when surface soil and husk moisture are lowest; morning harvesting of maize with dew on husks increases measured grain moisture by 2–3 percentage points compared to afternoon harvesting

For seed corn production in Dharwad's KMSSCL contract cultivation, stop irrigation 20–25 days before planned harvest date (earlier than grain corn cutoff) to accelerate field drying and achieve seed moisture below 20% at harvest, which is the target for safe seed processing

rule_name: Drip Fertigation Scheduling During Grain Filling
reason: Drip fertigation during grain filling in Dharwad maize is the most efficient method for delivering both water and potassium to the active root zone simultaneously. Grain filling requires 1.5–2 kg potassium per tonne of grain produced; a 5 tonne/acre yield target requires delivery of 7.5–10 kg K₂O/acre during grain filling alone. Conventional soil applications of potassium fertilizer are limited by the low mobility of potassium in soil (diffusion-dominated, <1 cm/day). Drip fertigation places dissolved potassium directly in the root zone with each irrigation event, achieving 3–4 times higher potassium uptake efficiency versus soil broadcast application during grain filling when root system activity is still high.
actions: Fertigate soluble potassium (potassium nitrate 13-0-45 @ 1.5 kg/acre or potassium sulfate @ 1 kg/acre) through the drip system in each irrigation event from 70 to 90 days after sowing to sustain potassium supply during the peak grain filling demand period

Maintain a drip run time of 3–4 hours daily during grain filling (30–35 mm per irrigation event per 2 days) to sustain root zone moisture at 60–70% FC; do not reduce irrigation frequency below alternate-day schedule during grain filling even when temperatures are mild

Flush the drip system with clean water for 30 minutes after each fertigation session to prevent salt crystallisation from evaporation of concentrated fertilizer solution at emitter orifices, which is the primary emitter blockage mechanism in fertigation systems

rule_name: Irrigation After Fertilizer Application on Dry Soil
reason: In Dharwad, top-dress urea applications are often made on dry soil during inter-cultivation, particularly in May-June before Kharif onset or between monsoon break periods. When urea is applied on soil with moisture below 40% FC and temperatures above 32°C, urease enzyme activity hydrolyses urea to ammonium and then ammonia (NH₃) within 2–4 days. Without subsequent irrigation to carry the resulting ammonium into the soil, up to 40–60% of surface-broadcast urea nitrogen volatilises as NH₃ gas into the atmosphere within a week, representing a complete waste of the applied fertilizer. This nitrogen volatilisation from dry-soil urea application is one of the largest avoidable input losses in Dharwad maize farming.
actions: Apply irrigation of 30–35 mm within 24–48 hours of urea top-dressing to dissolve and move the urea into the root zone before ammonia volatilisation can occur; this single practice can improve urea nitrogen recovery by 25–35%

If irrigation cannot be applied within 48 hours of urea application due to water unavailability, do not apply urea on dry, hot soil; defer urea application until either rain is forecast within 48 hours or irrigation can be scheduled

Use neem-coated urea (NCU) in place of plain urea when immediate incorporation irrigation cannot be guaranteed; the neem oil coating slows urease activity by 20–30%, extending the safe window between urea application and irrigation/rainfall to 5–7 days under Dharwad's high-temperature conditions

rule_name: Irrigation Duration Calibration for Flood Irrigation on Heavy Soils
reason: Black cotton Vertisol soils in Dharwad have a slow steady-state infiltration rate of 0.5–1.5 cm/hour after initial rapid infiltration in the first 30 minutes. A common farmer error is to allow flood irrigation to flow for 3–4 hours (applying 150–200 mm) because visual observation of water movement on the surface suggests insufficient coverage. In reality, a 2-hour flood irrigation on moist black cotton soil delivers 40–60 mm of actual infiltrated water — approximately the correct dose. Excess water beyond the soil's field capacity has no beneficial effect and contributes to waterlogging, nutrient leaching, and surface compaction when the flood recedes.
actions: Calibrate flood irrigation duration by measuring water intake: after each irrigation event, check if water is standing 24 hours later; if standing water persists for more than 12 hours post-irrigation on heavy soils, the irrigation duration was 30–40% too long

Reduce flood irrigation run time to 60–90 minutes for black cotton soils at 50–60% soil moisture FC; this delivers the correct 40–50 mm dose without overloading the soil's infiltration capacity and creating waterlogging

Use field length and width measurements to estimate actual applied water: for a 1-acre field (4047 m²), a 50 mm irrigation dose requires 200,000 litres of water; if your pump delivers 50,000 litres/hour, run time should be 4 hours total for the entire acre, not per row

rule_name: Soil Moisture Monitoring for Transition from Vegetative to Reproductive Stage
reason: The transition from vegetative to reproductive stage in Dharwad maize (approximately 45–55 days after sowing) is a critical monitoring window where good soil moisture management (55–70% FC) lays the foundation for maximum tassel and silk development. Maintaining this optimal moisture range during the transition phase ensures uniform tassel emergence, high pollen count per tassel, and full silk development. This is also the last practical window for soil-applied interventions (earthing-up, fertilizer incorporation, herbicide spot treatments) before canopy closure makes field entry difficult. In Dharwad's irrigated maize systems, this is the planning window for the critical tasseling-silking irrigation schedule.
actions: Apply irrigation to bring soil moisture to 65–70% FC at 45–48 days after sowing as a preparatory irrigation before the tasseling-silking critical window; this 'charging' irrigation ensures the crop enters the most critical reproductive stage with full moisture reserves

Take final soil moisture assessment and plan next 3 irrigation events: at approximately 52 days (tasseling start), 62 days (silking), and 72 days (early grain fill); having these dates planned and water source confirmed prevents last-minute failures during the critical window

Complete all mechanical operations (final earthing-up, last inter-row cultivation) before 50 days after sowing; entry into the field after canopy closure (55–60 days after sowing) causes significant physical damage to tassels, silks, and leaves that cannot be corrected

rule_name: Subsurface Drip Irrigation Placement Depth for Black Cotton Soils
reason: Drip irrigation on Dharwad's black cotton Vertisol soils presents unique challenges for water distribution due to the soil's swelling-shrinking nature. When drip laterals are placed at the surface on Vertisol soils with moisture below 55% FC (shrinkage phase), soil cracks 1–3 cm wide can bypass the emitter placement and create preferential flow paths that move water to deeper soil layers inefficiently. Placing drip laterals at 10–15 cm depth in Vertisol soils keeps emitters within the more stable subsoil zone below the active cracking layer, improving water distribution uniformity and reducing emitter exposure to surface UV degradation.
actions: Bury drip laterals at 10–12 cm depth in black cotton soil maize fields during installation to place emitters below the primary shrinkage cracking layer; use a sub-surface drip laying machine available through Dharwad DKVSSS cooperative for correct depth placement

Apply an initial wetting irrigation of 30 mm through the drip system before the first crop-cycle irrigation to close active soil cracks around the buried laterals before the main irrigation season begins; crack closure around emitters improves lateral water distribution by 25–35%

Inspect buried drip laterals annually before each season by excavating 3–5 random points per acre to check for root intrusion blockage; apply anti-root intrusion chemicals (Treflan® emulsifiable concentrate) through the drip system once per season to prevent root blockage of buried emitters

rule_name: Water Stress Index During Maximum Vegetative Growth
reason: The maximum vegetative growth period (25–50 days after sowing) in Dharwad maize is driven by high photosynthesis and rapid cell division in leaf, stem, and root meristems. When soil moisture drops below 40% FC while maximum temperatures exceed 34°C and humidity is below 50%, the crop exhibits both cellular dehydration (leaf rolling within 2 hours of morning) and stomatal closure that reduces CO₂ uptake and photosynthesis by 50–70%. Leaf rolling visible by 9–10 AM in Dharwad summer conditions is a clear field diagnostic of water stress at this stage. Extended stress (5+ days) during this period permanently reduces leaf area index and stalk diameter, reducing yield ceiling by 15–25%.
actions: Apply irrigation of 45–50 mm immediately when leaf rolling is visible by 10 AM on more than 30% of plants; leaf rolling by 10 AM (not the normal afternoon rolling that recovers after sunset) indicates permanent stress that requires immediate irrigation response

Apply 2% potassium chloride foliar spray simultaneously with irrigation scheduling to partially restore cell turgor through osmotic adjustment mechanisms, reducing the window of photosynthesis shutdown during the irrigation delay period

Monitor stalk girth at knee height (20 cm above ground) on 10 random plants every 10 days; stalk girth below 2.5 cm at 50 days after sowing indicates severe vegetative stress and predicts final grain yield below 3.5 tonnes per acre regardless of subsequent management

rule_name: Rainfall Uncertainty and Irrigation Pre-Planning for Kharif
reason: Dharwad's Kharif season rainfall is highly variable year-to-year (600–1100 mm total) with unpredictable monsoon break frequency and duration. At the time of Kharif sowing, farmers must pre-plan irrigation capacity for the 3 most critical windows (knee-high, tasseling, and grain filling). An irrigated Kharif maize crop in a dry year (600–700 mm rainfall) requires 2–3 supplementary irrigation events of 40–50 mm each at critical stages. A farmer who sows without confirming irrigation availability for tasseling-silking is taking an unnecessary risk that can result in complete yield loss in monsoon-break years. Pre-sowing irrigation planning is the most cost-effective risk management action available.
actions: Before Kharif sowing, confirm borewell water yield: pump for 4 hours continuously and verify water is still available; borewells that fail after 2–3 hours of continuous pumping cannot reliably supply tasseling-silking irrigation and alternative water sourcing plans must be made

For rain-fed maize fields without any irrigation access, consider constructing a minimum 200 m³ farm pond (sub-surface masonry type) with NABARD financial assistance to store monsoon runoff for 1–2 life-saving irrigations at critical stages

Join the local Dharwad district irrigation water users' association or maize farmers' cooperative to get advance information on canal water rotation schedule and register for priority tasseling-stage water turns before the Kharif season begins

rule_name: Sprinkler Wetting Pattern Check on Sandy Loam Soils
reason: Sprinkler irrigation on Dharwad's sandy laterite soils produces deep percolation losses if application rate exceeds the soil infiltration rate. The standard sprinkler head application rate of 8–12 mm/hour typically matches or slightly exceeds the infiltration rate of sandy Dharwad soils (10–20 mm/hour when dry, but falling to 2–5 mm/hour after 30 minutes of wetting due to surface sealing). This sealing on sandy soils creates surface ponding and runoff even under sprinkler application, reducing effective water penetration. If the wetting front from a 2-hour sprinkler run does not reach 25–30 cm depth in sandy Dharwad soils, the root zone is not receiving adequate water despite visual surface coverage.
actions: Test sprinkler irrigation penetration depth after each full irrigation event by inserting a metal rod (1 cm diameter) into the soil at 3–4 locations across the sprinkler coverage zone; resistance to rod insertion disappears at the wet-dry boundary, indicating actual wetting front depth

If wetting front depth is less than 20 cm after 2-hour sprinkler run, increase run time by 30–45 minutes and retest in 3 locations; sandy soils require longer run times due to seal development but benefit from intermittent operation (1 hour on, 30 minutes off) to allow infiltration before runoff develops

Apply gypsum @ 200 kg/acre on sandy laterite soils with surface sealing problems before the crop season to improve soil aggregate stability and increase the sustained infiltration rate under sprinkler application

rule_name: Irrigation Requirement Increase at High Plant Density
reason: Modern hybrid maize cultivation in Dharwad increasingly uses higher plant densities (27,000–30,000 plants/acre versus traditional 20,000–22,000 plants/acre) to maximise yield. Higher density creates 25–35% greater total crop water demand per acre, as each additional plant contributes its full transpiration demand. Under standard irrigation schedules designed for lower densities, high-density Dharwad maize reaches moisture stress 2–3 days earlier than the scheduled irrigation date, particularly under temperatures above 33°C. Farmers who adopt high-density planting without adjusting irrigation scheduling frequency consistently underperform the yield potential of high-density hybrids due to unrecognised moisture deficit in the critical vegetative and reproductive stages.
actions: Reduce irrigation interval by 2–3 days and increase dose by 5–8 mm (total 50–55 mm vs 45 mm) when plant density is above 27,000 plants per acre; the additional irrigation cost of ₹200–400 per acre per season is more than recovered through the higher yield enabled by high-density planting

Monitor soil moisture more frequently (every 4–5 days instead of every 7–8 days) after knee-high stage in high-density plantings; apply irrigation as soon as soil moisture drops to 55% FC rather than waiting until the scheduled date

Apply additional organic matter (compost or FYM @ 5 tonnes/acre) in high-density fields to improve soil water-holding capacity; soils with higher organic matter content buffer moisture depletion rate, reducing the irrigation frequency increase needed for high-density management

rule_name: Irrigation Efficiency Benchmark for Dharwad Seasonal Water Budget
reason: Rabi maize in Dharwad under flood irrigation typically requires 5–6 irrigation events totalling 250–330 mm of applied water over the full 110-day season. The optimal irrigation budget for different Dharwad soil types is: black cotton soil (5 irrigations × 50 mm = 250 mm), red laterite soil (6 irrigations × 50–55 mm = 300–330 mm). Farmers who apply more than 350 mm total in a Rabi season are over-irrigating, reducing nitrogen use efficiency and increasing crop disease risk. Farmers who apply less than 200 mm without adequate rainfall compensation are under-irrigating and limiting yield below achievable potential. A seasonal water budget provides the framework for cost-effective Rabi maize irrigation management in Dharwad.
actions: Plan the seasonal irrigation schedule before Rabi sowing: identify 5–6 irrigation windows at approximately 0 (pre-sow), 20, 35, 50, 65, and 85 days after sowing; schedule borewell operation and canal water turns around these dates 2–3 weeks in advance

Track cumulative irrigation applied using a simple notebook record; if cumulative irrigation exceeds 280 mm before 85 days after sowing for black cotton soil, assess whether late-season (85–100 day) irrigation is needed or whether natural rainfall has supplemented the budget

Calculate seasonal cost of irrigation per quintal of production: if spending more than ₹400 per quintal on irrigation alone (electricity + labour), the irrigation schedule is inefficient and drip irrigation conversion may be economically justified for Dharwad conditions at current electricity rates

rule_name: High Soil Moisture Restricting Root Zone Aeration at Seedling Stage
reason: Maize seedlings at 10–20 days after sowing have shallow root systems (10–15 cm depth) that are entirely dependent on the topsoil oxygen supply. When soil moisture exceeds 88% FC in the topsoil under warm conditions (26–34°C), oxygen diffusion to roots is insufficient to maintain aerobic root respiration. Seedlings show growth stagnation, purple leaf discolouration (phosphorus deficiency from impaired P uptake under anaerobic roots), and susceptibility to damping-off pathogens. In Dharwad's Kharif season, this condition is frequently created by over-enthusiastic irrigation applications in the first 2–3 weeks by farmers who fear drought but inadvertently create waterlogging at the seedling stage.
actions: Suspend all irrigation immediately and allow natural drainage and soil drying to reduce moisture to 65–70% FC; even 3–5 days of drying with no irrigation is beneficial for seedling recovery at this stage

Apply a small dose of Trichoderma viride @ 2.5 kg/acre as a soil drench after partial drainage to suppress opportunistic damping-off pathogens that colonise stressed seedling roots in the excess moisture zone

After soil drains to 65% FC, check all seedlings for recovery: healthy seedlings show new leaf unfurling from the whorl within 5 days of drainage; purple-coloured seedlings showing no new growth after 7 days of drainage are permanently damaged and should be replaced

rule_name: Irrigation to Support Earthing-Up and Topdress Incorporation
reason: Earthing-up (hilling soil around the base of maize plants) is a critical cultural operation at 28–40 days after sowing in Dharwad that provides mechanical support against lodging, covers surface-applied urea to reduce volatilisation, and severs horizontal weed roots. On black cotton Vertisol soils, effective earthing-up requires soil moisture of 45–60% FC — soil that is dry below 40% FC is cloddy and does not mould properly around plant bases, leaving air gaps that provide no support. Irrigating 48–72 hours before planned earthing-up softens the black cotton soil to the perfect plastic-moist state for earthing-up, ensuring a quality mound structure that provides root anchorage.
actions: Apply 25–30 mm irrigation 2–3 days before planned earthing-up operation on black cotton soils; this preparation irrigation brings soil to the ideal plastic-moist condition for forming firm earthing-up mounds at 12–15 cm height

Perform earthing-up immediately after topdress urea application (at 30–35 days after sowing); the hilling operation physically covers surface-applied urea with 5–8 cm of moist soil, reducing volatilisation losses by 50–60% compared to surface-applied urea in dry conditions

Do not perform earthing-up on wet (>80% FC) soil as the machinery compacts and smears the wet black cotton soil, creating a ploughpan at the earthing-up depth that restricts further root growth; soil at 50–65% FC is optimal for earthing-up quality

rule_name: Low Soil Moisture Combined with High Humidity Disease-Drought Paradox
reason: The disease-drought paradox in Dharwad's post-monsoon maize (October) creates a uniquely dangerous compound condition: soil dries rapidly as the monsoon withdraws (soil moisture falls to 40% FC or below), while ambient humidity remains high (80%+ RH from residual atmospheric moisture) and temperatures are elevated (>32°C). This combination means the crop is simultaneously moisture-stressed from the soil side and disease-pressured from the humid aerial side. Charcoal Rot, Fusarium Stalk Rot, and late foliar diseases all intensify under this paradox, creating the highest-risk compound yield-loss scenario in Dharwad's Kharif maize cycle.
actions: Apply irrigation of 40–45 mm immediately when this paradox condition is identified; restoring soil moisture to 60–65% FC simultaneously alleviates drought stress and reduces disease susceptibility, making irrigation the single most effective intervention for this compound risk

Apply Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/litre + Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 0.5 ml/litre foliar spray within 24 hours of irrigation to capitalise on restored plant vigour and deploy active fungicide residue on leaves and stalk surfaces simultaneously

Harvest at the very first indication of physiological maturity (black layer, husk yellowing); in the disease-drought paradox conditions, every day of delay post-maturity risks stalk collapse from Charcoal Rot in the rapidly drying, warm post-monsoon conditions of Dharwad's October harvest window

rule_name: Optimum Soil Moisture Triggering for Maximum Grain Weight
reason: Maximum kernel weight in Dharwad maize is achieved when soil moisture is maintained at 60–75% field capacity throughout the grain filling period (75–100 days after sowing), combined with temperatures of 22–28°C. At this moisture-temperature combination, phloem loading and unloading of sucrose to the developing endosperm is maximised, starch synthase activity is at peak efficiency, and plant respiration consumes the minimum proportion of daily photosynthate. In well-managed Dharwad Kharif plots under these conditions, 100-grain weights of 32–38 g are achievable versus 22–25 g under water or heat stress — a 40–60% difference that directly translates to market yield and price per quintal.
actions: Maintain irrigation schedule precisely at 60–75% FC trigger during grain filling; use the soil feel method every 5 days and irrigate when soil at 15 cm depth is just barely moist to the touch (approximately 55% FC trigger point to restore to 70% FC)

Apply 13-0-45 potassium nitrate @ 5 g/litre as a foliar spray twice during grain filling (at 75 and 88 days after sowing) to maximise kernel density and test weight under the favourable moisture and temperature conditions of this window

Record 100-grain weight at harvest by weighing 100 randomly selected kernels from different parts of 5 cobs; 100-grain weight above 30 g indicates successful grain filling management; below 25 g indicates moisture or temperature stress that should be addressed in the next season through improved irrigation scheduling

rule_name: Pump Failure Risk at Critical Stage Without Backup Plan
reason: Borewell pump failures during the critical tasseling-silking window in Dharwad are a significant unplanned risk for irrigated maize farmers. With soil moisture at 50% FC or below, no rainfall, and the crop approaching silking (50–72 days after sowing), a 3–5 day pump repair delay can cause the same yield loss as a monsoon break drought event. Mechanical pump failures (motor burnout, pump seizure, power supply failure) are most common in July–September when continuous Kharif irrigation demand puts maximum stress on ageing rural pump infrastructure. Having contingency plans for pump failure during the critical window is a practical resilience measure in Dharwad's irrigation-dependent maize system.
actions: Service and replace worn motor bearings and impellers on borewell pumps before Kharif sowing (May–June) to reduce in-season failure probability during the critical July–September irrigation peak demand period

Identify and confirm access to a neighbouring farmer's pump or village shared pump that can be used in case of own pump failure during critical irrigation windows; establish this arrangement before the Kharif season begins, not after pump failure occurs

Apply 2% potassium chloride foliar spray as an emergency drought management measure to extend the time between soil moisture deficit and irreversible crop damage during any pump repair delay period; this buys 2–3 additional days of partial stress tolerance in the critical stage

rule_name: Irrigation Demand Adjustment During Cloudy Low-Radiation Periods
reason: During Dharwad's peak monsoon (August–September), extended cloudy periods with low-intensity persistent rainfall (2–15 mm/day), high humidity (>88%), and moderate temperatures (22–27°C) reduce crop evapotranspiration demand to 2–4 mm/day (versus 7–10 mm/day in sunny conditions). Under these conditions, the combined water input from light rainfall alone (14–105 mm over 7 days) typically exceeds the crop's reduced demand. Farmers following a fixed calendar irrigation schedule that was set for sunny conditions will over-irrigate by 30–50% during these extended cloudy periods, increasing waterlogging risk, nitrogen leaching, and fungal disease pressure simultaneously.
actions: Suspend scheduled irrigation during continuous low-intensity rain + cloudy periods (>7 consecutive days with >5 mm/day rain and >88% RH); resume only when a 3+ day dry sunny window is forecast or when soil moisture drops below 60% FC

Inspect field drainage during these extended cloudy humid periods to ensure surface water does not accumulate; even 5–10 mm/day light rain accumulating over 7 days is 35–70 mm, which exceeds the water requirement and can create transient waterlogging in poorly drained Dharwad fields

Use this extended cloudy period as the optimal window for foliar disease management spraying; lower evapotranspiration and no need for irrigation frees up field operation time and equipment for fungicide applications that are agronomically urgent during high-humidity cloudy conditions

rule_name: Basal Nitrogen-Phosphorus-Potassium Application at Sowing
reason: Basal fertilizer application at sowing establishes the nutrient foundation for the entire maize crop cycle in Dharwad. Phosphorus (from DAP) and potassium (from MOP) must be placed in the seed zone at sowing because both nutrients have low soil mobility — phosphorus diffuses only 1–3 mm per day and potassium 2–5 mm per day in Dharwad's soils. Placement at 5–7 cm depth below the seed ensures roots reach the nutrient band within 10–14 days of germination. UAS Dharwad recommendation for Kharif maize is 80 kg N, 40 kg P₂O₅, and 40 kg K₂O per acre per season; the full phosphorus, full potassium, and 20–25% of nitrogen should be applied as the basal dose at sowing for maximum efficiency in Dharwad's soil types.
actions: Apply 75 kg DAP (18-46-0) per acre as basal fertilizer in the seed furrow at 5–7 cm below seed placement using a seed-cum-fertilizer drill to ensure precise seed-fertilizer separation and prevent germination damage from direct seed-fertilizer contact
Apply 25 kg MOP (0-0-60) per acre as basal potassium alongside DAP; mix DAP and MOP thoroughly before filling into the fertilizer box of the drill to ensure even distribution in every furrow

Apply 25 kg urea per acre as the basal nitrogen component mixed with the DAP+MOP blend to provide early nitrogen for rapid seedling establishment; supplement with Azospirillum bioinoculant (2 packets of 200 g each per acre) mixed with FYM and broadcast for biological nitrogen supplementation

rule_name: First Nitrogen Top-Dress at V4 Stage
reason: The V4 stage (4 fully expanded leaves, approximately 18–28 days after sowing in Dharwad conditions) marks the beginning of exponential nitrogen uptake in maize. Nitrogen uptake rate increases 5–8 fold between V4 and V8 stages, driven by rapid leaf area expansion and root development. Applying the first nitrogen top-dress precisely at V4 ensures that nitrogen is in the root zone when the plant's demand accelerates, preventing the nitrogen gap that causes pale-green colouration and growth check commonly seen at 25–35 days after sowing in Dharwad fields with delayed top-dressing. UAS Dharwad trials show that V4 nitrogen application increases season-end yield by 8–12% versus delayed V6 application at the same total dose.
actions: Apply 35 kg urea per acre in a band placement 7–8 cm from the plant base and 5 cm deep using inter-row hoe or tractor-mounted fertilizer applicator; band placement reduces nitrogen loss by 25–30% versus surface broadcast on Dharwad's open-textured soils

Irrigate within 24–48 hours of urea application to dissolve and move nitrogen into the root zone; application to dry soil without subsequent irrigation wastes 30–40% of applied urea through volatilisation at Dharwad's 28–32°C summer temperatures

Combine the urea application with inter-row cultivation (hoe weeding) at this timing to simultaneously control early weeds, aerate the topsoil, and mechanically incorporate the urea to a 3–5 cm depth which reduces ammonia volatilisation losses significantly

rule_name: Second Nitrogen Top-Dress at Knee-High Stage
reason: The knee-high stage (approximately 35–48 days after sowing in Dharwad, when plants are 50–70 cm tall) coincides with the period of maximum vegetative nitrogen demand in maize. Stem elongation and leaf area expansion are at maximum rates; ear shoot primordia are being determined, and the number of kernel sites per cob is being set. UAS Dharwad research indicates that the second top-dress nitrogen application at knee-high directly determines ear size and kernel row number — each 5 kg/acre additional nitrogen at this stage adds 0.3–0.5 kernel rows per ear in responsive varieties. The correct window is narrow (35–48 days after sowing) as late application past V8 is significantly less efficient for ear development.
actions: Apply 40 kg urea per acre as the second nitrogen top-dress at knee-high stage; this is the single most yield-responsive nitrogen application in the Dharwad maize season and should never be reduced or delayed even in tight cash-flow situations

Apply immediately before or after earthing-up operation so that the mounding of soil simultaneously covers the surface-applied urea and reduces volatilisation; the combination of urea+earthing-up at this stage is the most efficient nitrogen delivery method in Dharwad maize

Do not split this application with the subsequent grain-filling dose on poor black cotton soils susceptible to leaching; apply the full 40 kg urea at this single timing to ensure maximum availability during the rapid V8-to-tasseling growth surge that follows in Dharwad's Kharif season

rule_name: Zinc Deficiency Risk on Kharif Sandy Laterite Soils
reason: Zinc deficiency is the most widespread micronutrient deficiency in Dharwad district maize cultivation, affecting an estimated 60–70% of laterite and sandy soils in the eastern taluks (Kundgol, Navalgund, Kalghatgi). These soils are inherently low in plant-available zinc (DTPA-extractable Zn below 0.6 ppm versus the critical threshold of 0.8 ppm). Zinc-deficient maize seedlings show characteristic white striping on young leaves (White Bud or Khaira disease), purpling of older leaves, stunted internode elongation, and delayed emergence of the fifth leaf. Untreated zinc deficiency in Dharwad maize causes 15–30% yield loss and is preventable at very low cost (₹80–120 per acre for zinc sulfate).
actions: Apply zinc sulfate heptahydrate (ZnSO₄·7H₂O, 21% Zn) @ 10 kg per acre as a basal soil application mixed with FYM or DAP before sowing on all sandy laterite soils in Dharwad; this single application maintains zinc availability for 2–3 seasons

If soil application was missed, apply 0.5% zinc sulfate foliar spray (5 g per litre water) at 15–20 days after sowing when zinc deficiency symptoms first appear; foliar zinc corrects deficiency symptoms within 5–7 days of application in Dharwad conditions

Avoid applying zinc sulfate in direct contact with DAP or urea in the same fertilizer mixture as the high pH from DAP can precipitate zinc as zinc phosphate; apply zinc sulfate separately from other fertilizers either 1 week before or 1 week after

rule_name: Phosphorus Deficiency Risk in Cold Rabi Emergence
reason: Phosphorus uptake by maize roots is temperature-sensitive, with uptake rates declining by 50–70% when soil temperature drops below 15°C. In Dharwad's Rabi season (November–January), when minimum temperatures are 10–16°C, soil phosphorus mobility and root phosphatase enzyme activity are both suppressed, creating functional phosphorus deficiency even in soils with adequate total phosphorus. Diagnostic symptoms are purpling of the underside of young leaves (anthocyanin accumulation due to impaired sugar translocation) and stunted root development. This 'cold phosphorus deficiency' is temporary and resolves as temperatures warm in February but can permanently delay early Rabi crop development if not managed.
actions: Apply 19:19:19 NPK water-soluble fertilizer @ 5 g per litre as a foliar spray at 15–20 days after sowing for Rabi maize showing purple discolouration in cold weather; foliar phosphorus bypasses the cold-soil mobility limitation and reaches plant tissue directly

Use diammonium phosphate (DAP) as the basal phosphorus source for Rabi maize rather than single superphosphate (SSP); DAP's more soluble phosphate form has better cold-soil availability than SSP's calcium phosphate matrix in Dharwad's Rabi conditions

Apply 5 kg per acre additional DAP as a band top-dressing at 5 cm depth around plants at 20 days after sowing for Rabi crops showing severe purple colouration; this concentrated root-zone placement compensates for the cold-impaired diffusion of basal-applied phosphorus

rule_name: Nitrogen Deficiency Identification and Emergency Correction
reason: Nitrogen deficiency in Dharwad maize during the vegetative stage is most commonly caused by nitrogen leaching from heavy rainfall (40+ mm for 3+ days) on sandy soils. The diagnostic signature is yellowing beginning at the tip of the oldest (lowest) leaves and progressing toward the leaf base and midrib — the classic nitrogen deficiency 'V' pattern or 'fire' pattern on maize. This bottom-up yellowing pattern distinguishes nitrogen deficiency from sulphur deficiency (which yellows new top leaves) and magnesium deficiency (interveinal yellowing). Each day of uncorrected nitrogen deficiency during rapid vegetative growth in Dharwad reduces final yield by 1.5–2.5% as leaf area development is permanently curtailed.
actions: Apply 2% urea foliar spray (20 g urea per litre water) as emergency nitrogen intervention within 24 hours of identifying nitrogen deficiency symptoms; foliar urea provides nitrogen to the plant tissue within 12–24 hours, temporarily restoring leaf function while soil-applied nitrogen is being prepared

Follow the foliar spray with a soil application of 20–25 kg urea per acre banded at 7–8 cm depth in the inter-row space within 48 hours; the soil application provides sustained nitrogen supply over 2–3 weeks while the foliar application provides immediate relief

Switch from plain urea to neem-coated urea (NCU) for the corrective application on sandy soils to slow nitrification and reduce leaching risk from subsequent rainfall; the neem coating extends nitrogen availability by 2–3 weeks compared to plain urea under Dharwad's high-rainfall sandy soil conditions

rule_name: Potassium Application for Stalk Strength Before Tasseling
reason: Potassium is essential for maize stalk strength, as it regulates cell wall lignification and cellulose synthesis that determine stalk mechanical resistance to wind lodging. In Dharwad's sandy soils with inherently low potassium availability (due to low CEC), maize deficient in potassium produces stalks with significantly thinner cell walls and lower lignin content, making them 30–50% more susceptible to wind lodging than potassium-adequate plants. The knee-high stage is the last practical window for soil potassium application before root system depth exceeds the plough layer; after V8, potassium must be applied as foliar spray to have any crop-stage impact. High wind speeds (>20 km/h) common in Dharwad's pre-tasseling period increase the urgency.
actions: Apply 20–25 kg MOP (muriate of potash, 0-0-60) per acre as a top-dress application banded at 8–10 cm depth in the inter-row space at 35–45 days after sowing; deep band placement of potassium is essential on sandy soils where surface application results in leaching

Apply 2% potassium sulfate foliar spray (20 g per litre) as a supplement to soil-applied MOP on fields with known potassium deficiency history to provide rapidly available foliar potassium for stalk cell wall synthesis in the 4 weeks before tasseling

Conduct a simple stalk quality check at 50 days after sowing: pinch the second internode above soil — if it compresses easily (no resistance), potassium deficiency is affecting stalk quality and additional potassium sulfate foliar spray at 2% should be applied every 10 days until tasseling

rule_name: Boron Application for Pollen Viability and Silk Development
reason: Boron is essential for pollen germination, pollen tube elongation, and silk development in maize. Boron deficiency is common in Dharwad's leached sandy laterite soils (available boron below 0.5 ppm in 40–50% of surveyed laterite soils in Kundgol and Navalgund taluks). Boron-deficient maize plants produce tassels with poor pollen viability (60–70% vs >95% in boron-adequate plants) and silks that are sticky, fail to elongate fully, and have impaired sugar signalling for pollen tube attraction. Application at 40–55 days after sowing — approximately 10–15 days before tasseling — ensures boron reaches the developing floral organs before the critical pollination window in Dharwad.
actions: Apply borax (disodium tetraborate, 10.5% B) @ 1 kg per acre dissolved in 200 litres water as a foliar spray at 40–45 days after sowing; apply uniformly covering the entire plant canopy including the emerging whorl where the tassel is developing

Supplement with soil application of borax @ 1.5 kg per acre mixed with compost or dry sand for even distribution in fields with a history of poor pollination or irregular kernel rows that indicate boron deficiency in previous seasons

Do not apply boron foliar spray when temperature exceeds 35°C as boron can cause leaf burn above this temperature threshold on maize; apply in the early morning (before 9 AM) or evening (after 5 PM) to avoid phytotoxicity under Dharwad's high summer temperatures

rule_name: Urea Volatilisation Risk Under High Temperature
reason: Urea nitrogen volatilisation as ammonia (NH₃) is directly proportional to temperature and inversely proportional to soil moisture. At maximum temperatures above 34°C with moderate humidity (>70%) and dry soil surface (<45% soil moisture), the urease enzyme in Dharwad's soils hydrolyses surface-broadcast urea to ammonium within 24–48 hours, and the ammonium converts to volatile ammonia at alkaline soil surface pH. Under these conditions, 40–60% of surface-broadcast urea can be lost within 3–5 days of application. This is a critical efficiency problem in Dharwad Kharif maize where top-dress urea is often applied in July–August when temperatures and humidity are both elevated.
actions: Apply urea only by soil incorporation (using inter-row cultivator hoe at 5 cm depth) under high temperature-low moisture conditions; surface broadcast followed by incorporation within 2 hours reduces ammonia volatilisation by 55–65%

If incorporation machinery is unavailable, apply urea in the early morning (5–7 AM) when temperature is lowest, and immediately irrigate with 20–25 mm to dissolve and carry urea into the soil before afternoon heat accelerates urease activity and volatilisation

Use neem-coated urea (NCU) or sulphur-coated urea as alternatives to plain urea under high volatilisation risk conditions in Dharwad; NCU reduces ammonia volatilisation by 20–35% through inhibition of urease enzyme activity by neem coating compounds

rule_name: Sulphur Deficiency Risk in Kharif Leached Soils
reason: Sulphur deficiency is increasingly prevalent in Dharwad's sandy laterite soils under intensive Kharif maize cultivation. Sulphur is present as water-soluble sulfate (SO₄²⁻) that is highly mobile and leaches readily from sandy soils during heavy monsoon rainfall (30+ mm/day for 5+ days). Unlike nitrogen, sulphur deficiency in maize produces a distinctive new-leaf yellowing (interveinal chlorosis on the youngest leaves) because sulphur is relatively immobile within the plant and cannot be remobilised from old to new leaves. Sulphur is essential for chlorophyll synthesis, amino acid (cysteine, methionine) production, and enzyme function. With the progressive shift from SSP (containing sulphur) to DAP (sulphur-free) in Dharwad fertilizer use, sulphur deficiency has increased significantly over the past decade.
actions: Apply single superphosphate (SSP, 16% P₂O₅ + 11% S) instead of DAP as the basal phosphorus source on sandy soils in Dharwad; SSP delivers sulphur alongside phosphorus at no additional cost and prevents sulphur leaching during early Kharif monsoon rains

Apply ammonium sulphate (21% N + 24% S) @ 25 kg per acre as the first nitrogen top-dress application on all sandy laterite fields to simultaneously supply nitrogen and sulphur, replacing the standard urea dose for this application timing

If sulphur deficiency symptoms (new leaf interveinal yellowing) are already visible, apply gypsum (calcium sulphate, 18% S) @ 25 kg per acre as a top-dress application or spray 1% magnesium sulphate solution (Epsom salt @ 10 g per litre) as foliar correction — foliar sulphur via magnesium sulphate corrects symptoms within 7–10 days

rule_name: Iron Deficiency Foliar Correction in Alkaline Black Soils
reason: Iron chlorosis (lime-induced iron deficiency) affects maize grown in Dharwad's black cotton Vertisol soils with pH above 7.5–8.0, common in Hubli taluk and parts of Dharwad taluk. At high soil pH, iron is rapidly oxidised to insoluble ferric hydroxides, unavailable to plant roots. Rabi maize is more susceptible than Kharif maize because lower temperatures further reduce root iron uptake efficiency. Affected plants show interveinal yellowing on new leaves (young tissue first) while veins remain green — the classic iron chlorosis pattern. In severe cases, affected leaves are entirely white-yellow with no visible green. Iron deficiency reduces photosynthesis by 30–50% per affected leaf and, if uncorrected by 25 days after sowing, causes permanent yield loss of 15–25%.
actions: Apply ferrous sulphate (FeSO₄·7H₂O, 19% Fe) @ 0.5% solution (5 g per litre) as a foliar spray at 15–20 days after sowing for Rabi maize in high-pH black cotton soils; foliar iron application bypasses the soil pH-related fixation problem and delivers iron directly to chloroplasts within 3–5 days

Add 5 ml citric acid per litre to the ferrous sulphate foliar spray solution to chelate the iron and prevent oxidation before absorption; unchelated iron in spray solution can precipitate on leaf surfaces reducing effectiveness by 40–50%

Apply ferrous sulphate @ 25 kg per acre mixed with 500 kg well-decomposed FYM as a soil application in the season before sowing; organic matter complexes the iron in a plant-available form that resists alkaline soil fixation, providing 2–3 seasons of improved iron availability

rule_name: Third Nitrogen Top-Dress at Pre-Tasseling Stage
reason: In high-yield target maize production in Dharwad (target yield above 5 tonnes per acre), three nitrogen top-dress applications provide better nitrogen synchrony with crop demand than the standard two-split approach. The third application at pre-tasseling (48–58 days after sowing) targets the nitrogen demand of the rapidly developing tassel, silk, and ear structures, which collectively require 25–30% of the season's total nitrogen uptake within a 2-week window. For intensive Kharif maize on irrigated black cotton soils in Dharwad, the third nitrogen split can add 300–500 kg per acre of additional grain yield, making it economically justified at current maize market prices (₹1,600–1,800 per quintal at Dharwad APMC).
actions: Apply 20 kg urea per acre as the third nitrogen split at 50–55 days after sowing (approximately 7–10 days before expected tassel emergence); this pre-tassel application provides the nitrogen pool for ear and pollen development during the critical 2-week flowering window

Apply only to fields targeting above 40 quintals per acre yield potential; on lower-yield targets (below 35 quintals), this third split is not economically justified and the same nitrogen can be included in the second split at knee-high with similar results

Use ammonium nitrate or ammonium sulfate instead of urea for this third application to avoid the high volatilisation risk of surface-broadcast urea at the canopy-closure stage when mechanical incorporation is no longer possible without plant damage

rule_name: Manganese Deficiency in Waterlogged Sandy Soils
reason: Manganese deficiency occurs in Dharwad's sandy, well-drained, acidic to neutral laterite soils under dry Rabi conditions where soil moisture drops below 40% FC. Unlike waterlogging-induced iron toxicity (which releases excess iron), dry sandy soils with low organic matter have limited manganese release from primary minerals, and the low moisture reduces mass flow of manganese to roots. Affected maize plants show pale green to light yellow interveinal streaking on mid-canopy leaves (2nd and 3rd leaves from the top), which is distinct from iron chlorosis (affects newest leaves) and nitrogen deficiency (affects oldest leaves). Manganese deficiency at the vegetative stage reduces enzyme activity for photosynthesis (manganese is essential for oxygen evolution in Photosystem II) by 20–35%.
actions: Apply manganese sulfate (MnSO₄, 30–31% Mn) @ 0.5% foliar spray (5 g per litre water) at first appearance of interveinal striping on mid-canopy leaves; two applications at 10-day intervals are typically needed for full correction in Dharwad's sandy soils

Apply manganese sulfate @ 5 kg per acre mixed with 200 kg compost as a basal soil application in sandy Rabi fields with manganese deficiency history; the organic matter association improves manganese retention in sandy soils that otherwise have minimal manganese-holding capacity

Add irrigation to bring soil moisture to 55–65% FC before applying manganese; adequate soil moisture increases manganese diffusion rate to roots by 3–5 times and accelerates correction of deficiency symptoms even without additional manganese fertilizer in fields with borderline manganese status

rule_name: Magnesium Deficiency Risk in High-Rainfall Kharif Season
reason: Magnesium (Mg) is the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule and a cofactor for ATP synthesis and phosphorus translocation in maize. In Dharwad's sandy laterite soils, magnesium is present primarily as exchangeable Mg on clay mineral surfaces with low CEC. Under prolonged heavy monsoon rainfall (35+ mm/day for 7+ days), magnesium is leached from the soil's exchange sites, and the high potassium applied as MOP fertilizer further displaces magnesium through cationic competition. Magnesium deficiency appears as interveinal chlorosis on the oldest (lowest) leaves — a distinct striped green-yellow pattern between dark-green veins — at 35–60 days after sowing in Dharwad's heavy-rainfall Kharif seasons. Severe deficiency reduces photosynthesis by 25–40%.
actions: Apply kieserite (magnesium sulphate, MgSO₄·H₂O, 16% Mg + 13% S) @ 20 kg per acre as a soil top-dress application at 40–45 days after sowing on sandy soils in high-rainfall Kharif seasons; kieserite is more soil-stable than Epsom salt under leaching conditions

Apply 1% magnesium sulphate foliar spray (Epsom salt @ 10 g per litre) at 40 and 55 days after sowing as preventive nutrition on sandy soils in Dharwad's Kharif season when rainfall is high; foliar application delivers magnesium directly to chloroplasts bypassing leached soil

Maintain a potassium-to-magnesium soil ratio below 5:1 in Dharwad sandy soils; when applying MOP, limit dose to 20 kg per acre per application and add 5 kg kieserite alongside to maintain cation balance and prevent potassium-induced magnesium displacement

rule_name: Potassium Foliar Spray for Drought Stress Tolerance
reason: Potassium plays a central role in stomatal regulation — the potassium pump mechanism in guard cells controls stomatal opening and closing in response to water potential. When maize experiences drought stress (soil moisture <45% FC) under high temperatures (>34°C), adequate foliar potassium supply maintains stomatal regulation efficiency, reducing transpiration water loss by 15–25% without the same magnitude of photosynthesis reduction. Foliar potassium application (as potassium chloride or potassium nitrate) under stress conditions provides an osmolyte that improves cellular water retention (osmotic adjustment) and maintains grain filling under partial deficit conditions. This is particularly valuable during Dharwad's monsoon breaks at tasseling-grain filling when irrigation is limited.
actions: Apply 2% potassium chloride foliar spray (20 g KCl per litre water) during drought stress periods to enhance stomatal regulation and improve water use efficiency; apply in the early morning (before 9 AM) to allow leaf absorption before peak afternoon water demand

Combine potassium chloride spray with 1% urea foliar spray (10 g urea per litre) to simultaneously provide nitrogen and potassium for stress adaptation; this combination foliar spray is the most cost-effective emergency nutritional intervention per rupee spent in drought stress periods

Apply the potassium foliar spray every 7–10 days during the drought stress period until soil moisture recovers above 55% FC or until grain reaches physiological maturity; continuous potassium support through the critical pollination and grain filling windows is more effective than a single application

rule_name: Post-Waterlogging Nitrogen Recovery Application
reason: Waterlogging of 4+ days in Dharwad's black cotton soils triggers intense denitrification and nitrate leaching, together removing 40–70% of soil available nitrogen. Plants emerging from waterlogging show acute nitrogen deficiency within 5–7 days (yellowing from lower leaves upward), compounding the oxygen stress damage from the waterlogging itself. Without a rapid corrective nitrogen application post-waterlogging, maize recovery is slow and incomplete — plants that should be at knee-high remain stunted at seedling height for 2–3 weeks, permanently delaying tasseling. In Dharwad field trials, post-waterlogging nitrogen application within 3–5 days of drainage restored 60–70% of the yield loss that would otherwise have occurred from nitrogen starvation.
actions: Apply 2% urea foliar spray (20 g per litre) as the immediate nitrogen correction within 24–48 hours of field drainage becoming possible; foliar urea provides nitrogen directly to leaves that have already lost significant chlorophyll and cannot wait for soil-applied nitrogen to reach roots

Follow foliar spray with soil application of 25 kg urea per acre banded at 7 cm depth in inter-rows at 3–5 days post-drainage when soil is trafficable; the combination of foliar (immediate) + soil (sustained) nitrogen application maximises recovery rate

Apply PSB (phosphate solubilising bacteria) @ 2 kg per acre mixed in water as a soil drench post-waterlogging to restore biological phosphorus solubilisation activity in root zone soil whose microbial community was disrupted by anaerobic conditions during flooding

rule_name: Calcium Deficiency Risk in Tip Burn at High Humidity
reason: Calcium deficiency in Dharwad maize on sandy laterite soils manifests as tip burn — necrosis of the youngest leaf margins and tips — under high humidity and temperature conditions. Calcium is transported exclusively through the xylem (water stream) driven by transpiration. Under high humidity (>88%), transpiration rate is reduced because the vapour pressure gradient between leaf and air is small. The youngest, most rapidly growing leaves have the lowest transpiration rate and therefore the lowest calcium delivery rate, making them most susceptible to calcium deficiency even when soil calcium is adequate. The resulting cell wall failure at leaf tips and margins creates entry points for soft rot bacteria and Fusarium in Dharwad's humid Kharif season.
actions: Apply 0.5% calcium chloride foliar spray (5 g per litre) or 1% calcium nitrate foliar spray at first signs of tip burn on young leaves; calcium nitrate is preferred as it simultaneously provides nitrogen and delivers highly soluble calcium directly to deficient tissue

Apply gypsum (CaSO₄) @ 100 kg per acre on calcium-deficient sandy soils as a soil application before sowing; gypsum provides calcium in a soluble form that is not affected by soil pH and also supplies sulphur as a bonus nutrient for Dharwad's sandy soils

Ensure adequate plant spacing (25 cm within row, 60 cm between rows) to maximise air movement through the canopy; better airflow increases leaf transpiration rate, improving calcium mass flow to young leaves even under high ambient humidity conditions

rule_name: Micronutrient Cocktail Spray at Pre-Tasseling Stage
reason: Pre-tasseling (42–52 days after sowing) is the optimal stage for a comprehensive micronutrient foliar application in Dharwad maize. This timing ensures micronutrients reach the developing floral organs (tassel, ear primordia, silk) before they become enclosed and inaccessible in the plant tissue. Zinc (pollen viability), boron (pollen germination and tube growth), manganese (Photosystem II function), and copper (lignin synthesis for stalk strength) all have critical roles in the reproductive development that initiates at this stage. In Dharwad's micronutrient-depleted sandy and intensive cultivation soils, a single well-timed cocktail spray at pre-tasseling delivers measurable yield benefits of 5–12% compared to untreated controls in UAS Dharwad field trials.
actions: Prepare and apply a micronutrient cocktail spray: zinc sulfate 0.5% + borax 0.2% + manganese sulfate 0.3% + ferrous sulfate 0.3% dissolved in 200 litres water per acre; apply in the early morning on a day without forecast rain for the next 6 hours to allow full absorption

Add 0.5 ml per litre of agricultural sticker-spreader (Triton or similar) to the micronutrient spray solution to improve adhesion and penetration through the waxy cuticle of maize leaves, which has low natural wettability and reduces absorption of spray droplets without a surfactant

Keep records of micronutrient spray timing and the observed tassel quality (pollen shed duration, silk emergence uniformity) in the subsequent 2 weeks; consistent recording over 3 seasons provides field-specific data on which micronutrients produce the strongest response in each Dharwad plot

rule_name: Nitrogen Excess Risk Causing Delayed Maturity
reason: Over-application of nitrogen (total seasonal nitrogen exceeding 100 kg N/acre for Dharwad maize) or late-season nitrogen application after 60 days from sowing causes continued vegetative growth at the expense of reproductive development. Excess nitrogen during grain filling in Dharwad conditions stimulates secondary tillering, leaf area maintenance, and stem elongation at a time when the plant's resources should be channelled entirely to grain. This 'luxury nitrogen consumption' delays physiological maturity by 7–12 days, exposing the crop to post-monsoon rain and humidity risks, and increases susceptibility to stalk rot pathogens by producing lush, nitrogen-saturated tissue with thin cell walls in Dharwad's warm-humid conditions.
actions: Do not apply any soil nitrogen fertilizer after 60 days from sowing; the crop's nitrogen requirement is essentially complete by tasseling, and late applications delay maturity and increase stalk rot susceptibility without adding measurable grain yield

If excess nitrogen was applied (visible as very dark green, lush leaves remaining at 80+ days after sowing when some leaf senescence is normal), apply 1% potassium sulfate foliar spray to promote translocation of assimilates to grain and counterbalance the excess nitrogen's vegetative stimulation

Adjust the total seasonal nitrogen budget for the next season: calculate yield removed from the field (1 tonne grain removes approximately 14 kg N), and apply no more than 80–90 kg N per acre total for a 5-tonne yield target in Dharwad conditions, across all basal and top-dress applications

rule_name: FYM Application Benefit Before Kharif Sowing
reason: Well-decomposed farmyard manure (FYM) applied to Dharwad's sandy laterite soils before Kharif sowing improves the physical, chemical, and biological properties that determine maize productivity over multiple seasons. FYM increases CEC by 0.5–1.5 cmol/kg per tonne applied, improving nutrient retention against leaching. It supplies slow-release nitrogen (0.5–0.8% N), phosphorus (0.3–0.4% P₂O₅), and potassium (0.5–0.7% K₂O) equivalent to approximately 5–7 kg NPK per tonne. It also improves water holding capacity by 15–25% per tonne applied on sandy soils, reducing irrigation frequency requirement. UAS Dharwad research shows that FYM application of 5 tonnes per acre annually for 3+ years increases maize yield responsiveness to chemical fertilizers by 25–40%.
actions: Apply well-composted FYM @ 5 tonnes per acre broadcast and plough in at 15–20 cm depth at least 3 weeks before Kharif sowing to allow initial decomposition and nutrient release before crop establishment; fresh or partially decomposed FYM can cause temporary nitrogen immobilisation

Locate a nearby HDPE-lined FYM compost pit (minimum 6 m × 3 m × 1 m for a 1-acre farm's cattle manure) to ensure annual supply; contact Dharwad KWDP (Karnataka Watershed Development Programme) for composting training and HDPE liner subsidy under DDUGJY scheme

Inoculate FYM with Trichoderma viride @ 500 g per tonne of FYM and Azospirillum @ 500 g per tonne 7 days before application; the bioagents multiply in the FYM, bringing beneficial microbes directly to the seed zone and enhancing early root colonisation in Dharwad's maize fields

rule_name: Potassium Deficiency Causing Premature Leaf Senescence
reason: Potassium deficiency causes premature senescence of lower maize leaves, characterised by marginal and tip scorching (brown, crispy margins) that progresses inward on the oldest leaves. In Dharwad's sandy soils under heavy Kharif monsoon rainfall (25+ mm/day for 5+ days), potassium is leached from the sandy soil's limited exchange sites and becomes deficient relative to plant demand at the knee-high to tasseling growth stage when potassium accumulation rate in the plant is maximum. Potassium-deficient plants produce stalks 20–30% more susceptible to stalk rot pathogens (Fusarium, Colletotrichum) because cell wall lignification is impaired, reducing mechanical resistance to pathogen penetration.
actions: Apply MOP (muriate of potash) @ 15–20 kg per acre as an emergency top-dress application banded at 8–10 cm depth in the inter-row space when marginal leaf scorch symptoms are visible on more than 3 of the lower 5 leaves

Spray 2% potassium sulfate foliar solution (20 g K₂SO₄ per litre water) immediately on identification of potassium deficiency symptoms to provide rapid foliar potassium correction while soil-applied MOP requires 5–7 days to become plant-available through root uptake in Dharwad's sandy soils

In future seasons, apply potassium as a split: 50% at basal sowing (as MOP @ 15 kg/acre) and 50% at knee-high stage (MOP @ 15 kg/acre); split potassium application on sandy soils improves potassium use efficiency by 30–40% compared to full basal application under Dharwad's high monsoon leaching conditions

rule_name: Biofertilizer Application for Kharif Nitrogen Supplementation
reason: Azospirillum brasilense, a free-living nitrogen-fixing rhizobacterium, colonises maize root surfaces in Dharwad's Kharif season under warm (24–30°C), moist (55–75% soil moisture) conditions that are optimal for its nitrogen fixation activity. When applied as a seed treatment or soil application, Azospirillum can fix 15–25 kg N per acre equivalent per season in Dharwad's well-aerated soils. Combined with PSB (phosphate-solubilising bacteria such as Bacillus megaterium), biofertilizer applications can reduce chemical nitrogen and phosphorus requirements by 15–20%, saving ₹500–800 per acre in fertilizer costs while maintaining equivalent yields. UAS Dharwad on-farm trials confirm consistent yield parity with 20% reduced chemical fertilizer when biofertilizers are applied correctly.
actions: Treat seeds with Azospirillum @ 200 g per kg seed mixed in 10% jaggery solution as a slurry coating; dry seeds in shade for 30 minutes before sowing; do not mix biofertilizer-treated seeds with fungicide-treated seeds as fungicides inhibit the bacteria

Apply PSB (Bacillus megaterium) @ 2 kg per acre mixed with 200 kg compost as a soil application in the seed furrow; the compost matrix protects bacterial viability in Dharwad's warm soils and provides a carbon food source that maintains bacterial populations for 3–4 months
